VQ-VAE-2 is outperformed by GANs but provides:

Better mode coverage (no mode collapse)
Interpretable discrete latent space
Foundation for later models (DALL-E uses VQ-VAE)

title: 8  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
8.7 Practical Considerations
Architecture Choices:

Encoder/Decoder Depth: Deeper networks → better features, harder to train

Start simple: 3-4 conv layers each
Advanced: ResNet-style blocks

Latent Dimension: Trade-off between compression and reconstruction

Too small (\(d < 10\)): Poor reconstructions
Too large (\(d > 512\)): KL collapse (posterior collapses to prior)
Typical: \(d \in [32, 256]\)

KL Annealing: Gradually increase KL weight from 0 to 1 during training

Prevents early KL collapse
Allows decoder to learn before enforcing strong regularization



Training Issues:
1. Posterior Collapse: KL term goes to 0, model ignores latent code

Symptom: Decoder generates always the same output regardless of \(z\)
Solutions: KL annealing; free bits (minimum KL per dimension, i.e. optimize: \(\max(\text{KL}_j, \lambda)\) instead of \(\text{KL}_j\)); or \(\beta\)-VAE with \(\beta < 1\) initially

2. Blurry Reconstructions: MSE loss averages over modes

Symptom: Images look blurry compared to input
Cause: MSE loss \(= \mathbb{E}[\|x - \hat{x}\|^2]\) encourages averaging
Partial solutions: Perceptual loss (VGG similarity in deep feature space between input \(x\) and reconstruction \(\hat{x}\)); adversarial loss (VAE-GAN hybrid)

3. KL-Reconstruction Trade-off: Balancing two loss terms

High KL weight → regular latent space but poor reconstructions
Low KL weight → good reconstructions but irregular latent space
Solutions: Grid search for optimal weighting; β-VAE


Technical property:
VAEs use continuous latent spaces, allowing smooth interpolation and controllable generation: \[z_{\text{interp}} = (1-\alpha) z_1 + \alpha z_2, \quad \alpha \in [0,1],\] where interpolating between latent codes \(z_1\) and \(z_2\) produces meaningful intermediate output images.

title: 8  Variational Autoencoders (VAEs)
text:
8.8 Summary and Interview Preparation
Core Concepts Checklist:
Mathematical Foundation:

ELBO derivation from KL divergence
Why ELBO is lower bound on log-likelihood
Closed-form KL for Gaussian distributions
Reparameterization trick and why it’s needed

Architecture:

Encoder outputs distribution parameters \((\mu, \sigma^2)\)
Decoder is probabilistic: \(p_\theta(x|z)\)
Prior \(p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\)

VAE Variants:

β-VAE for disentanglement
CVAE for conditional generation
VQ-VAE: discrete codebook latents
VQ-VAE-2: hierarchical multi-scale

Training:

Two-term loss: reconstruction + KL
Posterior collapse problem
KL annealing strategy


Common Interview Questions:
1. “Derive the VAE loss function (ELBO).”
Answer: Start with log-likelihood: \(\log p(x) = \log \int p(x|z)p(z)dz\)
Introduce \(q(z|x)\): \(= \log \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}\left[\frac{p(x|z)p(z)}{q(z|x)}\right]\)
Jensen’s inequality: \(\geq \mathbb{E}_{q(z|x)}\left[\log p(x|z)\right] - \text{KL}(q(z|x)\|p(z))\)
This is ELBO. Maximizing ELBO = maximizing lower bound on likelihood.

2. “Explain the reparameterization trick and why it’s necessary.”
Answer: Problem: Sampling \(z \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)\) is not differentiable—can’t backprop through stochastic node.
Solution: Reparameterize as \(z = \mu + \sigma \odot \epsilon\) where \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\).
Now \(\epsilon\) is constant (sampled once), and gradients flow through \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\). Enables end-to-end training with backpropagation.

3. “Why do VAE reconstructions tend to be blurry?”
Answer: Cause: MSE loss \(\mathbb{E}[\|x - \hat{x}\|^2]\) encourages decoder to output mean of conditional distribution \(p(x|z)\).
When \(p(x|z)\) is multimodal (multiple valid reconstructions), mean is blurry average.
Solutions:

Perceptual loss (VGG features instead of pixels)
Adversarial loss (VAE-GAN hybrid)
Better decoder distributions (Mixture of Logistics)


4. “VAE vs. GAN—when to use each?”
Answer:
VAE:

✓ Stable training
✓ Computable likelihood (useful for anomaly detection)
✓ Good mode coverage
✓ Fast inference (encoder available)
✗ Blurry samples (MSE loss)

GAN:

✓ Sharp, high-quality samples
✗ Unstable training (mode collapse)
✗ No encoder (can’t infer \(z\) from \(x\) easily)
✗ No likelihood computation

Use VAE when: Need likelihood, stability, representation learning Use GAN when: Need highest quality samples, don’t need encoder

5. “Explain VQ-VAE and why it’s useful.”
Answer: VQ-VAE uses discrete codebook latents instead of continuous:

Encoder outputs feature map, each spatial location quantized to nearest codebook vector
No posterior collapse (discrete codes)
Compatible with autoregressive priors (learn \(p(z)\) with PixelCNN)

Why useful:

Foundation for DALL-E (VQ-VAE + GPT generates images)
Better than continuous for capturing discrete modes
Used in Stable Diffusion latent space compression


6. “What is posterior collapse in VAEs and how to fix it?”
Answer: Posterior collapse: KL term → 0, \(q(z|x) \approx p(z)\).
Decoder ignores \(z\), generates from marginal \(p(x)\) only.
Causes:

Decoder too powerful (can model \(p(x)\) without \(z\))
KL weight too high initially

Solutions:

KL annealing: Start with low β, gradually increase
Free bits: Minimum KL per dimension (don’t push below threshold)
β-VAE with β < 1 initially, then increase
Weaker decoder: Limit capacity to force latent usage


Company Context:
OpenAI:

DALL-E uses VQ-VAE for discrete tokens + GPT for prior
Exploring VAEs for representation learning

Stability AI:

Stable Diffusion uses VAE encoder/decoder (compress to latent space)
Diffusion in latent space (not pixel space)

Google/DeepMind:

VQ-VAE-2 research
Hierarchical VAEs for video (VideoGPT)

Meta:

VAE-based compression for videos
Research on disentangled representations (β-VAE)


Further Reading:
Foundational Papers:

Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (VAE, 2013)
β-VAE: Learning Basic Visual Concepts (2017)
Neural Discrete Representation Learning (VQ-VAE, 2017)
Generating Diverse High-Fidelity Images with VQ-VAE-2 (2019)

Tutorials:

Tutorial on Variational Autoencoders (Carl Doersch)
Understanding Variational Autoencoders


This completes Variational Autoencoders—the foundation of latent variable generative modeling, combining efficient inference with structured latent spaces, and serving as the basis for modern approaches like latent diffusion models.




Rocca, Joseph. 2021. “Understanding Variational Autoencoders (VAEs).” https://medium.com/data-science/understanding-variational-autoencoders-vaes-f70510919f73.

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.1 Introduction
Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) learn to generate data through a two-player game between competing neural networks. Unlike VAEs which use explicit density modeling, GANs learn an implicit generative model through adversarial training.
Core Idea: Train two networks in opposition:
Key Insight: The generator never sees real data directly—it only receives gradients from the discriminator’s judgment. This indirect supervision produces remarkably sharp, high-quality samples.

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
Generator \(G\): Creates fake samples to fool the discriminator
Discriminator \(D\): Distinguishes real data from generated fakes




9.1.1 Minmax Game Formulation
Generator and discriminator play a minimax game with value function \(V(G, D)\):
\[\min_G \max_D V(D, G) = \min_G \max_D \Big(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z(z)}[\log(1 - D(G(z)))]\Big)\]
Discriminator’s objective:
Maximize \(V(D, G)\);   by correctly classifying real data (\(D(x) \to 1\)) and fake data (\(D(G(z)) \to 0\)).
Generator’s objective:
Minimize \(V(D, G)\);   by fooling the discriminator (\(D(G(z)) \to 0\)).



9.1.2 Architecture Components
Generator \(G: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{X}\):

Input: Latent code \(z \sim p(z) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) (typically)
Output: Generated sample \(\hat{x} = G(z) \in \mathbb{R}^D\)
Architecture: Transposed convolutions (images) or MLPs (tabular)

\[z \to \text{FC} \to \text{Reshape} \to \text{TransposedConv} \times N \to \text{Tanh} \to \hat{x}\]
Discriminator \(D: \mathcal{X} \to [0,1]\):

Input: Sample \(x\) (real or fake)
Output: Probability that \(x\) is real: \(D(x) \in [0,1]\)
Architecture: Convolutional network (images) or MLPs

\[x \to \text{Conv} \times N \to \text{Flatten} \to \text{FC} \to \text{Sigmoid} \to D(x)\]



9.1.3 Training Algorithm
Alternating optimization—train discriminator and generator in turns:
for epoch in epochs:
    # Train Discriminator (k steps, typically k=1)
    for _ in range(k):
        # Sample real data
        x_real ~ p_data(x)
        
        # Sample noise and generate fakes
        z ~ p(z)
        x_fake = G(z)
        
        # Discriminator loss (binary cross-entropy)
        L_D = -[log D(x_real) + log(1 - D(x_fake))]
        
        # Update discriminator
        θ_D ← θ_D - η ∇_θD L_D
    
    # Train Generator (1 step)
    z ~ p(z)
    x_fake = G(z)
    
    # Generator loss (non-saturating)
    L_G = -log D(G(z))
    
    # Update generator
    θ_G ← θ_G - η ∇_θG L_G
Key design choice: Update discriminator more frequently (\(k\) times) per generator update to maintain discriminator strength.

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.2 Unconditional Image Generation

9.2.1 DCGAN (Deep Convolutional GAN, 2015)
Key contribution: Stable architecture guidelines for training GANs on images.
Architecture principles: 1. Replace pooling layers with strided convolutions (discriminator) and transposed convolutions (generator) 2. Use batch normalization in both networks (except generator output and discriminator input) 3. Remove fully connected hidden layers 4. Use ReLU in generator (except output: Tanh) 5. Use LeakyReLU in discriminator
Generator architecture (for 64×64 images):
z (100) → FC(4×4×1024) → Reshape
  → TransposedConv(512, 4×4, stride=2) → BN → ReLU  # 8×8
  → TransposedConv(256, 4×4, stride=2) → BN → ReLU  # 16×16
  → TransposedConv(128, 4×4, stride=2) → BN → ReLU  # 32×32
  → TransposedConv(3, 4×4, stride=2) → Tanh          # 64×64
Impact: Enabled stable training, became foundation for future GAN research.



9.2.2 WGAN (Wasserstein GAN ,2017)
Motivation: Address training instability through better distance metric.
Key idea: Instead of Jensen-Shannon divergence, use Wasserstein distance (Earth Mover’s Distance):
\[W(p_r, p_g) = \sup_{\|f\|_L \leq 1} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_r}[f(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[f(x)]\]
WGAN objective: \[\min_G \max_{D \in \mathcal{D}} \mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}}[D(x)] - \mathbb{E}_{z \sim p_z}[D(G(z))]\]
Key differences from standard GAN:



Aspect
Standard GAN
WGAN




Discriminator output
Sigmoid (probability)
Linear (score)


Loss
Binary cross-entropy
Wasserstein distance


Constraint
None
1-Lipschitz


Stability
Sensitive to hyperparameters
More stable



Advantages: Provides meaningful gradients even when distributions don’t overlap, more stable training.
Enforcing Lipschitz constraint: The Wasserstein GAN optimizes the Earth-Mover distance, which requires the critic to be 1-Lipschitz. This smoothness constraint is essential for the distance to be valid (via the Kantorovich–Rubinstein duality). The original WGAN enforces this constraint by clipping the critic’s weights, a simple but crude way to bound the gradients.
# Enforcing 1-Lipschitz constraint (original WGAN)
for p in discriminator.parameters():
    p.data.clamp_(-0.01, 0.01)
Problems with weight clipping:

Limits discriminator model capacity
Can lead to unstable or flat value surfaces
Slows Convergence




9.2.3 WGAN-GP (2017)
Improvement: Replace weight clipping with gradient penalty.
Gradient penalty: \[\lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x} \sim p_{\hat{x}}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]\]
for any interpolated point \(\hat{x}\) between a real data sample and a generated sample
(i.e., convex combinations of the form \(\hat{x} = \epsilon x + (1-\epsilon)G(z), \, \epsilon \in [0,1]\)).
Complete loss: \[\mathcal{L}_D = \mathbb{E}_z[D(G(z))] - \mathbb{E}_x[D(x)] + \lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]\]
Benefits: Better gradient behavior, no weight clipping issues.
Standard practice for Wasserstein GANs (typically \(\lambda = 10\)).

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.3 Conditional Image Generation

9.3.1 Conditional GAN (cGAN, 2014)
Idea: Condition both networks on labels \(y\):
\[\min_G \max_D \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\log D(x|y)] + \mathbb{E}_{z,y}[\log(1 - D(G(z|y)|y))]\]
Implementation:
# Generator
y_embedded = embedding(y)
z_cond = concat([z, y_embedded])
x = G(z_cond)

# Discriminator  
x_cond = concat([x, y_embedded])
score = D(x_cond)
Applications:

Class-conditional image generation (ImageNet)
Text-to-image synthesis
Image-to-image translation (pix2pix)
Super-resolution


Having covered conditional GANs, we now move to advances in unconditional high-resolution image generation, which ultimately led to StyleGAN.

Prior to StyleGAN, Progressive GAN introduced progressive growing — a key technique that allowed stable training at very high resolutions (up to 1024×1024), and was later adopted in early versions of StyleGAN.


9.3.2 Progressive GAN (2017)
Key idea: Train generator & discriminator by gradually increasing resolution
(4×4 → 8×8 → 16×16 → … → 1024×1024)
Fade-in mechanism: Smooth transition when adding layers
x_lowres = upsample(prev_block(x))
x_highres = new_block(x)
x = α * x_highres + (1 - α) * x_lowres  # α: ramps from 0→1
Benefits:

Stable training at high resolution
Faster convergence
Much sharper high-resolution results than prior GANs




9.3.3 StyleGAN (2018-2019)
Key innovation: Style-based generator with explicit control over image features at different scales.
Architecture overview:
1. Mapping Network \(f: \mathcal{Z} \to \mathcal{W}\):

8-layer MLP maps \(z\in \mathcal{Z}\) to disentangled latent \(w \in \mathcal{W}\)

2. Synthesis Network: Generates image from \(w\)

Starts from learned constant tensor (not latent vector)
Progressive upsampling; each layer modulated by style vector \(w\) through Adaptive Instance Normalization (AdaIN)

AdaIN (Style Modulation): Applies style controls by normalizing activations and re-scaling them with learned scale/bias from \(w\): \[\text{AdaIN}(x_i, y) = y_{s,i} \frac{x_i - \mu(x_i)}{\sigma(x_i)} + y_{b,i}\]
3. Hierarchical Style Control:

Coarse (4×4–8×8): pose, face shape
Middle (16×16–32×32): facial features, hair
Fine (64×64–1024×1024): colors, pores, micro-structure

Style mixing regularization: Inject different \(w\) vectors at different layers to encourage disentanglement and prevent the network from encoding all variation in early layers.
4. Noise Injection: Per-pixel Gaussian noise at each layer → stochastic realism (hair strands, pores, skin variation)
x = conv(x)
x = x + noise * learned_weight  # Uncorrelated Gaussian noise
x = activation(x)
Results: State-of-the-art 1024×1024 image quality (FID ~3 on FFHQ faces dataset).
StyleGAN2 later removed progressive growing and improved normalization to eliminate artifacts.

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.4 Image-to-Image Translation
Goal: Learn a mapping between two visual domains \(X\) and \(Y\). Given input \(x \in X\), generate \(y \in Y\).

Paired setting: explicit aligned pairs \((x_i, y_i)\) are available
Unpaired setting: only samples from each distribution, no direct correspondences


9.4.1 Pix2Pix (2016) — Paired Translation
Setting: Learn \((G: X \rightarrow Y)\) with paired examples \((x, y)\).

Generator: U-Net (skip connections preserve spatial details)
Discriminator: PatchGAN (classifies local patches as real/fake)

Loss: \[\mathcal{L}_\text{Pix2Pix} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}} + \lambda \mathcal{L}_{\text{L1}}\]

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{L1}} = \mathbb{E}[\|y - G(x)\|_1]\)
\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}} = \mathbb{E}_{x,y}[\log D(x,y)] + \mathbb{E}_{x}[\log(1 - D(x, G(x)))]\)
GAN loss encourages realistic textures; L1 keeps output close to the paired target.

Applications: Conditional generation across paired domains, including:

edges → photos
labels → scenes (semantic → realistic)
image colorization
super-resolution



9.4.2 CycleGAN (2017) — Unpaired Translation
Setting: Unsupervised translation (no paired data). Learn mappings both ways: \[
G: X \rightarrow Y, \quad F: Y \rightarrow X
\]
Key idea — Cycle Consistency: Translating forward then back should reconstruct the original:
\[
F(G(x)) \approx x, \quad G(F(y)) \approx y
\]
Loss: \[\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(G) + \mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(F) +
\lambda_1 \mathcal{L}_{\text{cyc}} +
\lambda_2 \mathcal{L}_{\text{id}}
\]
Adversarial loss:   enforces that translating to the other domain and back recovers the original image

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(G)=
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\text{data}}(y)}[(D_Y(y) - 1)^2]+
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[D_Y(G(x))^2]\)
\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}(F)=
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_{\text{data}}(x)}[(D_X(x) - 1)^2]+
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p_{\text{data}}(y)}[D_X(F(y))^2]\)

Cycle Loss:   enforces that translating to the other domain and back recovers the original image

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{cyc}} =
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)}[\|F(G(x)) - x\|_1] +
\mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)}[\|G(F(y)) - y\|_1]\)

Identity Loss:   preserves content when input already resembles target domain

\(\mathcal{L}_{\text{id}} \,\ = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim p(y)} \left[ \lVert G(y) - y \rVert_1 \right]+
\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p(x)} \left[ \lVert F(x) - x \rVert_1 \right]\)

Applications: Cross-domain translation without paired supervision, e.g.,

season transfer
horse ↔︎ zebra
apples ↔︎ oranges
photo ↔︎ painting style

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.5 Evaluation Metrics
Evaluating generative models is challenging because we cannot compute exact likelihoods for GANs. Instead, we rely on proxy metrics that measure different aspects of generation quality.

9.5.1 Inception Score (IS)
Motivation: Good generated images should satisfy two properties:

Sharpness: Each image should clearly belong to one class → \(p(y|x)\) has low entropy
Diversity: Generated images should cover many classes → marginal \(p(y)\) has high entropy

Formula: \[\text{IS} = \exp\left(\mathbb{E}_{x \sim p_g}[\text{KL}(p(y|x) \| p(y))]\right)\]

\(p(y|x)\) is Inception-v3’s predicted class distribution,
\(p(y) = \mathbb{E}_x[p(y|x)]\) is the marginal.

Intuition:
\[\ln(\text{IS}) = \underbrace{H(y)}_{\text{diversity across dataset}} -
\underbrace{\mathbb{E}[H(y|x)]}_{\text{avg. uncertainty per image}}\]






TipMathematical Derivation (click to expand)





\[\text{KL}(p(y|x) \| p(y)) = \sum_y p(y|x) \log p(y|x) - \sum_y p(y|x) \log p(y)\] \[= -H(y|x) - \sum_y p(y|x) \log p(y)\]
Taking expectation over \(x \sim p_g\): \[\mathbb{E}_x[\text{KL}(p(y|x) \| p(y))] = -\mathbb{E}_x[H(y|x)] + H(y)\]
Therefore: \[\boxed{\ln(\text{IS}(G)) = H(y) - \mathbb{E}_{x}[H(y|x)]}\]





High \(H(y)\): Generator produces many different classes (diversity)
Low \(H(y|x)\): Each image is sharp and recognizable (quality)

Critical limitation:

Depends on Inception network
IS evaluates \(p_g\) in isolation—not comparing it to real distribution \(p_{\text{data}}\).
A generator could game a high IS by:

Producing a single perfect image per class (high \(H(y)\), low \(\mathbb{E}[H(y|x)]\))
Memorizing training set (Overfitting)
Generating unrealistic but sharp images (Deviation from real distribution)





9.5.2 Fréchet Inception Distance (FID)
Measure distance between real and generated distributions in feature space.
Key difference:

IS: Evaluates \(p_g\) in isolation (requires only generated samples)
FID: Compares \(p_g\) to \(p_{\text{data}}\) (requires both real and generated samples)

Method:

Extract features from Inception-v3 (before final classification layer) for real and generated images
Assume feature distributions follow multivariate Gaussians:
Compute Fréchet distance (Wasserstein-2 distance between Gaussians)

Formula: \[\text{FID}(p_r, p_g) = \|\mu_r - \mu_g\|^2 + \text{Tr}\left(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2(\Sigma_r \Sigma_g)^{1/2}\right)\]

\(\mu_r, \Sigma_r\) are mean and covariance of real data features
\(\mu_g, \Sigma_g\) are mean and covariance of generated data features

Interpretation of terms:

Lower FID is better: closer match to real data. FID = 0 when distributions are identical.
\(\|\mu_r - \mu_g\|^2\):   Distance between feature means.

Measures how far the average generated sample is from the average real sample in feature space (if this term is large, the generator is producing images that, on average, look different from real ones - wrong global appearance, color tone, style bias, etc..).


\(\text{Tr}(\Sigma_r + \Sigma_g - 2\sqrt{\Sigma_r \Sigma_g})\):   Difference in covariances.

Measures if generated samples have similar diversity and correlations as real data
Penalizes mode collapse (when generator produces only a few types of images).


Best practice: Use FID as primary metric (measures distance to real distribution), IS for quick checks only.



9.5.3 Precision and Recall
FID is a single number that doesn’t distinguish between quality and diversity failures.
Precision and Recall separately measure quality from diversity:

Precision: Fraction of generated samples that are realistic (quality)
Recall: Fraction of real data modes covered by generator (diversity)

Computation (using k-NN in feature space):
# Extract Inception features
real_features = Inception(real_images)
fake_features = Inception(generated_images)

# Precision: fraction of fake samples with real neighbor nearby
distances_fake_to_real = knn_distance(fake_features, real_features, k=3)
precision = (distances_fake_to_real < threshold).mean()

# Recall: fraction of real samples with fake neighbor nearby
distances_real_to_fake = knn_distance(real_features, fake_features, k=3)
recall = (distances_real_to_fake < threshold).mean()
Diagnosis:

High precision, low recall → mode collapse
Low precision, high recall → diverse but low quality

Use case: Diagnose specific failures when FID insufficient.

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.6 Training Challenges

9.6.1 Mode Collapse
Problem: Generator produces limited variety, ignoring parts of data distribution.
Symptoms:

Generated samples look similar
Low Recall metric
Discriminator loss oscillates

Fixes:

WGAN-GP (stable gradients)
Minibatch discrimination (penalize lack of diversity)
Unrolled GANs (look ahead in discriminator updates)




9.6.2 Vanishing Gradients
Problem: Discriminator becomes too strong → generator receives tiny or zero gradients.
Why it happens:
In the vanilla GAN objective, when \(D(G(z)) \to 0, \,\, \nabla_G \log (1 - D(G(z))) \to 0\).
Fixes:

Non-saturating loss: \(\max_G \mathbb{E}[\log D(G(z))]\)
Feature matching: Match statistics of discriminator’s intermediate features
One-sided label smoothing: Real labels = 0.9 (not 1.0)




9.6.3 Training Instability
Problem: GANs optimize a min–max game, not a single objective → unstable fixed point behavior. Training dynamics can oscillate wildly and the minmax game may fail to converge.
Symptoms:

Losses do not correlate with image quality
Discriminator and generator take turns “winning”
Sudden collapse in sample quality

Solutions:

Architecture Stabilization:

Spectral normalization → enforces Lipschitz constraint on \(D\)
Batch normalization in G (avoid in final layer of \(D\))
LeakyReLU in D → prevents dead units
Residual connections / skip connections (modern GANs)

Optimization stabilization

TTUR (Two-Time-Scale Update Rule):

# Two Time-Scale Update Rule (TTUR)
lr_D = 4e-4  # Higher discriminator learning rate
lr_G = 1e-4  # Lower generator learning rate
optimizer = Adam(lr, betas=(0.0, 0.9))  # Different from default

Balanced update ratio e.g., 1 D step, per 1 G step; or 5:1 in WGANs.

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.7 Training Monitoring
What to plot:
1. Losses (but interpret carefully):
# Discriminator loss should be stable, not too low
plot(D_loss_real, D_loss_fake, D_loss_total)

# Generator loss should decrease (but may oscillate)
plot(G_loss)
⚠️ Warning: GAN losses are NOT good indicators of quality!

Discriminator loss approaching 0 → too strong (generator gets no gradient)
Generator loss approaching 0 → fooling discriminator (might be mode collapse)
Oscillating losses can indicate healthy adversarial dynamics

2. Generated samples (most important):
# Save samples every N iterations
if iter % save_freq == 0:
    with torch.no_grad():
        fake = G(fixed_noise)  # Use same noise for comparison
        save_image(fake, f'samples_{iter}.png')
3. Evaluation metrics:
# Compute every epoch or few epochs
if epoch % eval_freq == 0:
    FID_score = compute_FID(real_images, generated_images)
    IS_score = compute_IS(generated_images)
    log(FID_score, IS_score)
Red flags:

Generator produces identical samples → mode collapse
Generator produces noise or blurry blobs → vanishing gradient
Discriminator loss drops to 0 early → generator stops improving (Discriminator is too strong)
Sudden quality degradation → training instability

title: 9  Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs)
text:
9.9 Interview Preparation

9.9.1 Core Concepts Checklist

GAN minimax objective and Nash equilibrium
Non-saturating loss vs saturating loss
Mode collapse: causes and solutions
Wasserstein distance vs JS divergence
WGAN-GP gradient penalty mechanism
FID vs Inception Score
StyleGAN architecture innovations




9.9.2 Key Interview Questions
Q1: “What is mode collapse and how do you prevent it?”
Answer: Mode collapse is when generator produces limited variety, ignoring parts of data distribution. Generator finds samples that fool discriminator and exploits these without exploring other modes.
Detection: Visual inspection (similar samples), low Recall metric, oscillating discriminator loss.
Solutions:

WGAN-GP (better gradients, less prone to collapse)
Minibatch discrimination (penalizes lack of diversity)
Multiple discriminators/generators


Q2: “Why use Wasserstein distance instead of Jensen-Shannon divergence?”
Answer: When real and fake sample distributions don’t overlap:

JS divergence stops providing learning signal,
since \(\text{JS}(p_{\text{data}} | p_g)  \equiv \log 2\) is constant when \(p_{\text{data}}\) and \(p_g\) have disjoint supports.
The Wasserstein distance gives non-zero gradients during training,
since it always measures the “cost” of moving probability mass from \(p_g\) to \(p_r\).

Advantages:

Continuous and differentiable everywhere
Provides meaningful gradients even with disjoint distributions
More stable training

Disadvantage:: Requires enforcing Lipschitz constraint (gradient penalty).

Q3: “Explain WGAN-GP’s gradient penalty. Why better than weight clipping?”
Answer:
Goal: Enforce 1-Lipschitz constraint on discriminator.
Weight clipping (original WGAN):

Limits capacity (parameters stuck at boundaries)
Pathological optimization surfaces

Gradient penalty (WGAN-GP): \[\lambda \mathbb{E}_{\hat{x}}[(\|\nabla_{\hat{x}} D(\hat{x})\|_2 - 1)^2]\]
where \(\hat{x}\) are interpolations between real and fake.
Why better: Soft constraint, discriminator uses full parameter space, smoother optimization.

Q4: “Compare GANs, VAEs, and Diffusion models.”
Answer:

Use GAN: Need speed + quality (real-time applications).
Use VAE: Need stability + latent manipulation.
Use Diffusion: Need quality + diversity (current SOTA).

Q5: “How do you evaluate GAN performance?”
Answer:
FID (primary metric):

Measures distance between real/generated distributions in feature space
Lower is better
Sensitive to mode collapse
Correlates with human judgment

Inception Score (secondary):

Measures sharpness and diversity
Doesn’t compare to real distribution
Can be fooled

Precision/Recall:

Separately measure quality vs diversity
Diagnose specific failures

Best practice: FID + visual inspection + Precision/Recall for diagnosis.



9.9.3 Company Context
Anthropic:

Focus is on safety & interpretability
GANs less central than transformers/diffusion
Safety research - GANs used in synthetic data augmentation for adversarial attacks/robustness;
Interpretability research - GANs used in Understanding learned latent features.

Google DeepMind:

Research on GAN theory and variants
BigGAN, VQ-GAN (for video)

NVIDIA:

Focus on high-resolution generation

OpenAI / Stability AI:

Moved away from GANs toward diffusion models
But GAN descriminators used in: latent compression (Stable Diffusion VAE), for sharper reconstructions




9.9.4 Further Reading
Foundational Papers:

This completes the Generative Adversarial Networks theory, architectures and training techniques. While GANs revolutionized image synthesis through adversarial learning, their training remains notoriously unstable. Diffusion models emerged as a more robust alternative — easier to train, more interpretable, and capable of producing samples with unprecedented fidelity.

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.1 Introduction and Intuition
Diffusion models generate data by learning to reverse a gradual noising process. Instead of directly mapping noise to data—as in GANs—or compressing and decoding data as in VAEs, diffusion models treat generation as a sequence of small denoising steps. Each step is simple, which makes the overall learning problem stable and well-behaved.
Core idea:

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
Forward process: Add Gaussian noise to data over \(T\) steps until it becomes nearly pure noise. This process is analytically tractable.
Reverse process: Train a model to remove small amounts of noise at each step, gradually reconstructing samples from the data distribution.

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.2 Forward Diffusion Process

10.2.1 Noise Schedule
Forward diffusion is a discretized stochastic Markov process with transition probability at time \(t\) given by:
\[q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(x_t; \sqrt{1-\beta_t} x_{t-1}, \beta_t I)\]
where \(\beta_t \in (0, 1)\) is the noise schedule, controlling how much Gaussian noise is added at each step.
Equivalently, using a reparameterization: \[ \boxed{x_t = \sqrt{1-\beta_t} x_{t-1} + \sqrt{\beta_t} \epsilon_{t-1},
\quad \, \mathbf{\epsilon_{t-1} \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}}\]
Because each state depends only on the previous, the full forward process factorizes as a Markov chain: \[q(x_{1:T} | x_0) = \prod_{t=1}^T q(x_t | x_{t-1})\]



10.2.2 Closed-Form Forward Process
The forward diffusion process allows direct sampling of \(\mathbf{x_t}\) from \(\mathbf{x_0}\) in a single step — no need to iterate through all intermediate steps. Define: \[\alpha_t = 1 - \beta_t \text{ and } \bar{\alpha}_t = \prod_{s=1}^t \alpha_s\]
Closed form: \[q(x_t | x_0) = \mathcal{N}(x_t; \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0, (1 - \bar{\alpha}_t) I)\]
Reparameterization (sampling in one step): \[\boxed{x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0 + \sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t} \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)}\]
Intuition:

As \(t \to T\), \(\bar{\alpha}_t \to 0\), so \(x_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) — i.e., pure noise.
The forward process smoothly interpolates between the data \(x_0\) and standard Gaussian noise.

Noise schedule design:

Linear: \(\beta_t = \beta_{\min} + (t/T)(\beta_{\max} - \beta_{\min})\),   e.g., \(\beta_1 = 10^{-4}, \beta_T = 0.02\)
Cosine: Slower increase at endpoints, improved for high-resolution images

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.3 Reverse Diffusion Process

10.3.1 Theory
The reverse diffusion process aims to invert the forward noising process.
For sufficiently small \(\beta_t\), the reverse transition is approximately Gaussian: \[p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t) = \mathcal{N}(x_{t-1}; \mu_\theta(x_t, t), \Sigma_\theta(x_t, t))\]
The full reverse process is a Markov chain starting from pure noise: \[p_\theta(x_{0:T}) = p(x_T) \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(x_{t-1} | x_t), \quad \text{where } p(x_T) = \mathcal{N}(0, I)\]



10.3.2 Training


DDPM (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model, 2020)
The goal of training is to learn a network that can denoise \(x_t\) and approximate the reverse process.
Intuition:

At each timestep \(t\), we generate \(x_t\) from \(x_0\) by adding known Gaussian noise.
The network \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\) is trained to predict that exact noise.
Once we have this noise estimate, we can plug it into the analytic reverse-mean formula \(\mu_\theta(x_t, t)\) to obtain a slightly denoised estimate of \(x_{t-1}\) during sampling.

Reverse mean used in sampling::
\[
\mu_\theta(x_t, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}} \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\Big)
\]
Training objective:

Full ELBO objective (like in VAEs): \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{VLB}} = \mathbb{E}_q\left[D_{\text{KL}}(q(x_T|x_0) \| p(x_T)) + \sum_{t=2}^T D_{\text{KL}}(q(x_{t-1}|x_t, x_0) \| p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t)) - \log p_\theta(x_0|x_1)\right]\]
Simplified, practical objective (predict noise directly):

\[\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}} = \mathbb{E}_{t \sim \text{Uniform}(1,T), x_0, \epsilon}\left[\|\epsilon - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\|^2\right]}\]
where \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t} x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} \epsilon\).



10.3.3 Sampling
Once trained, the reverse process can generate samples by starting from pure Gaussian noise \(x_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\) and iteratively applying the learned transitions: \[
x_{t-1} = \mu_\theta(x_t, t) + \sigma_t z, \quad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)
\]

Repeat this from \(t=T\) down to \(t=1\) to obtain \(x_0\), a sample from the learned data distribution.
Different noise schedules or accelerated samplers (e.g., DDIM) can be used to reduce the number of steps or improve sample quality.




10.3.4 Algorithms
Training Algorithm:
# Training
for x_0 in dataloader:
    # Sample timestep and noise
    t ~ Uniform(1, T)
    ε ~ N(0, I)
    
    # Forward process (closed form)
    x_t = sqrt(α̅_t) * x_0 + sqrt(1 - α̅_t) * ε
    
    # Predict noise
    ε_pred = ε_θ(x_t, t)
    
    # Loss: MSE between true and predicted noise
    loss = ||ε - ε_pred||²
    
    # Update network
    θ ← θ - η ∇_θ loss
Network architecture: Typically a time-conditional U-Net with:

Timestep embeddings (sinusoidal or learned)
Self-attention at lower resolutions (16×16, 8×8)
Residual blocks with group normalization
Skip connections between encoder and decoder


Sampling Algorithm:
\[x_{t-1} = \mu_\theta(x_t, t) + \sigma_t z, \quad z \sim \mathcal{N}(0, I)\]
# Sampling
x_T ~ N(0, I)

for t = T, T-1, ..., 1:
    if t > 1:
        z ~ N(0, I)
    else:
        z = 0  # No noise at final step
    
    # Predict noise
    ε_pred = ε_θ(x_t, t)
    
    # Compute mean
    μ = (1/sqrt(α_t)) * (x_t - (β_t/sqrt(1-α̅_t)) * ε_pred)
    
    # Compute variance (can be learned or fixed)
    σ_t = sqrt(β_t)  # or sqrt(β̃_t) = sqrt((1-α̅_{t-1})/(1-α̅_t) * β_t)
    
    # Sample x_{t-1}
    x_{t-1} = μ + σ_t * z

return x_0
Cost: Requires \(T\) forward passes (typically \(T = 1000\)) → slow compared to GANs (1 pass).

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.4 Improvements and Variants

10.4.1 DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models, 2021)
Problem: DDPM requires many sampling steps (\(T \sim 1000\)), making image generation quite slow.
Key idea: DDIM reformulates the reverse diffusion process to allow deterministic sampling and arbitrary timestep skipping, while preserving the same marginal distributions \(q(x_t \mid x_0)\).
Deterministic reverse sampling (setting \(\sigma_t = 0\)): \[x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}} \underbrace{\left(\frac{x_t
- \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}}\right)}_{\text{predicted } x_0}
+ \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}} \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\]

Here, \(x_{t-1}\) is expressed in terms of \(x_t\) and the predicted \(\hat{x}_0\).
This formulation makes it mathematically consistent to skip multiple timesteps (e.g., from \(t\) to \(t-S\)) without iterating through all intermediate steps.

Benefits:

Faster sampling: Can reduce the number of steps from \(T\) to \(S \ll T\) (e.g. 50 instead of 1000 steps)
Deterministic: Same initial noise \(x_T\) always produces the same final image
Inversion: Can encode images back into latent codes

Trade-offs:

Potential quality degradation: Skipping many steps may slightly reduce image fidelity compared to full-step DDPM.
Reduced stochastic diversity: Deterministic sampling eliminates randomness, so multiple runs produce the same image.

Optional tip: For partial stochasticity, a multiplicative factor \(\eta \in [0,1]\) can scale the variance, allowing a continuum between fully deterministic (DDIM, \(\eta=0\)) and stochastic DDPM (\(\eta=1\)).

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.5 Conditional Image Generation

10.5.1 Score-Based View
Diffusion models can be interpreted as learning the score function \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\) rather than the density itself. This connection enables principled conditioning approaches.
Score formulation: From the forward process, the unconditional score at timestep \(t\) is: \[\nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t) = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}} \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\]
Conditional generation: To sample from \(p(x|y)\) where \(y\) is conditioning (class, text), we need the conditional score \(\nabla_x \log p(x|y)\). By Bayes’ theorem: \[\nabla_x \log p(x|y) = \nabla_x \log p(x) + \nabla_x \log p(y|x)\]
This suggests two different approaches for conditional generation: use a classifier to model \(p(y|x)\) (classifier guidance), or learn both terms jointly (classifier-free guidance).



10.5.2 Classifier Guidance
Method (Dhariwal and Nichol 2021): Train a separate classifier \(p_\phi(y|x_t)\) on noisy images at all noise levels \(t\).
Guided score: \[\nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t|y) = \nabla_{x_t} \log p(x_t) + w \cdot \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y|x_t)\]
where \(w\) is the guidance scale controlling conditioning strength.
Training:

Train unconditional diffusion model \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)\)
Separately train classifier \(p_\phi(y|x_t)\) on noisy images
At sampling, combine both using guidance scale \(w\). For noise prediction, the guided update is: \[\boxed{\tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, t, y) = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t) - w\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} \nabla_{x_t} \log p_\phi(y|x_t)}\]

Limitations:

Requires training a separate classifier robust to noisy inputs.
Classifier must be trained for each noise level \(t\).
Computationally expensive (extra gradient computation per step).




10.5.3 Classifier-Free Guidance
Key insight (Ho and Salimans 2022): Learn both conditional and unconditional models jointly in a single network, eliminating the need for a separate classifier.
Derivation: Rewrite the conditional term from Bayes’ theorem: \[\nabla_x \log p(y|x) = \nabla_x \log p(x|y) - \nabla_x \log p(x)\]
Substituting into the conditional score: \[\nabla_x \log p(x|y) = \nabla_x \log p(x) + w[\nabla_x \log p(x|y) - \nabla_x \log p(x)]\]
Rearranging: \[\nabla_x \log p(x|y) = (1-w)\nabla_x \log p(x) + w \nabla_x \log p(x|y)\]
In terms of noise prediction: \[\boxed{\tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, t, y) = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset) + w \cdot [\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, y) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset)]}\]
where \(\emptyset\) denotes the unconditional (null) condition.
Training: Single model learns both conditional and unconditional generation by randomly dropping conditioning \(y\) during training (typically 10-20% dropout rate): \[\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) \text{ where } c = \begin{cases} y & \text{with prob. } 0.9 \\ \emptyset & \text{with prob. } 0.1 \end{cases}\]
Guidance scale interpretation:

\(w = 0\): Unconditional generation
\(w = 1\): Standard conditional generation

\(w > 1\): Amplified conditioning (sharper, more aligned with \(y\), less diverse)

Advantages over classifier guidance:

No separate classifier needed (simpler training pipeline)
Better empirical results
Single model handles both conditional and unconditional generation

Classifier-free Guidance is the standard conditional generation approach in most modern text-to-image models (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2)



10.5.4 Classifier-Free Guidance (2022)
Goal: Generate samples conditioned on class labels or text without training a separate classifier.
Method: Train a single model unconditionally and conditionally by randomly dropping conditioning \(c\) during training:
\[\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) = \begin{cases}
\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) & \text{with prob. } p \\
\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset) & \text{with prob. } 1-p
\end{cases}\]
Guided sampling: Interpolate between conditional and unconditional predictions: \[\tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, t, c) = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset) + w \cdot (\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset))\]
where \(w\) is the guidance scale (typically \(w = 7\)-\(10\)).
Effect: - \(w = 0\): Unconditional generation - \(w = 1\): Standard conditional generation - \(w > 1\): Stronger conditioning (sharper, more aligned with condition, less diverse)
Why it works: Moves away from unconditional distribution toward conditional, amplifying the effect of conditioning.
Impact: Enables high-quality text-to-image generation (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2) without classifier networks.



10.5.5 Latent Diffusion Models (Stable Diffusion, 2022)
Problem: Running diffusion on high-resolution images (\(512 \times 512 \times 3\)) is computationally expensive.
Solution: Run diffusion in latent space of a pretrained autoencoder (VAE).
Architecture:

Encoder \(\mathcal{E}\): Compress image to latent: \(z = \mathcal{E}(x)\) (e.g., \(512^2 \times 3 \to 64^2 \times 4\))
Diffusion model: Operate on \(z\) (much smaller)
Decoder \(\mathcal{D}\): Reconstruct image: \(\hat{x} = \mathcal{D}(z)\)

Training:
# Encode to latent space
z_0 = Encoder(x)

# Diffusion in latent space
t ~ Uniform(1, T)
ε ~ N(0, I)
z_t = sqrt(α̅_t) * z_0 + sqrt(1 - α̅_t) * ε

# Predict noise in latent space
ε_pred = UNet(z_t, t, text_embedding)

# Loss
loss = ||ε - ε_pred||²
Benefits:

8× memory reduction (64² vs 512² spatial dimensions)
Faster training and sampling
Better quality (learned latent space is more structured)

Applications: Stable Diffusion, ImageGen, DALL-E 2 decoder.



10.5.6 Score-Based Models Connection
Alternative view: Diffusion models learn the score function \(\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t)\).
Score matching: Train model \(s_\theta(x_t, t) \approx \nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t)\).
Relation to noise prediction: \[\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t | x_0) = -\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}\]
So predicting noise \(\epsilon_\theta\) is equivalent to predicting score (up to scaling).
Continuous-time formulation: Stochastic differential equations (SDEs):

Forward SDE: \(dx = f(x, t)dt + g(t)dw\)
Reverse SDE: \(dx = [f(x, t) - g(t)^2 \nabla_x \log p_t(x)]dt + g(t)d\bar{w}\)

Benefits: Unified framework, flexible sampling (ODE/SDE), better theoretical understanding.
Key papers: Song et al. (2020) Score-Based Generative Modeling, Song et al. (2021) Score-Based SDEs.

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.6 Conditioning and Control

10.6.1 Text-to-Image
Method: Cross-attention between image features and text embeddings.
Architecture (Stable Diffusion):
Text → CLIP/T5 → text_embeddings

UNet layers:
  self_attention(image_features)
  cross_attention(image_features, text_embeddings)  # Condition here
  conv/resnet blocks
Training: Condition diffusion model on text captions from large datasets (LAION-5B).



10.6.2 ControlNet (2023)
Goal: Add spatial control (edges, pose, depth) to pretrained diffusion models without retraining from scratch.
Method: 1. Copy UNet encoder weights to create “control network” 2. Add conditioning image (edge map, pose, etc.) as input 3. Inject control features into main UNet via zero-initialized convolutions
Zero convolution trick: Initialize final layer with zeros, so initially ControlNet contributes nothing (preserves pretrained model).
Result: Precise spatial control while maintaining quality of pretrained model.
Applications: Sketch-to-image, pose-to-image, depth-to-image.



10.6.3 IP-Adapter (2023)
Goal: Image conditioning via cross-attention (like text, but with images).
Method: Add image cross-attention layers parallel to text cross-attention.
Applications: Image variations, style transfer, composition.

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.8 Practical Training Tips

10.8.1 Hyperparameters
Noise schedule: - Linear: \(\beta_1 = 10^{-4}\), \(\beta_T = 0.02\), \(T = 1000\) - Cosine: Better for high resolution, smoother at endpoints
Network: - U-Net with self-attention at 16×16, 8×8 resolutions - Timestep embedding: sinusoidal + 2-layer MLP - Channel multipliers: [1, 2, 4, 8] typical
Optimizer:
optimizer = Adam(lr=1e-4)  # Or AdamW with weight decay
ema_model = EMA(model, decay=0.9999)  # Use EMA for sampling
EMA (Exponential Moving Average): Critical for good results. Use EMA weights for sampling, not training weights.



10.8.2 Sampling Strategies
Trade-offs: - DDPM (1000 steps): High quality, diverse, slow - DDIM (50-100 steps): Faster, deterministic, slightly lower quality - DPM-Solver / UniPC: Fast ODE solvers (10-20 steps)
Guidance scale tuning: - Higher (\(w = 10\)-\(15\)): More aligned with prompt, less diverse - Lower (\(w = 5\)-\(7\)): More diverse, may drift from prompt



10.8.3 Monitoring Training
What to track: 1. Loss curve: Should decrease steadily (easier than GANs) 2. Generated samples: Visual inspection at regular intervals 3. FID score: Quantitative quality metric
Validation: Generate samples at fixed noise seeds to track progress.
Training time: ~1 week on 8× A100 for high-quality models (ImageNet 256×256).

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.9 Recent Advances (2023-2024)

10.9.1 DiT (Diffusion Transformer, 2023)
Key idea: Replace U-Net with Vision Transformer architecture.
Architecture: - Patch embeddings + positional encodings - Standard transformer blocks - AdaLN (adaptive layer norm) for conditioning
Results: Scales better than U-Net, achieves state-of-the-art FID on ImageNet.



10.9.2 Consistency Models (2023)
Problem: Diffusion requires many steps even with DDIM.
Solution: Train model to map any \(x_t\) directly to \(x_0\) (one-step generation).
Method: Enforce self-consistency: \(f_\theta(x_t, t) = f_\theta(x_{t'}, t')\) for all \(t, t'\) along same trajectory.
Result: Single-step generation with competitive quality.



10.9.3 Flow Matching (2023)
Idea: Learn vector fields that transport noise to data via optimal transport.
Advantage: Simpler training (no noise schedule), faster sampling, better likelihood.
Relation: Generalizes diffusion models, connects to continuous normalizing flows.



10.9.4 Rectified Flow (2023)
Improvement: Use straight-line paths in probability space (not curved SDEs).
Benefit: Fewer sampling steps needed, better for distillation.

title: 10  Diffusion Models
text:
10.11 Interview Preparation

10.11.1 Core Concepts Checklist
Mathematical Foundation: - [ ] Derive forward process closed form: \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon\) - [ ] Explain why we predict noise instead of mean - [ ] Understand score matching connection - [ ] Derive reverse process from forward
Training and Sampling: - [ ] DDPM training algorithm - [ ] DDIM vs DDPM sampling differences - [ ] Classifier-free guidance mechanism - [ ] Latent diffusion advantages
Advanced Topics: - [ ] ControlNet architecture - [ ] Score-based SDE formulation - [ ] Flow matching basics



10.11.2 Key Interview Questions
Q1: “Explain the forward and reverse diffusion process. Why is the forward process useful?”
Answer:
Forward process: Gradually add Gaussian noise over \(T\) steps: \[q(x_t | x_{t-1}) = \mathcal{N}(x_t; \sqrt{1-\beta_t}x_{t-1}, \beta_t I)\]
Key property: Has closed form—can sample \(x_t\) directly from \(x_0\): \[x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\]
Reverse process: Learn to denoise step-by-step: \[p_\theta(x_{t-1}|x_t) = \mathcal{N}(x_{t-1}; \mu_\theta(x_t,t), \Sigma_\theta(x_t,t))\]
Why forward process is useful: 1. Closed form enables efficient training (sample any \(t\) directly) 2. Provides training targets (known true noise \(\epsilon\)) 3. Ensures \(x_T \approx \mathcal{N}(0,I)\) (tractable starting point for sampling)

Q2: “Why do we predict noise \(\epsilon\) instead of directly predicting \(x_0\) or the mean \(\mu\)?”
Answer:
Theoretical reason: Equivalent formulations have different gradient properties. Predicting noise \(\epsilon\) gives the best loss weighting across timesteps.
From forward process: \(x_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon\)
Can rearrange to get mean: \[\mu(x_t, t) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\left(x_t - \frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}\epsilon\right)\]
Predicting noise advantages: 1. Single network output works for all timesteps (noise is same distribution) 2. Empirically more stable training 3. Naturally weighted—loss is uniform in \(\epsilon\), but implied loss on \(x_0\) varies by \(t\)
Equivalence: Predicting \(\epsilon\), \(x_0\), or \(\mu\) are mathematically equivalent (can convert between them), but \(\epsilon\) trains best.

Q3: “Explain DDIM. How does it achieve faster sampling?”
Answer:
Key insight: DDPM’s forward process is not unique. Can design different forward processes with same marginals \(q(x_t|x_0)\) but different conditionals \(q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0)\).
DDIM forward: Non-Markovian—\(q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0)\) depends on \(x_0\), not just \(x_t\).
Sampling update (deterministic when \(\sigma=0\)): \[x_{t-1} = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\underbrace{\left(\frac{x_t - \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}}\right)}_{\text{predicted }x_0} + \sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\]
Why faster: - Can skip timesteps (subsample \(\{t_1, t_2, ..., t_S\}\) where \(S \ll T\)) - Each step is deterministic, not stochastic - Typically 50-100 steps vs 1000 for DDPM
Trade-off: Slightly less diverse samples than DDPM (deterministic), but much faster.

Q4: “What is classifier-free guidance and why is it important?”
Answer:
Goal: Generate samples strongly aligned with conditioning (class/text) without training separate classifier.
Method: Train single model with conditioning randomly dropped: - Train unconditional \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset)\) and conditional \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c)\) jointly
Sampling: Interpolate predictions: \[\tilde{\epsilon}_\theta(x_t, t, c) = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset) + w \cdot (\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t, \emptyset))\]
Intuition: - Difference \((\epsilon_c - \epsilon_\emptyset)\) points toward conditional distribution - Scale \(w > 1\) amplifies this direction - Moves sample away from unconditional, toward conditional
Impact: - Enables high-quality text-to-image (Stable Diffusion, DALL-E) - No need for separate classifier network (simpler) - Controllable trade-off between alignment and diversity via \(w\)
Typical values: \(w = 7\)-\(10\) for text-to-image.

Q5: “Explain latent diffusion. Why is it better than pixel-space diffusion?”
Answer:
Idea: Run diffusion in latent space of pretrained autoencoder (VAE), not pixel space.
Architecture: 1. Encoder \(\mathcal{E}\): \(x \to z\) (e.g., \(512^2 \times 3 \to 64^2 \times 4\)) 2. Diffusion: Operate on \(z\) 3. Decoder \(\mathcal{D}\): \(z \to \hat{x}\)
Advantages: 1. Efficiency: 8× smaller spatial dimensions → 64× less memory 2. Speed: Faster training and sampling 3. Quality: Learned latent space is more semantically structured 4. Perceptual loss implicitly included (VAE decoder trained with perceptual objectives)
Trade-off: Adds VAE reconstruction artifacts (usually minor).
Impact: Enabled open-source high-resolution generation (Stable Diffusion on consumer GPUs).

Q6: “Compare diffusion models to GANs and VAEs. When would you use each?”
Answer:
Diffusion: - Pros: Best quality + diversity, stable training, excellent mode coverage - Cons: Very slow sampling (50-1000 steps) - Use when: Quality and diversity critical, generation time acceptable
GAN: - Pros: Fast sampling (1 step), high quality - Cons: Training instability, mode collapse, no likelihood - Use when: Real-time generation needed, willing to handle training difficulty
VAE: - Pros: Fast, stable training, explicit latent space, likelihood - Cons: Blurry samples (posterior collapse) - Use when: Need latent manipulation, representation learning, anomaly detection
Current trend (2024): - Diffusion dominant for image generation (quality + diversity) - GANs still used in latent diffusion VAE decoders - Research on fast diffusion samplers (consistency models, flow matching)

Q7: “How would you speed up diffusion model sampling?”
Answer:
Approaches (in order of ease):
1. DDIM sampling (easiest): - Use 50-100 steps instead of 1000 - Deterministic sampling allows step skipping - Minimal quality loss
2. Better ODE/SDE solvers: - DPM-Solver, UniPC: 10-20 steps - Leverage numerical methods from differential equations
3. Distillation: - Train student model to match teacher in fewer steps - Progressive distillation: 1000 → 500 → 250 → … → 4 steps - Consistency models: Single-step generation
4. Latent diffusion: - Operate in compressed latent space (8× speedup) - Stable Diffusion approach
5. Architectural improvements: - DiT (transformer-based): Better scaling - Efficient attention mechanisms
Trade-offs: - Fewer steps → faster but slightly lower quality/diversity - Distillation → fast but requires teacher model - Latent space → efficient but VAE artifacts
Practical recommendation: Start with DDIM (50 steps), then explore DPM-Solver if need faster.

Q8: “What is ControlNet and how does it work without retraining the base model?”
Answer:
Goal: Add spatial control (edges, pose, depth) to pretrained diffusion model without full retraining.
Architecture: 1. Copy pretrained UNet encoder → “control network” 2. Add conditioning image as input to control network 3. Inject control features into main UNet via zero-initialized convolutions
Zero convolution trick:
# Initialize final convolution layer with zeros
control_output = zero_conv(control_features)  # Initially outputs 0
main_features = main_features + control_output
Initially contributes nothing (preserves pretrained model), gradually learns control.
Training: Only train control network + zero conv layers (freeze main UNet).
Why it works: - Preserves pretrained model’s quality - Zero initialization ensures smooth learning - Encoder copy provides good features for control
Applications: Canny edges, pose skeletons, depth maps, semantic segmentation → image.

Q9: “Explain the connection between diffusion models and score-based models.”
Answer:
Score function: \(\nabla_x \log p(x)\) (gradient of log probability).
Key insight: Diffusion models implicitly learn scores.
Connection: From forward process, can derive: \[\nabla_{x_t} \log q(x_t|x_0) = -\frac{x_t - \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}x_0}{1-\bar{\alpha}_t} = -\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}\]
So predicting noise \(\epsilon_\theta\) is equivalent to predicting score \(s_\theta\) (up to scaling): \[s_\theta(x_t, t) = -\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_t}}\]
Score-based view: Train model to estimate \(\nabla_x \log p_t(x)\) at all noise levels \(t\).
Continuous time: Formulate as Stochastic Differential Equations (SDEs): - Forward SDE adds noise continuously - Reverse SDE removes noise using learned scores
Advantages of score view: - Unified theoretical framework - Flexible sampling (ODE vs SDE) - Connection to Langevin dynamics
Practical impact: Mostly equivalent, but score perspective enables better samplers (DPM-Solver, flow matching).

Q10: “You’re training a diffusion model but samples are blurry. What could be wrong?”
Answer:
Likely causes:
1. Not using EMA model (most common): - EMA (exponential moving average) critical for quality - Use EMA weights for sampling, not training weights
ema_model = EMA(model, decay=0.9999)
# Sample with ema_model, not model
2. Too few sampling steps: - Try increasing from 50 to 250-1000 steps - DDIM needs more steps for high quality
3. Poor noise schedule: - Linear schedule may not be optimal for high resolution - Try cosine schedule (smoother at endpoints)
4. Model undertrained: - Diffusion needs long training (days on GPUs) - Check if loss still decreasing
5. Variance schedule wrong: - If predicting variance, check initialization - Can fix variance to \(\beta_t\) or \(\tilde{\beta}_t\) initially
6. Conditioning issues (if conditional): - Check cross-attention is working - Verify text embeddings have correct dimensionality
Debugging steps: 1. Verify EMA is enabled 2. Generate with more steps (1000) 3. Check training loss curve 4. Compare to pretrained model samples



10.11.3 Company-Specific Context
Anthropic: - Focus on safety, controllability, interpretability - Diffusion useful for: data augmentation, understanding representations - Interest in: controllable generation, alignment
OpenAI: - DALL-E 2/3 (cascaded diffusion + CLIP) - Focus on text-to-image, safety, prompt alignment
Stability AI: - Stable Diffusion (open-source latent diffusion) - Focus on efficiency, democratization
NVIDIA: - DiT (diffusion transformers) - Focus on efficiency, GPU optimization, fast sampling
Google DeepMind: - Imagen (high-quality text-to-image) - Research on theoretical foundations, SDE formulations



10.11.4 Further Reading
Foundational Papers: - Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM, Ho et al., 2020) - Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM, Song et al., 2021) - Score-Based Generative Modeling through SDEs (Song et al., 2021)
Key Improvements: - Classifier-Free Guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2022) - High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion (Stable Diffusion, Rombach et al., 2022) - Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (DiT, Peebles & Xie, 2023)
Control and Conditioning: - Adding Conditional Control to Text-to-Image Diffusion (ControlNet, Zhang et al., 2023) - Prompt-to-Prompt Image Editing (Hertz et al., 2022)
Fast Sampling: - Consistency Models (Song et al., 2023) - Flow Matching for Generative Modeling (Lipman et al., 2023)

This chapter provides a rigorous yet intuitive understanding of diffusion models, covering theory, training, key innovations, and practical considerations for research roles in top AI labs.

title: Video
text:
Overview
Video extends images with a temporal dimension, turning visual understanding into a spatiotemporal problem. This section covers the full stack across five chapters: representing and measuring motion and the discriminative architectures built on top of it, vision-language models that understand, retrieve, and reason over video, the structural task of splitting video into shots and scenes, the benchmark landscape used to evaluate all of it, and generative models that synthesize temporally coherent clips.
Chapter Scope:
Interview Relevance: Video understanding and generation are central to roles at Meta (Reels ranking, Movie Gen), Google DeepMind (Gemini, Veo, Genie), OpenAI (Sora), Tesla and Waymo (temporal scene understanding), and TikTok/YouTube (recommendation, search, and moderation at scale). Expect questions on extending image architectures to video efficiently, token-budget trade-offs for long-context video LLMs, how modern video generators (Sora, CogVideoX) differ architecturally from image diffusion models, how a video is split into shots/scenes for retrieval, and how to evaluate video understanding or generation quality.
Prerequisites: Part II (CNNs, Vision Transformers), Part III (Self-Supervised Learning), Part IV (Diffusion Models), and the Foundation Models for Segmentation chapter (§sec-segmentation). Familiarity with 2D convolution, multi-head self-attention, rotary positional embeddings, and the DDPM training objective.

title: Video
text:
Video Fundamentals: Motion and Spatiotemporal Architectures (Chapter 10): Video as a spatiotemporal signal, optical flow (classical and learned), 3D CNNs (C3D, I3D, R(2+1)D, SlowFast), video transformers (TimeSformer, Video Swin, ViViT), and self-supervised pretraining (VideoMAE, V-JEPA)
Video Understanding (Chapter 11): Downstream video tasks (action recognition, temporal grounding, VQA, retrieval, tracking), vision-language model architectures from Q-Former to M-RoPE, the Qwen-VL evolution, specialized and contrastive video VLMs, and the two-stage retrieval-and-reranking pipeline
Video Temporal Segmentation (Chapter 12): Shot boundary detection and scene boundary detection as the two-stage pipeline that turns raw frames into searchable, retrieval-ready units — classical signals, learned detectors, and Scene-VLM-style sequence labelling
Video Understanding Benchmarks (Chapter 13): A systematic tour of the benchmark landscape — action recognition, long-video, VQA/reasoning, temporal grounding, captioning/retrieval, and egocentric benchmarks, plus practical guidance for choosing one
Video Generation (Chapter 14): Diffusion fundamentals for video (3D-VAE compression, DiT vs. U-Net), training-from-scratch (VDM, Imagen Video, Sora, CogVideoX), fine-tuning image models (Make-A-Video, Video LDM), training-free adaptation (Text2Video-Zero), autoregressive video generation, and evaluation (FVD, VBench)

11.1 Video as a Spatiotemporal Signal
Formal Representation: A video is a spatiotemporal signal \(I: \Omega \times [0, T] \to \mathbb{R}^C\), where:
In the discrete setting, a video is represented as a tensor: \[\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times C}\] with \(T\) frames, each of spatial resolution \(H \times W\) and \(C\) color channels.
Key Challenges relative to image processing:
Core Tasks:
This chapter focuses on the encoder side: representing motion and building spatiotemporal architectures. Vision-language models for captioning, QA, retrieval, and temporal grounding are covered in the next chapter; video generation (the rightmost column above) gets its own chapter.

title: 11  Video Fundamentals: Motion and Spatiotemporal Architectures
text:
11.2 Optical Flow
Optical flow captures the motion in a scene: for each pixel and each time step, it estimates the displacement vector between consecutive frames.

11.2.1 The Optical Flow Constraint
Definition: The optical flow field is a mapping: \[\mathbf{v}: \Omega \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^2, \quad (x, y, t) \mapsto (u, v)\] where \((u, v)\) denote the horizontal and vertical displacement of the pixel at \((x, y)\) between frames \(t\) and \(t+1\).
Brightness Constancy Assumption: The intensity of a moving pixel is approximately preserved across frames: \[I(x + u,\; y + v,\; t + 1) = I(x, y, t)\]
Linearization (first-order Taylor expansion for small displacements): \[I(x+u, y+v, t+1) \approx I(x,y,t) + I_x u + I_y v + I_t\]
Substituting into the brightness constancy assumption yields the optical flow constraint equation: \[\boxed{I_x u + I_y v + I_t = 0}\] where \(I_x = \partial I/\partial x\), \(I_y = \partial I/\partial y\), \(I_t = \partial I/\partial t\) are spatiotemporal image gradients.
The Aperture Problem: At each pixel, the OFC gives 1 equation with 2 unknowns \((u, v)\). Only the component of motion parallel to the image gradient is recoverable from local measurements—motion along isoluminance contours (perpendicular to the gradient) remains ambiguous. Additional constraints are required to recover the full flow field.



11.2.2 Classical Methods
Both classical methods impose extra constraints to resolve the aperture problem.

11.2.2.1 Lucas–Kanade (1981)
Assumption: Flow is locally constant within a spatial window \(\mathcal{W}\) centered on each pixel.
Lucas-Kanade finds \((u,v)\) that minimizes the sum of squared OFC residuals over the window: \[\min_{u,v} \sum_{(x,y) \in \mathcal{W}} \left(I_x u + I_y v + I_t\right)^2\]
Collecting the OFC equation at every pixel \((x_i, y_i) \in \mathcal{W}\): \[\mathbf{A} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = -\mathbf{b}, \quad \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} I_x(x_1) & I_y(x_1) \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ I_x(x_n) & I_y(x_n) \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{b} = \begin{bmatrix} I_t(x_1) \\ \vdots \\ I_t(x_n) \end{bmatrix}\]
This overdetermined system (\(n \gg 2\)) is solved in the least-squares sense: \[\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} = -(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A})^{-1} \mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{b}\]
The \(2 \times 2\) matrix \(\mathbf{A}^\top \mathbf{A}\) is the structure tensor (also used in the Harris corner detector). The system is well-conditioned only when both eigenvalues are large—meaning the window contains gradients in multiple directions. This is exactly the condition for a well-defined corner.
Limitation: Fails for large displacements (linearization breaks down) and at motion discontinuities (where the constant-flow assumption is violated). Addressed in practice via image pyramids (coarse-to-fine refinement).



11.2.2.2 Horn–Schunck (1981)
Assumption: The flow field is globally smooth—motion should vary slowly across the image.
Minimize the energy functional: \[E(u, v) = \iint_\Omega \underbrace{\left(I_x u + I_y v + I_t\right)^2}_{\text{data term}} + \lambda^2 \underbrace{\left(|\nabla u|^2 + |\nabla v|^2\right)}_{\text{smoothness term}} \; dx \, dy\]
The Euler–Lagrange equations for \(u\) and \(v\) yield a coupled system of PDEs solved iteratively via Gauss-Seidel or Jacobi updates.
Trade-off: \(\lambda\) controls the smoothness–accuracy balance. Large \(\lambda\) → smoother flow; small \(\lambda\) → more faithful to the brightness constancy assumption, but noisier at motion discontinuities.
Limitation: Global smoothness is physically incorrect at object boundaries, where flow should be discontinuous.




11.2.3 Deep Optical Flow
Modern methods learn optical flow end-to-end from paired data \(\{(I_t, I_{t+1}, \mathbf{v}^*)\}\).
FlowNet (2015): First CNN for optical flow. Two variants: - FlowNetS (Simple): Concatenate both frames, pass through encoder–decoder U-Net. - FlowNetC (Correlation): Compute feature correlation volume \(C(\mathbf{f}_1, \mathbf{f}_2)\) explicitly at bottleneck, then decode.
RAFT (2020): Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms. Current state-of-the-art approach:

Feature extraction: Shared encoder produces feature maps \(\mathbf{g}_1, \mathbf{g}_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{H/8 \times W/8 \times D}\).
All-pairs correlation: Compute 4D correlation volume \(\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times H \times W}\): \[\mathbf{C}(\mathbf{g}_1, \mathbf{g}_2)_{ijkl} = \langle \mathbf{g}_1[i,j],\, \mathbf{g}_2[k,l] \rangle\] Pool over multiple scales to handle large displacements.
Recurrent update: A ConvGRU iteratively refines the flow estimate \(\mathbf{v}^{(r)}\) using correlation lookups: \[\mathbf{v}^{(r+1)} = \mathbf{v}^{(r)} + \Delta\mathbf{v}^{(r)}, \quad \Delta\mathbf{v}^{(r)} = f_\theta(\mathbf{h}^{(r)}, \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{v}^{(r)}))\]

Training: Supervised on FlyingChairs, FlyingThings3D synthetic datasets; fine-tuned on real data (Sintel, KITTI).
Interview Insight: “Why a correlation volume?” Lucas-Kanade is essentially computing local correlation between templates. RAFT computes all pairwise correlations globally, then lets a recurrent module learn which correlations to use given the current flow estimate.



11.2.4 Using Optical Flow in Deep Video Models
Optical flow and raw frames are complementary:

Frames → appearance (texture, color, object identity)
Flow → dynamics (motion, trajectories, temporal consistency)

Integration strategies:

Two-Stream Networks (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2014): Independent spatial stream (RGB) and temporal stream (stacked optical flow \([u_t, v_t, \ldots, u_{t+L}, v_{t+L}]\)). Late fusion via score averaging.
Flow as warping operator: Given flow \(\mathbf{v}(x,y,t) = (u,v)\), warp frame \(I_t\) to predict \(I_{t+1}\): \[\hat{I}_{t+1}(x, y) = I_t(x + u,\; y + v)\] Used in video prediction, tracking, and temporal consistency constraints.
Self-supervision signal: Optical flow provides geometric constraints without labels:

Temporal consistency loss: \(\|F_t(x,y) - F_{t+1}(x+u, y+v)\|\), encouraging features to move consistently with the scene.
Future frame prediction: Predict \(I_{t+1}\) from \(I_t\) via flow; minimize reconstruction error.


Practical note: Computing optical flow per-frame is expensive ($$100ms per pair with RAFT on GPU). Modern architectures increasingly learn motion implicitly via 3D convolutions or temporal attention, avoiding explicit flow. Optical flow is most valuable when motion is the primary discriminative cue (e.g., subtle human pose changes) or when labeled data is scarce.

11.3.2 3D Convolutional Networks

11.3.2.1 C3D (2015)
Core idea: Replace 2D convolutions with 3D convolutions that jointly model space and time.
A 3D convolution with kernel \(\mathbf{K} \in \mathbb{R}^{k_t \times k \times k \times c_\text{in} \times c_\text{out}}\) applied to a volume \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{T' \times H' \times W' \times c_\text{in}}\): \[\mathbf{Y}[\tau, i, j, c] = \sum_{c'} \sum_{p=0}^{k_t-1} \sum_{q=0}^{k-1} \sum_{r=0}^{k-1} \mathbf{X}[\tau+p, i+q, j+r, c'] \cdot \mathbf{K}[p,q,r,c',c]\]
C3D Architecture: VGG-like network with 3×3×3 kernels throughout. Pre-trained on Sports-1M.
Limitation: 3D convolutions are computationally expensive ($$3× the FLOPs of 2D) and cannot leverage 2D ImageNet pretrained weights.



11.3.2.2 Two-Stream Networks (2014)
Motivation: Decouple appearance and motion modeling.
RGB frames ──► Spatial CNN ──► Spatial scores ──┐
                                                 ├──► Fusion ──► Action class
Optical flow ─► Temporal CNN ──► Temporal scores─┘
Temporal stream input: Stack of \(L\) consecutive flow fields \([u_t, v_t, u_{t+1}, v_{t+1}, \ldots, u_{t+L-1}, v_{t+L-1}] \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 2L}\), treated as a multi-channel image.
Fusion strategies: Late fusion (score-level averaging) outperforms early fusion in practice. The temporal stream alone achieves $\(85\%\) of the full model’s accuracy on UCF-101.
Interview Insight: “Why stack flow fields rather than feed them frame-by-frame?” The stack gives the temporal stream a wider temporal context in a single forward pass—it sees \(L\) consecutive motions simultaneously, allowing it to reason about motion trajectories rather than instantaneous displacements.



11.3.2.3 I3D: Inflated 3D (2017)
Core idea: Bootstrap 3D CNNs from 2D ImageNet pretrained weights by “inflating” 2D convolutions to 3D.
Inflation procedure: For a 2D kernel \(\mathbf{K}^{2D} \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k \times c_\text{in} \times c_\text{out}}\), construct a 3D kernel \(\mathbf{K}^{3D} \in \mathbb{R}^{k_t \times k \times k \times c_\text{in} \times c_\text{out}}\) by repeating and rescaling: \[\mathbf{K}^{3D}[p, :, :, :, :] = \frac{1}{k_t} \mathbf{K}^{2D}, \quad p = 0, \ldots, k_t - 1\]
This ensures that at initialization, the 3D conv collapses to the 2D conv when applied to a video with identical frames — so the pretrained ImageNet performance is preserved.
Two-Stream I3D: Apply the inflation independently to the spatial (RGB) and temporal (flow) streams. At the time of publication, Two-Stream I3D achieved state-of-the-art on Kinetics-400.
Why it works: ImageNet pretraining provides strong appearance priors. Inflation provides a meaningful initialization for temporal filters rather than random initialization from scratch.



11.3.2.4 R(2+1)D: Factorized Spatiotemporal Convolutions (2018)
Core idea: Decompose a 3D convolution into a 2D spatial convolution followed by a 1D temporal convolution.
A \(t \times d \times d\) 3D convolution is replaced by: 1. \(1 \times d \times d\) spatial convolution: \(\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times c_\text{in}} \to \mathbb{R}^{T \times H' \times W' \times M}\) 2. \(t \times 1 \times 1\) temporal convolution: \(\mathbb{R}^{T \times H' \times W' \times M} \to \mathbb{R}^{T' \times H' \times W' \times c_\text{out}}\)
where \(M\) is an intermediate channel count chosen to match the parameter count of the original 3D convolution.
Advantages over full 3D convolution: - An additional non-linearity between the two convolutions doubles the number of nonlinearities. - Easier optimization (closer to 2D pretrained initialization). - Factorized structure aids interpretability.

11.3.2.5 SlowFast Networks (2019)
Core idea: Use two pathway networks operating at different temporal resolutions to separately capture spatial semantics and temporal dynamics.

Slow Pathway: Low frame rate (e.g., 4 fps), high spatial resolution, large channel capacity → captures spatial semantics.
Fast Pathway: High frame rate (e.g., 32 fps), low spatial resolution, small channel capacity ($$1/8 of Slow channels) → captures fine-grained motion.

Lateral connections: Fuse Fast-to-Slow at multiple stages via time-strided convolution (to match temporal dimensions): \[F^{\ell}_\text{fused} = \text{Concat}\left[F^{\ell}_\text{Slow},\; \text{Conv}(F^{\ell}_\text{Fast})\right]\]
Rationale: Not all video information requires temporal detail. Object identity and scene context can be determined from a few frames; subtle motions (hand gestures, facial expressions) need high temporal resolution. SlowFast allocates compute accordingly.
Interview Insight: “What does the Fast pathway actually learn?” Visualization shows that Fast pathway channels respond primarily to motion rather than appearance—they exhibit low selectivity for object classes but high sensitivity to temporal differences. This supports the design intuition.




11.3.3 Video Transformers
Self-attention over space and time enables global context modeling but requires careful management of the quadratic cost.
For a video with \(T\) frames and \(N = (H/P)^2\) patches per frame, the sequence length is \(TN\). Naive full spatiotemporal attention has complexity: \[\mathcal{O}\left((TN)^2 \cdot D\right)\]
For \(T=8\), \(N=196\), \(D=768\): \((8 \times 196)^2 \times 768 \approx 1.5 \times 10^{12}\) operations per layer.
The practical methods below all propose factorized or windowed attention to reduce this cost.


11.3.3.1 TimeSformer (2021)
Approach: Divide the full spatiotemporal attention into separate spatial and temporal attention operations applied sequentially at each layer — “Divided Space-Time Attention”.
Within each Transformer block, for token \((t, i)\) (frame \(t\), patch \(i\)):

Temporal attention: attend over all frames at the same spatial position: \[\mathbf{z}'^{(t,i)} = \text{Attn}\!\left(\mathbf{z}^{(t,i)},\; \{\mathbf{z}^{(t',i)}\}_{t'=1}^T\right)\]
Spatial attention: attend over all patches in the same frame: \[\mathbf{z}''^{(t,i)} = \text{Attn}\!\left(\mathbf{z}'^{(t,i)},\; \{\mathbf{z}'^{(t,j)}\}_{j=1}^N\right)\]

Complexity: \(\mathcal{O}(T^2 N D + TN^2 D)\) — linear in \(TN\) rather than quadratic.
Initialization: Weights from pretrained ViT. Temporal attention weights initialized to zero (so at initialization, the model reduces to a spatial-only ViT — a well-conditioned starting point).



11.3.3.2 Video Swin Transformer (2021)
Approach: Extend the shifted window mechanism from Swin Transformer to 3D — compute attention within local 3D windows of size \(P_t \times P_h \times P_w\) tokens.
Each attention operation is restricted to a local window of \(P_t \times P_h \times P_w\) spatiotemporal tokens: \[\mathcal{O}(T H W \cdot P_t P_h P_w \cdot D)\]
which is linear in \(THW\) for fixed window sizes.
Cyclic shifting: Alternate window partitions between layers (identical to 2D Swin) to enable cross-window communication without added cost.
Result: Strong performance on Kinetics and Something-Something with better compute efficiency than TimeSformer.



11.3.3.3 ViViT (2021, Google)
Proposes four factorization strategies; the best-performing:
Model 2 — Factorised Encoder: First apply spatial Transformer (ViT) to each frame independently → get \(T\) frame-level tokens. Then apply temporal Transformer over these \(T\) tokens.
\[\text{ViViT: } \mathbf{V} \xrightarrow{\text{Spatial ViT per frame}} \{z_1, \ldots, z_T\} \xrightarrow{\text{Temporal Transformer}} y\]
This decouples spatial and temporal pretraining — the spatial ViT can be initialized from ViT-pretrained weights directly.
Interview Insight: “How do you choose between TimeSformer, Video Swin, and ViViT?” At equal scale: Video Swin is most efficient (locality bias reduces compute); TimeSformer is simpler to implement and flexible; ViViT’s factorized encoder is cleanest for transfer from image models. For standard benchmarks (Kinetics), Video Swin and ViViT are broadly comparable.

title: 11  Video Fundamentals: Motion and Spatiotemporal Architectures
text:
11.4 Self-Supervised Learning for Video
The same paradigms from image SSL (§6 in this book) extend naturally to video, with temporal structure providing additional self-supervision signals.

11.4.1 Masked Video Modeling: VideoMAE (2022)
Core idea: Extend Masked Autoencoders (MAE) to video. Given a video clip, mask a large fraction of spatiotemporal patches and train a Transformer encoder-decoder to reconstruct the masked patches.
High masking ratio: VideoMAE uses \(90\%\) masking (vs. \(75\%\) for image MAE). This is motivated by the high redundancy in video—adjacent patches are strongly correlated. Aggressive masking forces the model to reason about long-range spatiotemporal structure rather than copying neighboring patches.
Tube masking: Masks are sampled as spatiotemporal tubes — the same spatial positions are masked across all frames. This prevents the trivial solution of copying visible patches from adjacent frames at the same location.
\[\text{Mask} \in \{0,1\}^{T \times N}, \quad \text{Mask}[t, i] = \text{Mask}[t', i] \;\forall t, t'\]
Training objective: Pixel-level MSE reconstruction on masked patches (same as MAE): \[\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{|\mathcal{M}|} \sum_{(t,i) \in \mathcal{M}} \|\hat{\mathbf{x}}_{t,i} - \mathbf{x}_{t,i}\|^2\right]\]
Efficiency: Because \(90\%\) of tokens are masked, the encoder only processes \(10\%\) of tokens → the computational cost of SSL pre-training is comparable to supervised training.
Result: VideoMAE pre-trained representations transfer competitively with or surpass fully supervised training on Kinetics-400 when fine-tuned.



11.4.2 Contrastive and Distillation Approaches
Video contrastive learning: Extend image contrastive methods (SimCLR, MoCo) by defining temporal augmentations as additional views: - Two temporally-distant clips from the same video → positive pair - Clips from different videos → negative pairs
V-JEPA (2024, Meta): Extends I-JEPA to video. Predict representations of masked spatiotemporal regions using context regions in feature space (not pixel space), avoiding the need to reconstruct high-frequency details. This encourages the model to learn semantic rather than textural features.
Interview Insight: “Why does VideoMAE use such a high masking ratio?” The spatial redundancy in video is much higher than in images — nearby pixels and frames are nearly identical. Low masking ratios allow the decoder to reconstruct patches from adjacent visible neighbors without learning meaningful semantics. High masking forces global reasoning.
