Three deployment regimes follow, and they want different things:

Data curation at scale (video-generation training corpora, Chapter 15). Only stage one matters, but it must be transition-aware and sudden-jump-aware: a clip with a dissolve at its head or a discontinuity in its middle is training poison for a temporal VAE. This is OmniShotCut’s target, and the 3.3× gap in transition IoU over TransNet V2 is the argument.
Retrieval indexing. PySceneDetect for shots, keyframe captions + adjacent-shot clustering for scenes, and the 2 s / 60 s cleanup rules of Section 13.2. Scene boundaries need only be good enough that the retrieved segment is watchable, and the cheap pipeline clears that bar at a fraction of the cost.
Media operations with human review. Confidence scores and rationales stop being niceties: an editor triaging boundary proposals needs to sort by confidence and to check the model’s reasoning against narrative intent. This is the regime that justifies Scene-VLM’s price, and the 8.3× cheaper “concise” variant is the fallback when precision–recall control is not required.







Important



The two stages are trained and evaluated in isolation, and this hides a real failure mode. MovieNet ships ground-truth shot boundaries, so every published scene model has been evaluated on perfect shot input. In deployment the shot detector runs first, and its errors — a missed gradual transition, a dissolve boundary placed mid-dissolve — silently corrupt the shot representations the scene model consumes. No published benchmark measures this propagation.

title: 13  Video Temporal Segmentation
text:
13.6 Open Problems
The scene is not well defined. No published inter-annotator agreement exists for MovieNet scene boundaries, so nobody knows whether F1 0.62 is halfway to the ceiling or nearly at it. This is the single most important missing measurement in the task, and it is cheap to obtain.
Cascade error is unmeasured. See the note above. An end-to-end benchmark that runs a real shot detector into a scene model would tell us how much of the scene-segmentation gap is actually shot-detection debt.
Domain generalisation is poor in both directions. On MovieNet, Chapter-LLaMA trails Scene-VLM by 23.5 F1 (38.6 vs 62.1), because caption-based reasoning discards the visual structure that carries cinematic scene changes. On VidChapters the ordering reverses: Chapter-LLaMA with its native LLaMA-3.1 backbone reaches 42.6 F1 against Scene-VLM’s 32.2 — though under a matched Qwen backbone Scene-VLM leads (32.2 vs 28.4), so part of that gap is backbone rather than method. Either way, no published system covers both regimes without retraining.
Audio is barely used. Scene-VLM consumes transcripts, not audio. Score, ambience, and silence are among the strongest scene cues a film editor deliberately places — a music cue frequently is the boundary — and the cross-modal agreement heuristic of Section 13.2 suggests the signal is easy to exploit. The sound-event and audio-scene machinery of Chapter 33 is sitting unused here.
Online and streaming variants are absent. Both formulations are offline: OmniShotCut reads a 100-frame clip, Scene-VLM needs a right-context margin by construction. Live segmentation has to commit to boundaries without future evidence, and nothing in either literature addresses the resulting latency/accuracy trade-off.
One stage instead of two? The two-stage split is justified by cost, not by correctness, and the cost argument weakens as long-context video models improve. A model that reads a whole video and emits a semantic partition directly would avoid cascade error entirely. Nothing today comes close on either accuracy or cost, but this is the direction the cost curve points.
Synthetic supervision has a horizon. OmniShotCut’s own limitation section is honest: a parameterised synthesiser reproduces the transitions someone thought to parameterise. Elaborate cinematic transitions built from industry template libraries lie outside the generated distribution, and there is no obvious way to discover what is missing except by finding failures.

title: 13  Video Temporal Segmentation
text:
13.7 Summary
Temporal segmentation is where video understanding starts, and it splits cleanly into two problems that share a name and nothing else.
Shot detection is a signal-processing problem with a physically real ground truth. It has been essentially solved on legacy hard-cut benchmarks since the first 3D CNNs, and OmniShotCut’s contribution is to show that the metric which certified this — range F1 — was hiding the part that still fails. Once you ask where exactly a dissolve begins and what kind of discontinuity a boundary is, prior detectors score 0.18–0.25 transition IoU. The fixes are a richer output space (intra- and inter-shot relations), a formulation that exploits the problem’s structure (contiguous shots make queries intrinsically ordered, so no Hungarian matching; discrete frame indices instead of coordinate regression, so no thresholding), and supervision generated forward from editing operations rather than annotated backward from pixels, with the synthesiser’s marginal distribution treated as a first-class hyperparameter.
Scene detection is a narrative-understanding problem with a constructed ground truth, and it is not close to solved. A decade of encoder methods converged on point-wise classification of independent shots from visual-centric features; Scene-VLM’s gain comes from dropping both assumptions — autoregressive decoding makes each decision condition on the last, and multimodal input lets dialogue and character identity carry the three-quarters of the scene definition that pixels do not. Two engineering details generalise beyond this task: valid-padding in time (the context–focus window) is necessary whenever a sequence model emits predictions over a windowed input, and a generated token’s logit is informative only where the token sits at a genuine branch point in the output distribution.
The gap between F1 0.97 and F1 0.62 is the honest state of the field. Whether the second number is near a human ceiling nobody has measured, or whether it is genuine headroom, is the question the next benchmark should answer.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.1 Action Recognition Benchmarks
This is a companion chapter to Chapter 12. The benchmark survey lives here so that the main chapter can move quickly through architectures while still pointing to a definitive index of every evaluation set worth knowing about. The structure mirrors the task taxonomy of Section 12.2: one subsection per family of tasks, each with a few headline benchmarks expanded into fact blocks and the rest listed compactly.
Every benchmark below is written as a compact fact block with the same six fields so the section can be scanned at speed:
The oldest video task and still the default reported number for every encoder paper. The action-recognition benchmarks split into three flavours: large-scale clip classification (Kinetics family), motion- and interaction-heavy classification (SSv2, Diving48), and multi-label / spatio-temporal (Charades, AVA).

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
Kinetics-400 / -600 / -700 (Kay et al. 2017; Carreira et al. 2018, 2019) (2017–2019)

Domain: YouTube clips, third-person, single dominant human action.
Size & length: K400 ≈ 306K clips × 10 s ≈ 850 h, 400 classes; K600 ≈ 480K × 10 s, 600 classes; K700 ≈ 650K × 10 s, 700 classes.
Task: action recognition (clip classification).
Modalities: video (audio usually stripped).
Probes: generic action recognition at scale; the de facto pretraining benchmark for video encoders.
Importance: saturated on K400 (best encoders > 90 % top-1; VideoMAEv2 (L. Wang et al. 2023), InternVideo2 (Y. Wang et al. 2024)) but still the default reported number in every encoder paper. K700 is the harder, less-saturated current target. Metric: top-1 / top-5 accuracy.

Something-Something v2 (SSv2) (Goyal et al. 2017) (2017)

Domain: crowdsourced clips of someone manipulating an object on a tabletop, filmed against a plain background.
Size & length: ∼220K clips × 4 s, 174 fine-grained action classes (e.g. “pushing X from right to left”, “pretending to put X on Y”).
Task: action recognition, motion-heavy.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: temporal understanding — the same scene can yield different labels depending solely on the direction of motion, so a model that looks at one frame cannot win.
Importance: critical for any paper that wants to argue its model has temporal understanding (separates frame-bag classifiers from real video models). Metric: top-1 accuracy.

UCF-101 (Soomro et al. 2012) (2012)

Domain: sports + everyday action clips from YouTube.
Size & length: 13K clips × 7 s, 101 action classes.
Task: action recognition.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: historic ImageNet-of-video; 3-split protocol still used for tiny-data ablations and zero-shot transfer.
Importance: saturated (top-1 > 98 %); also widely used as an FVD reference for video generation. Metric: top-1 accuracy.

HMDB-51 (Kuehne et al. 2011) (2011)

Domain: movie clips + YouTube; 51 action classes.
Size & length: 7K clips × ∼4 s; 3 official train/test splits.
Task: action recognition.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: small-scale transfer; harder than UCF-101 due to cluttered scenes and inter-class similarity.
Importance: saturated; legacy benchmark; usually quoted as a triplet with UCF-101 and K400. Metric: top-1 accuracy across the three splits.

Moments in Time (MiT) (Monfort et al. 2019) (2019)

Domain: very short web clips spanning humans, animals, objects, weather, abstractions.
Size & length: ∼1M clips × 3 s, 339 classes; a multi-label extension (Multi-Moments) has ∼1M clips with 313 classes.
Task: action recognition (extremely short clips).
Modalities: video + audio.
Probes: generalisation across agents (not just humans) and very short events; large training scale.
Importance: standard as an auxiliary pretraining corpus, less common as a final eval. Metric: top-1 / top-5 accuracy.

Charades (Sigurdsson et al. 2016) (2016)

Domain: crowdsourced Hollywood-in-Homes — people perform scripted indoor activities.
Size & length: ∼10K untrimmed videos × ∼30 s, 157 daily-activity classes.
Task: multi-label action classification and temporal localization (multiple actions can overlap).
Modalities: video + audio.
Probes: dense multi-label classification under heavy overlap; activity recognition in unscripted-looking settings.
Importance: standard for multi-label classification and as the source of the Charades-STA grounding split. Metric: mAP (multi-label), mAP@IoU (localization).

AVA (Gu et al. 2018) (2018)

Domain: 15-min movie segments densely annotated.
Size & length: ∼430 movies, ∼1.6M actor-action labels at 1 Hz, 80 atomic action classes (e.g. stand, sit, hand-wave).
Task: spatio-temporal action detection — per-actor bounding box + action labels.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: combines detection (where) with action recognition (what) on long-form video.
Importance: critical and non-saturated for any model that claims spatial-temporal localisation; SlowFast (Feichtenhofer et al. 2019) and MViTv2 (Li et al. 2022) benchmark here. Metric: frame-level mAP @ spatial IoU 0.5.

Diving48 (Li et al. 2018) (2018)

Domain: competitive diving videos.
Size & length: ∼18K clips × ∼5 s, 48 fine-grained dive classes.
Task: action recognition, motion-only (background and equipment are uninformative).
Modalities: video only.
Probes: isolation of motion cues from scene/object bias — designed as a counter-example to Kinetics-style “context cheating”.
Importance: niche but the cleanest test that a model uses motion; pairs well with SSv2. Metric: top-1 accuracy.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.2 Long-Video Understanding Benchmarks
The 2023–2026 wave of benchmarks built specifically for video VLMs with minute- to hour-long inputs. All are MCQ-style by construction (so they can be auto-scored at the LLM-judge-free level of reliability) and all emphasise aggregation and narrative reasoning over per-frame perception.

LongVideoBench (LVB) (Wu et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: 3 763 web videos across multiple genres, paired with their original subtitles.
Size & length: 8 s – 1 h per video; 6 678 human-written MCQ questions over 17 fine-grained categories.
Task: long-video MCQ VQA with referring-query structure — every question explicitly cites a sub-window the answer is grounded in.
Modalities: video + subtitles.
Probes: memory and segment retrieval under interleaved video+text input; the referring clause forces the model to pick from many candidate windows.
Importance: critical — together with Video-MME the de facto pair every long-video VLM reports (Qwen2.5-VL, InternVL3, LLaVA-Video). Metric: MCQ accuracy, with separate splits by duration (8–15 s / 15–60 s / 3–10 min / 15–60 min).

Video-MME (Fu et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: 900 hand-picked YouTube videos spanning 6 high-level genres (knowledge, film/TV, sports, life, multilingual, artistic).
Size & length: ∼254 h total, durations from 11 s to ∼1 h split into short / medium / long sub-splits; 2 700 expert-written MCQs (3 per video × 4-way).
Task: general video MCQ VQA — the eval is also commonly reported in with-subtitles mode.
Modalities: video + subtitles + audio (some questions are answerable only from subtitles).
Probes: general video understanding across the full duration spectrum in one suite; the long sub-split (30 min – 1 h) is the de facto long-video number.
Importance: the most-reported video VLM benchmark of 2024–2026. Gemini 1.5 / 2.x, GPT-4o, Qwen2.5/3-VL, InternVL2.5/3, LLaVA-OneVision, Apollo, LongVU all report on it. Metric: MCQ accuracy, separately no-subs and w/ subs.

MLVU (Multi-task Long Video Understanding) (Zhou et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: very diverse — movies, surveillance, cartoons, games, egocentric, life vlogs, etc.
Size & length: ∼1 700 videos, 3 min – 2 h long; ∼3K questions across 9 sub-tasks (plot QA, action order, needle-in-haystack, sub-scene captioning, summarisation, …).
Task: MCQ VQA + open-ended captioning/summarisation — the only major long-video benchmark with non-MCQ sub-tasks.
Modalities: video only (no subtitles).
Probes: multi-task long-video understanding — exposes models that are tuned only for MCQ.
Importance: standard in 2025–2026 long-video papers; complementary to Video-MME because it has open-ended generation sub-tasks. Metric: MCQ acc for MCQ tasks; generation metrics (CIDEr / LLM-judge) for the open ones.

LVBench (W. Wang et al. 2024) (2024) — distinct from LongVideoBench above

Domain: publicly sourced long videos (TV episodes, sports, surveillance, …).
Size & length: ∼500 videos, mean ∼68 min, max several hours; ∼1.5K MCQs.
Task: long-video MCQ VQA, with a focus on hour-scale reasoning.
Modalities: video + subtitles.
Probes: the very long tail (> 30 min) where Video-MME has only ∼100 videos.
Importance: important for hour-scale specialists (LongVU, Video-XL-2, LongVA, LongVILA all report). Metric: MCQ accuracy.

EgoSchema (Mangalam et al. 2023) (2023)

Domain: egocentric (head-mounted camera) clips drawn from Ego4D.
Size & length: ∼5K MCQs over 3-minute clips, ∼250 h total.
Task: long-form egocentric MCQ VQA, 5-way.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: intrinsic temporal certificate — by design every question requires reasoning over the full 3 min (the certificate length is ∼10× prior egocentric benchmarks).
Importance: critical for any long-video or egocentric model (Gemini, Qwen2.5-VL, Apollo all report). Metric: 5-way MCQ accuracy; the subset split has 500 fully validated questions, the fullset has all 5K.

HourVideo (Chandrasegaran et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: 1-hour egocentric videos from Ego4D.
Size & length: 500 videos, mean ∼45 min, range 20–120 min; ∼13K MCQs.
Task: very-long-form MCQ VQA with task categories summarisation / perception / visual reasoning / navigation.
Modalities: video only (audio available).
Probes: hour-scale reasoning specifically, with a curated task taxonomy.
Importance: emerging — released late 2024, gaining traction in 2025–2026 long-video work. Metric: MCQ accuracy.

MomentSeeker (Hu et al. 2025) (2025)

Domain: long videos (mean 20 min) for video corpus moment retrieval (VCMR).
Size & length: 268 long videos, 1 800 multi-modal queries.
Task: locate a relevant temporal segment within a corpus of long videos (not a single video).
Modalities: video + audio + subtitles; multi-modal queries.
Probes: the corpus version of moment retrieval at long-video scale; needs efficient retrieval and fine grounding.
Importance: emerging — the de facto VCMR-at-scale benchmark for 2025–2026 retrieval research. Metric: R@1/R@5 at IoU.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
section: 14.3 General Video VQA and Reasoning Benchmarks
text:
14.3 General Video VQA and Reasoning Benchmarks
The workhorses for short / medium-clip evaluation. MVBench and the Video-MME short split are now the must-haves; the older ActivityNet-QA / MSRVTT-QA / MSVD-QA generation benchmarks are still reported but generally regarded as saturated and replaced by MCQ ones above.

MVBench (Li et al. 2024) (2024, introduced with VideoChat2)

Domain: clips reused from Charades, EPIC-Kitchens, SSv2, NTU RGB+D, Perception Test, FunQA, etc.
Size & length: ∼4K MCQ examples spanning 20 temporal-reasoning task types (action order, object existence, action prediction, scene transition, counterfactual, …); short clips (mostly < 30 s).
Task: MCQ VQA, temporal-reasoning-specific.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: designed so the answer cannot be inferred from a single frame nor from world knowledge alone — the 20 task categories are constructed to force inter-frame reasoning.
Importance: the canonical short-clip video VLM benchmark of 2024–2026. Every video VLM paper reports it. Metric: 4-way MCQ accuracy, with optional per-task breakdown.

TVBench (Cores et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: filtered subset of MVBench’s source clips with newly written questions.
Size & length: ∼2.5K MCQs over 10 temporal-skill categories.
Task: MCQ VQA, temporal-only.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: addresses a known weakness of MVBench — its questions are partly solvable from a single frame or from text alone. TVBench filters those out: most published 2024 video LMs score near chance at release.
Importance: standard, used alongside MVBench as a “true temporal” sanity check. Metric: MCQ accuracy.

TempCompass (Liu et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: ∼500 carefully edited videos (paired clips that differ only in their temporal dimension — direction, speed, order).
Size & length: ∼7K MCQs spanning action, direction, speed, event order, attribute change.
Task: MCQ VQA, temporal-only.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: controlled-pair tests for temporal sensitivity, with paired-video accuracy as an additional metric (model must answer both clips in a contrastive pair correctly to score 1).
Importance: standard for any paper making a temporal-reasoning claim (Qwen2.5-VL, Apollo, VideoLLaMA3 report). Metric: MCQ accuracy + paired accuracy.

Vinoground (J. Zhang et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: 1 000 short-clip pairs that differ only in their temporal counterfactual content (e.g. cause vs effect).
Size & length: ∼1K pairs × ∼5 s each.
Task: binary MCQ + dense temporal-counterfactual judgement.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: the temporal analogue of the Winoground image benchmark — counterfactual reasoning that requires distinguishing two near-identical clips.
Importance: emerging; the strongest published 2024 video LMs score below random on the paired metric. Metric: pair accuracy + group accuracy.

Perception Test (Patraucean et al. 2023) (2023)

Domain: scripted real-world “perception probes” filmed in lab settings — people manipulating objects, performing physical demos, illusions.
Size & length: 11 600 videos, ∼23 s each; densely annotated with 190K object tracks, 73.5K action segments, 137K sound segments, 38K MCQ-VQA + 6K grounded VQA.
Task: combined — VQA + temporal action localisation + object tracking + sound localisation + grounded VQA.
Modalities: video + audio + dense annotations.
Probes: a capability matrix — 4 reasoning skills (memory, abstraction, physics, semantics) × 4 reasoning types (descriptive, explanatory, predictive, counterfactual). Designed as a diagnostic, not a single number.
Importance: important multi-task diagnostic; widely reported in 2024–2026 video VLM papers (Qwen2.5-VL, Apollo, VideoLLaMA3). Metric: top-1 MCQ accuracy by default; per-skill breakdown.

MMBench-Video (Fang et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: ∼600 YouTube videos × 10 s – 6 min.
Size & length: ∼2K open-ended QAs across 26 fine-grained capability dimensions (counting, reasoning, OCR, captioning, …).
Task: open-ended VQA scored by LLM-as-judge (GPT-4 by default).
Modalities: video only.
Probes: capability-axis breakdown for VLMs, generation-style (vs MCQ).
Importance: standard for VLM papers that want a generation-style number alongside MCQ. Metric: LLM-judge score (0–3) averaged per dimension.

NeXT-QA (Xiao et al. 2021) (2021) and NeXT-GQA (Xiao et al. 2024) (2024)

Domain: ∼5.4K trimmed YouTube clips of daily-life activity.
Size & length: ∼44s avg; ∼52K MCQs in NeXT-QA covering causal, temporal, descriptive; NeXT-GQA adds temporal grounding annotations for 5.6K causal/temporal QAs.
Task: MCQ VQA (NeXT-QA) and grounded MCQ VQA (NeXT-GQA).
Modalities: video only.
Probes: causal and temporal reasoning specifically (NeXT-QA); whether MCQ accuracy is grounded in the actual evidence window (NeXT-GQA).
Importance: NeXT-QA standard; NeXT-GQA important and unique — it measures the grounding gap, the fraction of correct MCQs that are also temporally well-grounded. Metric: MCQ accuracy + IoU@0.5 grounding accuracy for NeXT-GQA.

STAR (Wu et al. 2021) (2021)

Domain: filtered Charades clips.
Size & length: ∼22K MCQs across interaction / sequence / prediction / feasibility situations.
Task: situated reasoning MCQ VQA, with object-relation graphs in the supervision.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: compositional and counterfactual reasoning, especially the feasibility and prediction questions which require physical-world common sense.
Importance: standard — frequently reported by VLM papers as an OOD reasoning test. Metric: MCQ accuracy per situation type.

AGQA / AGQA-Decomp (Grunde-McLaughlin et al. 2021) (2021)

Domain: Charades clips with auto-generated compositional questions.
Size & length: ∼9.6M compositional MCQs (filtered subsets of 192K and 3M widely used).
Task: compositional, multi-step VQA.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: compositional reasoning chains over object relations.
Importance: niche — auto-generated questions are sometimes noisy; cited mainly for compositional ablations. Metric: MCQ accuracy.

TVQA / TVQA+ (Lei et al. 2018, 2020a) (2018 / 2020)

Domain: clips from 6 popular TV shows (sitcom + medical + crime drama).
Size & length: ∼22K clips × 60–90 s; 152K MCQs; TVQA+ adds bounding boxes + frame indices for 29K of those.
Task: MCQ VQA (TVQA), grounded MCQ VQA (TVQA+).
Modalities: video + subtitles (subtitle text is often essential to answer).
Probes: dialogue-heavy reasoning where subtitles dominate.
Importance: standard for subtitle-aware VLMs; metric: MCQ accuracy.

ActivityNet-QA (Yu et al. 2019) (2019)

Domain: ActivityNet web videos.
Size & length: 5.8K videos × ∼2 min, 58K open-ended QAs.
Task: open-ended VQA (short answers, often single words).
Modalities: video only.
Probes: generic action-and-object questions over short web videos; the historical open-ended VQA baseline.
Importance: standard but declining — increasingly replaced by MCQ benchmarks. Metric: accuracy (exact match by GPT-judge), sometimes WUPS.

MSRVTT-QA / MSVD-QA (Xu et al. 2017) (2017)

Domain: MSR-VTT and MSVD web clips.
Size & length: MSRVTT-QA — 10K clips, 244K QAs; MSVD-QA — 1 970 clips, 50K QAs.
Task: open-ended VQA, short clips.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: very short web-video VQA; historical baseline.
Importance: deprecated for SOTA papers (saturated, single-frame solvable for most questions) but still reported as a sanity number. Metric: accuracy (GPT-judge or exact match).

VideoChatGPT-bench (VCG-Bench) (Maaz et al. 2024) (2023)

Domain: subset of ActivityNet videos.
Size & length: ∼3K open-ended QAs.
Task: generation-style VQA scored on 5 axes — correctness of information, detail orientation, contextual understanding, temporal understanding, consistency.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: dialogue quality of an end-to-end video chatbot.
Importance: standard in video-chat papers (VideoChat2, Video-LLaVA, LLaVA-Video). Metric: GPT-judge 1–5 scores per axis.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
section: 14.4 Temporal Grounding and Moment Retrieval Benchmarks
text:
14.4 Temporal Grounding and Moment Retrieval Benchmarks
Given a natural-language query, find when the described event occurs. The metric of choice is Recall@N at IoU \(\tau\) (see Equation 12.2).

Charades-STA (Gao et al. 2017) (2017)

Domain: indoor daily-activity videos from Charades.
Size & length: 9 848 videos × ∼30 s, ∼16K query–moment pairs.
Task: sentence-conditioned moment retrieval (Video Moment Retrieval / Temporal Moment Localization).
Modalities: video only.
Probes: mid-length indoor moment retrieval; the canonical introductory grounding benchmark.
Importance: standard — every temporal grounding paper reports it, though now considered too short and too easy to differentiate modern systems. Metric: R@1 and R@5 at IoU ∈ {0.3, 0.5, 0.7}; mIoU.

ActivityNet Captions (Krishna et al. 2017) (2017)

Domain: ActivityNet web videos.
Size & length: 20K videos × ∼2 min, ∼100K densely annotated event captions (∼3.6 captions per video).
Task: dense video captioning and (separately) sentence-conditioned moment retrieval.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: longer multi-event narratives; dense captioning evaluates event detection + captioning jointly.
Importance: critical for dense captioning, standard for grounding. Metric: dense — CIDEr / METEOR @ tIoU + SODA_c (Fujita et al. 2020); grounding — R@N IoU.

DiDeMo (Hendricks et al. 2017) (2017)

Domain: Flickr web clips, descriptive of everyday scenes.
Size & length: ∼10K untrimmed videos × ∼30 s, ∼41K query–moment pairs; moments are quantised to 5-s bins (a defining feature).
Task: sentence-conditioned moment retrieval.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: short-clip retrieval with discretised time — simpler metric than continuous IoU.
Importance: standard; metric: Recall@N over bins, plus mIoU.

QVHighlights (Lei et al. 2021) (2021)

Domain: ∼10K YouTube vlogs (lifestyle, news, travel) × ∼150 s.
Size & length: ∼10K queries with both moment annotations (1+ relevant segments per query) and saliency scores per 2-s clip.
Task: joint moment retrieval and highlight detection.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: the only widely used benchmark that scores moment retrieval and highlight ranking in the same dataset.
Importance: critical for temporal grounding papers since 2022 (Moment-DETR, QD-DETR, TimeChat). Metric: R@1 IoU={0.5, 0.7} + mAP for moments; mAP @ HIT@1 for highlights.

TACoS (Regneri et al. 2013) (2013)

Domain: cooking videos.
Size & length: 127 videos × ∼5 min, ∼17K query–moment pairs.
Task: moment retrieval, long-clip cooking domain.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: dense fine-grained step-level grounding within long cooking videos.
Importance: standard; metric: R@N IoU.

HiREST (Zala et al. 2023) (2023)

Domain: instructional YouTube videos.
Size & length: ∼3.4K videos × 0.5–8 min, multi-step retrieval annotations.
Task: hierarchical retrieval — moment retrieval and step segmentation and clip-level retrieval, evaluated jointly.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: hierarchical-task generalisation; multi-task evaluation.
Importance: emerging — used by long-video / instructional-video specialists. Metric: R@N for retrieval; step-level F1.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.5 Video Corpus Moment Retrieval (VCMR)
Strictly a generalisation of moment retrieval: the query is matched against all moments in all videos in a corpus rather than against moments in a single given video. The metric is the same (R@N IoU) but the corpus size makes retrieval indexing essential.

TVR (Lei et al. 2020b) (2020) — built from the TVQA TV-show corpus; ∼22K videos × 60–90 s, ∼109K query–moment annotations across visual + subtitle + audio modalities. Modalities: video + subtitles + audio. Probes: multi-modal moment retrieval; the standard VCMR benchmark since 2020.
MAD (Moment Anything Dataset) (Soldan et al. 2022) (2022) — ∼650 long movies × ∼110 min from the LSMDC source, ∼384K natural-language queries from movie audio descriptions. Probes: moment retrieval over a corpus of full-length movies, where most clips are far from any given query. Importance: the canonical long-video VCMR benchmark.
TVR-Ranking (Lei et al. 2020b) — a re-scored split of TVR that converts the original retrieval task into a ranking problem with relevance judgments, used for evaluating rerankers.
MomentSeeker (Hu et al. 2025) (2025) — see Section 14.2; the modern VCMR-at-scale benchmark.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.6 Captioning and Retrieval Benchmarks
The classical text↔︎video alignment benchmarks. Almost all of them sit between training corpus and test set — the same MSR-VTT collection appears as MSRVTT-QA above, as a retrieval test here, and as a generation test for video generators.

MSR-VTT (Xu et al. 2016) (2016)

Domain: YouTube clips from 20 categories (music, sports, news, …).
Size & length: 10K clips × 10–30 s, 20 captions per clip (200K captions).
Task: clip captioning + text↔︎video retrieval (canonical 1K-A / 1K-B test splits).
Modalities: video + audio.
Probes: general short-clip caption / retrieval; long-running leaderboard.
Importance: critical historical benchmark, still reported by every contrastive paper (CLIP4Clip (Luo et al. 2021), ViCLIP (Y. Wang et al. 2023), LanguageBind-Video (Zhu et al. 2023)). Metric: captioning — BLEU-4/METEOR/CIDEr; retrieval — R@1/5/10, median rank, mean rank.

VATEX (Wang et al. 2019) (2019)

Domain: Kinetics-600 clips re-captioned by humans.
Size & length: ∼41K clips × 10 s, ∼826K captions (10 EN + 10 ZH each).
Task: clip captioning + retrieval; explicitly multilingual.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: parallel EN/ZH evaluation; the standard multilingual video benchmark.
Importance: standard for multilingual evaluation; metric: same as MSR-VTT.

YouCook2 (Zhou et al. 2018) (2018)

Domain: instructional cooking videos from YouTube.
Size & length: 2K videos × ∼5.3 min, ∼14K step segments with captions.
Task: dense video captioning + step localisation + retrieval.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: instructional procedural understanding; pre-training signal for cooking-oriented models.
Importance: standard for instructional-video work (TimeChat (Ren et al. 2024), HiREST (Zala et al. 2023)). Metric: CIDEr / METEOR @ tIoU.

LSMDC (Rohrbach et al. 2017) (2017)

Domain: movie clips with audio-description tracks (subtitles for the blind).
Size & length: ∼118K clips × ∼5 s from 200 movies, 1 caption each.
Task: clip captioning, retrieval, and fill-in-the-blank.
Modalities: video + audio.
Probes: narrative-style descriptions; movie-domain bias.
Importance: standard but declining; metric: same as MSR-VTT.

MSVD (Chen and Dolan 2011) (2011)

Domain: very short YouTube clips of single events.
Size & length: 1 970 clips × ∼10 s, ∼80K captions.
Task: clip captioning + retrieval.
Modalities: video only.
Probes: simplest possible single-event captioning.
Importance: deprecated (saturated); metric: same as MSR-VTT.

DiDeMo (see Section 14.4) — also a standard retrieval benchmark in addition to its grounding role; 10K videos, 41K text–video pairs.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.7 Tracking, Detection and Segmentation Benchmarks
Closer to classic computer vision than to video VLMs, but worth listing because (i) representation models often pretrain on them and (ii) some VLM extensions (e.g. SAM-2, Mol-2Track) compete on them.

LaSOT (Fan et al. 2019) (2019) — single-object tracking; 1.4K sequences, mean 84 s; metric: AUC of success plot.
GOT-10k (Huang et al. 2019) (2019) — SOT with class-disjoint train/test (zero-shot tracking); 10K videos; metric: average overlap (AO).
TrackingNet (Müller et al. 2018) (2018) — SOT in the wild; 30K training + 511 test sequences; metric: AUC + precision.
MOT17 / MOT20 (Dendorfer et al. 2020) (2017 / 2020) — multi-object tracking; pedestrians; metric: HOTA (Luiten et al. 2021) + MOTA.
DanceTrack (Sun et al. 2022) (2022) — MOT for dancers (uniform appearance, complex motion); metric: HOTA + AssA — a particularly hard association benchmark.
DAVIS-2017 (Pont-Tuset et al. 2017) (2017) — semi-supervised VOS, ∼150 sequences × 4 s; metric: \(\mathcal{J} \& \mathcal{F}\).
YouTube-VOS (Xu et al. 2018) (2018) — semi-supervised VOS at scale; 4K videos; metric: \(\mathcal{J} \& \mathcal{F}\) split into seen and unseen classes.
MeViS (Ding et al. 2023) (2023) — motion-guided referring VOS; 2K videos, ∼28K motion-expression queries. Probes phrase-level grounding that requires temporal cues (e.g. “the bird that flies up”); a strong test for VLM-grounded segmenters. Metric: \(\mathcal{J} \& \mathcal{F}\).
V-HICO (Chao et al. 2020) (2020) — human-object interaction detection in video; 6K video segments, 244 verb categories. Probes spatio-temporal HOI specifically. Metric: mAP for interaction detection + temporal IoU.
DALY (Weinzaepfel et al. 2016) (2016) — Daily Action Localisation in Youtube; 510 untrimmed videos × ∼3 min, weakly supervised action localisation. Niche but instructive: weakly supervised setup mirrors what we have at web scale. Metric: video-mAP + frame-mAP.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.8 Egocentric Benchmarks
Distinct enough from the third-person setting that it warrants its own section. The dominant data source is Ego4D, and most egocentric papers report on its native task suite plus EgoSchema for long-form reasoning (see Section 14.2).

Ego4D (Grauman et al. 2022) (2022)

Domain: egocentric video from 9 countries, daily activities (cooking, crafts, sport, driving, …).
Size & length: ∼3 670 h across 931 unique camera-wearers, clips up to 10 h.
Task: a 5-benchmark suite — Episodic Memory, Hands-and-Objects, Audio-Visual Diarisation, Social, Forecasting (each with its own splits and metrics).
Modalities: video + audio + IMU + gaze + 3D scans (varies by clip).
Probes: generic egocentric understanding at unprecedented scale; the data source for most modern egocentric pretraining.
Importance: critical; metric: task-dependent (e.g. Natural Language Queries — R@1 IoU; Object State Change Classification — accuracy).

EPIC-Kitchens-100 (Damen et al. 2022) (2020)

Domain: egocentric kitchen activity (cooking sessions, single-person).
Size & length: 100 h, 90K narrated action segments, 97 verbs × 300 nouns.
Task: action recognition (verb / noun / verb+noun), action detection, action anticipation, retrieval.
Modalities: video + audio + narration.
Probes: fine-grained activity recognition in a constrained domain; strong hand-object interaction signal.
Importance: critical for any egocentric encoder (VideoMAE, V-JEPA2, InternVideo2 all report). Metric: top-1 / top-5 accuracy per axis.

Charades-Ego (Sigurdsson et al. 2018) (2018)

Domain: the same activities as Charades but filmed simultaneously from third-person and egocentric.
Size & length: ∼8K paired video pairs × ∼30 s.
Task: action recognition; the canonical dataset for studying third-person ↔︎ first-person transfer.
Modalities: video + audio.
Probes: view-invariance of learned representations.
Importance: niche but important; metric: mAP (multi-label) and view-invariance gap.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.9 Pretraining Corpora
Not test benchmarks — they have no canonical held-out split — but worth listing because almost every model in Section 12.3 cites at least one of them as training data. Quality and scale here dominate downstream benchmark scores.

HowTo100M (Miech et al. 2019) (2019) — 136M YouTube-clip / ASR-caption pairs from ∼1.2M instructional videos (∼23 years of video). Noisy by construction; the original “scale beats quality” pretraining corpus.
WebVid-10M (Bain et al. 2021) (2021) — 10M video-caption pairs scraped from a stock-footage site. Taken down in late 2024 after a copyright dispute; pre-2024 papers that cite it are increasingly unreproducible. The standard mid-scale captioned-video corpus 2021–2024.
VideoCC3M / VideoCC (Nagrani et al. 2022) (2022) — ∼10M auto-matched (CC3M-derived) caption / video clip pairs; cleaner alternative to HowTo100M.
InternVid / InternVid-10M-FLT (Y. Wang et al. 2023) (2024) — ∼7M videos × ∼234M re-captioned sentences (re-captioned with multimodal-LLM judges). The standard “modern” video-caption corpus, used by ViCLIP, InternVideo2, and many 2024–2026 VLMs.
Panda-70M (T.-S. Chen et al. 2024) (2024) — 70M video clips × ∼ 1 caption each; auto-captioned by an ensemble of VLMs and filtered. The largest open captioned-video corpus as of 2026.
HD-VG-130M / HD-VILA-100M (Xue et al. 2022) (2022) — 100M+ clips at HD resolution for video-language pretraining; useful for higher-resolution work.
VAST-27M (Chen et al. 2023) (2023) — 27M video clips with omni-modality captions (separate captions describing video, audio, subtitles) — designed for video-audio-language pretraining.
LLaVA-Video-178K (Y. Zhang et al. 2024) (2024) — 178K videos with synthetic dense captions + 1.3M QA pairs; the de facto SFT recipe for late-2024 / 2025 video VLMs (LLaVA-Video-7B, Apollo, VideoLLaMA3 all use it).
ShareGPT4Video (L. Chen et al. 2024) (2024) — 40K human + 4.8M GPT-4V detailed video captions; used widely as a quality signal on top of larger noisy corpora.

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.11 Choosing a Benchmark: Practical Recommendations
The benchmark choice is forced by two things — what task we want to prove and what budget we have. The recommendations below reflect a specific model trajectory: an autoregressive image-LM in the Molmo / Qwen2.5-VL line, first extended to video frames, later turned into a contrastive representation model via token-average + contrastive head.

Stage 1 — autoregressive image-LM extended to video
Five-benchmark suite, ordered by priority:

MVBench (Li et al. 2024). Short-clip MCQ over 20 temporal-reasoning task types. The fastest, cheapest test that proves the model has any temporal understanding above a frame-bag baseline. Run this first.
Video-MME (Fu et al. 2024) (full + short split). The de facto industry-standard video VLM benchmark; lets us position against Qwen2.5-VL / InternVL3 / LLaVA-OneVision on a single axis. Report both with-subtitles and no-subtitles.
TempCompass (Liu et al. 2024) (or TVBench (Cores et al. 2024)). A paired-clip test that catches the “looks at one frame and guesses” failure mode. Pick TempCompass for clarity, TVBench if we want to share an axis with VideoChat2 and Qwen2.5-VL.
Perception Test (Patraucean et al. 2023) (validation split, MCQ only). Diagnostic-style breakdown into Memory / Abstraction / Physics / Semantics × Descriptive / Explanatory / Predictive / Counterfactual; tells us where the model is weak.
LongVideoBench (Wu et al. 2024) (validation, MCQ only). Only if we have decided to invest in long-context training; otherwise expect near-chance on the > 15 min split. Defers to Video-MME-long if budget is tight.

What we are explicitly not running first:

No K400 / SSv2 — these are encoder benchmarks. We will get a number from K400 zero-shot if we ever turn the model into a representation model in Stage 2; otherwise it tells us very little about the autoregressive head.
No MSRVTT-QA / MSVD-QA — generation-style, saturated, and replaced by MCQ benchmarks above.
No ActivityNet-QA — same, with one exception: cite it once for continuity with the older video-chat lineage.



Stage 2 — representation model (token-average + contrastive head)
Five-benchmark suite for the contrastive variant:

Kinetics-400 zero-shot (Kay et al. 2017). The canonical zero-shot action-classification number. Compare to ViCLIP and InternVideo2.
MSR-VTT 1K-A retrieval (Xu et al. 2016). Both directions (text → video and video → text), R@1/5/10. The default retrieval leaderboard.
DiDeMo retrieval (Hendricks et al. 2017). Shorter clips, simpler IoU bins; pair with MSR-VTT.
Charades-STA moment retrieval (Gao et al. 2017) (if the representation supports temporal grounding via similarity-over-time). R@1 IoU={0.5, 0.7}.
SSv2 zero-shot or linear-probe (Goyal et al. 2017). The motion-heavy counterpoint to K400 — if a representation has not learned motion, this is where it shows. Skip if the model is purely frame-pooled (it will score at chance by design).

If we add a long-video retrieval/grounding axis later, the canonical pair is EgoSchema (long-form egocentric MCQ) and ActivityNet-Captions retrieval (medium-length narrated web). For corpus-scale moment retrieval, the canonical pair is TVR (short-form, multi-modal) and MAD (long-form movie).

title: 14  Video Understanding Benchmarks
text:
14.12 2026 Trends in Video Benchmarks
A compressed read of the field as the chapter is being written:

Saturated, still reported anyway: K400 (encoders > 90 % top-1), UCF-101, HMDB-51, MSVD-QA. These remain on every results table for continuity, but moving the needle on them no longer signifies a real capability gain.
The 2024–2026 short-clip de facto trio: MVBench + Video-MME + Perception Test. Almost every video VLM paper from 2025 onwards reports all three; if a benchmark is missing from a paper it is usually because the authors didn’t like the result.
Long-video has consolidated: LongVideoBench + Video-MME-long + MLVU form the de facto long-video trio. LVBench and HourVideo are the dataset-papers’ newer hour-scale tests, used mainly by long-video specialists.
The “true temporal” wave: TVBench, TempCompass, and Vinoground exist specifically because most 2023–2024 video VLMs can answer MVBench-style questions from a single frame or from world knowledge. Expect any 2026 paper that claims temporal understanding to report at least one of these.
Egocentric has its own axis: EgoSchema (long-form) + EPIC-Kitchens-100 (fine-grained) + Ego4D NLQ are the canonical trio; if a paper claims egocentric understanding it has to hit all three.
The grounded-MCQ frontier: NeXT-GQA’s grounding gap — the fraction of correct MCQs that are also temporally well-grounded — is the most informative single number for “does the model actually know when the answer is?”. The field is collectively bad at this and that is where the next gains will come from.
VCMR at scale: TVR remains the standard, but MAD and MomentSeeker have moved the frontier to long-form / multi-modal queries. Combined with the rise of LLM-based rerankers (UniME-V2 (Gu et al. 2025)), 2025–2026 sees retrieval pipelines become two-stage (coarse first-stage embedding retrieval → LLM cross-encoder reranker) rather than single-stage.
Pretraining-corpus shake-up: the take-down of WebVid-10M in 2024 forced a switch to InternVid / Panda-70M / LLaVA-Video-178K. Quality + re-captioning has displaced raw scale as the dominant axis; expect 2026 papers to spend pages on data composition rather than architecture.
What is not reported and probably should be: open-ended captioning under SODA_c (only ActivityNet-Captions and YouCook2 do this routinely); spatio-temporal grounding for VLMs (no good benchmark in 2026); fairness/cultural-coverage of egocentric data outside North America and Europe (Ego-Exo4D partially addresses this, an emerging story).

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.1 Diffusion Fundamentals
Video generation is a generalisation of image generation: a model samples a clip \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{T \times H \times W \times 3}\) from a distribution \(p_{\theta}(\mathbf{V} \mid \mathbf{c})\) conditioned on some control signal \(\mathbf{c}\) — most commonly a text prompt, but also an image (image-to-video), a previous clip (extension), a reference identity (subject-driven generation), or a structured pose / depth / camera trajectory (control-net style generation).
An image is the degenerate case \(T = 1\), so anything that works for image generation is a candidate for video. But the temporal axis adds two new requirements that change the engineering substantially:
The 2022–2026 landscape splits naturally along two axes:
This chapter follows that taxonomy. We first review the diffusion fundamentals (Section 15.1), then walk through the three families in order of increasing training cost (Section 15.2), discuss the orthogonal autoregressive line (Section 15.3), survey the closed-source flagships (Section 15.4) and the open-weights landscape (Section 15.5), and close with the evaluation question (Section 15.6).
Almost every video generator in this chapter is a diffusion model. This section recaps the minimum prerequisite vocabulary. Readers familiar with image diffusion can skim straight to Section 15.2.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.1.1 Denoising Diffusion
Diffusion models (Ho et al. 2020; Sohl-Dickstein et al. 2015) define a forward noising process that gradually turns a real sample \(\mathbf{x}_0\) into Gaussian noise \(\mathbf{x}_T \sim \mathcal{N}(0,
\mathbf{I})\) over \(T\) steps:
\[
q(\mathbf{x}_t \mid \mathbf{x}_{t-1}) =
\mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}_t; \sqrt{1 - \beta_t}\,\mathbf{x}_{t-1},
\beta_t\mathbf{I})
\tag{15.1}\]
with a variance schedule \(\{\beta_t\}_{t=1}^{T}\). The forward process has a closed-form marginal, \(\mathbf{x}_t = \sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_t}\,\mathbf{x}_0 +
\sqrt{1 - \bar{\alpha}_t}\,\boldsymbol{\epsilon}\) with \(\bar{\alpha}_t
\;=\; \prod_{s \leq t} (1 - \beta_s)\). A denoiser \(\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c})\) is trained to predict the noise added at step \(t\), optimising
\[
\mathcal{L}_{\text{simple}}(\theta) \;=\;
\mathbb{E}_{t, \mathbf{x}_0, \boldsymbol{\epsilon}}
\bigl[ \| \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, t, \mathbf{c}) -
\boldsymbol{\epsilon} \|_2^2 \bigr].
\tag{15.2}\]
Sampling reverses the chain: starting from \(\mathbf{x}_T \sim
\mathcal{N}(0, \mathbf{I})\) and iterating \(\mathbf{x}_t \to \mathbf{x}_{t-1}\) using the predicted noise. A 1000- step DDPM trajectory is wasteful; DDIM (Song et al. 2021) replaces it with a deterministic ODE solve and 20–50 steps are typical in 2024– 2026. Faster solvers (DPM-Solver-2 / 3, UniPC) push this to single digits.


Classifier-Free Guidance
Almost all video generators use classifier-free guidance (CFG) (Ho and Salimans 2021): train the denoiser jointly with conditional and unconditional inputs (drop the conditioning \(\mathbf{c}\) with probability ~10 %), then at sampling time blend them:
\[
\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{c}) \;=\;
\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \varnothing)
\;+\; w \bigl[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \mathbf{c})
- \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t, \varnothing)\bigr]
\tag{15.3}\]
with guidance scale \(w > 1\) (typically 4–7.5 for image, 6–9 for video). CFG is the lever that trades sample diversity for prompt fidelity.


Latent Diffusion
Running diffusion on raw pixels is prohibitively expensive for video. Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) (Rombach et al. 2022) compress \(\mathbf{x}\) to a low-dimensional latent \(\mathbf{z} = \mathcal{E}(\mathbf{x})\) via a frozen VAE, run diffusion in \(\mathbf{z}\)-space, and decode back at the end via \(\hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathcal{D}(\mathbf{z}_0)\). For video this matters even more: a 3D VAE (space + time, typically 8 × 8 × 4 compression — CogVideoX 1.5 uses 16 × 16 × 4, Sora uses an “undisclosed but aggressive” 3D VAE) reduces a 16 × 720 × 1280 × 3 clip to a 4 × 90 × 160 × 16 latent — a 24× memory saving.


Text Conditioning
Text prompts enter the denoiser via cross-attention from a frozen language encoder. The three dominant choices in 2024–2026:

CLIP-text (OpenAI / OpenCLIP) — fast, strong on short prompts, weak on compositional language. The default for the Stable Diffusion 1.x / 2.x line.
T5-XXL / Flan-T5-XXL (Raffel et al. 2020) — the heavyweight in Imagen, Imagen Video, DeepFloyd-IF, Sora, and CogVideoX. Excellent at long prompts and compositions, expensive to run.
LLM-as-text-encoder — direct hidden states from a Llama-3-class LLM, often distilled into a smaller adapter. Used by HunyuanVideo and several 2025 open-weights models; trades T5’s robustness for better instruction-following.



Denoiser architectures: U-Net vs DiT
For image diffusion, the original choice was a U-Net with cross- attention to text (Ronneberger et al. 2015; Rombach et al. 2022). Peebles & Xie (Peebles and Xie 2023) showed that a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) — a plain transformer over a tokenised latent grid — scales better and beats the U-Net once data and compute are abundant. The video field has followed the same trajectory:

2022–2023 video models (VDM, Make-a-Video, Video LDM, Stable Video Diffusion) used U-Net + factorised space-time attention or 3D convolutions.
2024 onwards (Sora, CogVideoX, Mochi-1, HunyuanVideo, Wan-2.1, LTX-Video, Open-Sora-Plan) uses DiT-style transformers over a 3D-VAE latent.

The DiT wins for the same reason it does in image generation: a plain transformer scales cleanly, parameter-shares across all spatial and temporal positions, and benefits from every infrastructure improvement made for LLMs (FlashAttention, pipeline parallelism, sequence parallelism, etc.).

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.2 Three Families of Video Generation
The video-diffusion approaches of 2022–2026 fall into three families distinguished by how much video training they do.

15.2.1 Family 1 — Train from Scratch on Video
The cleanest baseline: train a denoiser on video data only, with no image pretraining. Used by the biggest closed flagships (Sora) and by recent open-weights efforts that have the compute (CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo). The early open-academic example is VDM.

Video Diffusion Models (VDM, 2022)
VDM (Ho, Salimans, et al. 2022) (Ho et al., 2022) introduced the modern video-diffusion template. The denoiser is a 3D U-Net factorised over space and time:

Each spatial 2D convolution is extended to a “space-only 3D convolution” with kernel size \((1, 3, 3)\) — only the spatial axes see the kernel; frames are processed independently.
Each spatial self-attention layer is left as is, but with the frames axis treated as a batch dimension.
After every spatial self-attention block, a temporal attention block is inserted, with the spatial axes folded into the batch dimension. The temporal positional embedding is a relative one (no absolute notion of time, so the model works across arbitrary clip lengths).

This factorised design — spatial blocks operating on frames in parallel, temporal blocks acting only across time — became the canonical pattern. Almost every video diffusion model of 2022–2024 inherits it; the DiT variants of 2024–2026 generalise it with a single transformer that attends across (t, h, w) jointly but still often uses block-sparse masks that recover the factorised form for compute efficiency.


Imagen Video (2022)
Imagen Video (Ho, Chan, et al. 2022) (Google, 2022) tackled the resolution problem: generating long, high-resolution videos directly is too expensive, so use a cascade of seven diffusion models that progressively refine spatial and temporal resolution:

A base diffusion model produces a low-resolution, short clip (40 × 24 × 24, 16 frames at ~3 FPS).
Three spatial super-resolution (SSR) models progressively upscale: 24×24 → 80×80 → 240×240 → 720×720.
Three temporal super-resolution (TSR) models interpolate in time: 16 frames → 32 → 64 → 128 frames (≈5 s at 24 FPS).

Each stage is conditioned on T5-XXL text embeddings and on the output of the previous stage. The base model is a 3D-conv U-Net with spatio-temporal self-attention; the upsamplers use cheaper alternatives — temporal convolutions instead of attention (linear in frames, not quadratic) and no spatial attention at the highest resolution (where it would dominate compute). The result was the first text-to-video model widely regarded as “production quality” by the standards of 2022, and it set the cascade template that Sora later inherited.


Sora (2024)
Sora (OpenAI 2024) (OpenAI, Feb 2024) is the headline closed-flagship that made transformer-based video generation mainstream. Two architectural breaks with the 2022 line:

DiT denoiser. Replace the 3D U-Net with a plain transformer.
3D space-time patches. Instead of 2D patches from a single image, Sora extracts \(p_t \times p_h \times p_w\) spacetime patches (e.g. \(2 \times 16 \times 16\) pixels) from the 3D-VAE-compressed latent. Each patch becomes a token; the transformer applies self- attention across all spacetime tokens to model spatial and temporal dependencies jointly (rather than via the factorised pattern of VDM/Imagen Video).

The conditioning stack is standard — cross-attention from a T5-XXL text encoder, with classifier-free guidance for sampling. The training data and exact 3D-VAE design are not disclosed, but the inferred recipe is: a high-compression-ratio 3D VAE (likely \(8 \times 8 \times 4\) or finer), a billion-parameter DiT, and multi-aspect-ratio / multi-duration training so the same model serves 5-second portrait clips and 60-second landscape clips. Sora 2 (2024) and the disclosed Wan, HunyuanVideo, Mochi, CogVideoX designs follow the same pattern with smaller, public weights.


CogVideoX / CogVideoX 1.5 (Tsinghua + Zhipu AI, 2024)
CogVideoX (Yang et al. 2024) (Aug 2024, 1.5 released Nov 2024) is the canonical open-weights train-from-scratch video DiT. Three contributions:

3D-VAE with \(4 \times 8 \times 8\) compression (1.5 raised this to \(4 \times 16 \times 16\)).
Expert Adaptive Layer Normalisation. Conditioning signals (timestep, text) modulate the transformer through dedicated AdaLN “experts” rather than via cross-attention. This was influential — many 2024–2026 video DiTs followed.
Multi-resolution / multi-duration training with bucketing, similar to Sora’s inferred recipe but disclosed.

CogVideoX-5B (5 B-parameter DiT) and 1.5-5B are the most-used open references for academic comparisons in 2025–2026.



15.2.2 Family 2 — Fine-tune a Pretrained Image Model
The pragmatic majority of 2022–2024 work. Start from a strong image diffusion model (Stable Diffusion 1.5 / 2.1, eDiff-I, IF) and add temporal layers. Often only the new temporal layers are trained, with the image weights kept frozen — this is cheap, the image model has already learned visual priors, and the resulting generator inherits the image model’s compositional strength.

Make-A-Video (2022)
Make-A-Video (Singer et al. 2022) (Meta, Sep 2022) — the first widely cited example. Composition of three modules:

A pretrained text-to-image diffusion model (eDiff-I-class).
A spatiotemporal super-resolution model that upgrades the image generator to a video generator by adding (2+1)D layers:

(2+1)D convolutions: each pretrained 2D conv is followed by a new 1D temporal conv, initialised to the identity. The 2D conv first generates a stack of frames in parallel; the 1D conv smooths across time.
(2+1)D attention: each spatial attention layer is followed by a new temporal attention layer that attends only across frames at each spatial position.

A frame interpolation network that increases frame rate.

Only the new temporal modules are trained; the image weights stay frozen, so the model inherits Make-a-Scene-class image quality at roughly the training cost of a temporal-only model. The (2+1)D factorisation became standard for years.


Video LDM / Align-Your-Latents (2023)
Align-Your-Latents (Blattmann, Rombach, et al. 2023) (Blattmann et al., 2023, NVIDIA / LMU Munich) — the canonical latent variant of the Make-A-Video idea. Build on a Stable-Diffusion-style LDM:

Insert temporal layers (3D convolutions + temporal attention) between the frozen spatial layers of the image LDM.
Train only the temporal layers with the spatial LDM weights frozen.
Use a personalised decoder: the original LDM decoder produces flickering artefacts when frames are decoded independently, so a video-aware decoder is fine-tuned — temporal layers are added, spatial encoder weights are kept frozen, and the decoder is trained jointly with a reconstruction loss and a GAN-style 3D-conv patch discriminator that distinguishes real from generated video clips.

Video LDM is the template for Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) (Blattmann, Dockhorn, et al. 2023) (Stability AI, Nov 2023), the most-downloaded open-weights video model of 2023–2024. SVD trains the SD-2.1 U-Net with added temporal layers on a curated 5-million-clip subset of the LVD corpus and produces 14- or 25-frame 1024 × 576 clips. It is the default image-to-video baseline in most 2024 papers.



15.2.3 Family 3 — Train-Free Adaptation
Inference-time tricks that produce video from a pretrained image diffusion model with no weight updates. Cheap, fast, sufficient for short demos, but lacking the realism of trained models. Useful mainly as a baseline and for one-off effects.

Text2Video-Zero (2023)
Text2Video-Zero (Khachatryan et al. 2023) (Picsart AI Research, Mar 2023) — the reference train-free method. Two tricks:

Camera-motion noise initialisation. Start with one random latent \(\mathbf{z}_T\). Run a single DDIM backward step to denoise it slightly. Apply a sequence of translations to the resulting latent (simulating a panning camera). Then take a DDPM forward step to obtain a sequence of noised latents, each related to the first by a known linear shift in latent space. This injects coherent inter-frame motion at the noise level.
Cross-frame attention. Reprogram the U-Net’s self-attention so that each frame’s queries cross-attend (using the image model’s pretrained Q, K, V matrices) to the first frame’s keys and values. The first frame thus acts as an anchor for object identity and background.

The result is short, somewhat coherent video from a frozen image diffusion model. Not competitive with trained models on benchmarks, but a useful diagnostic — when an image diffusion model produces better short clips with these tricks than a poorly-trained video diffusion model produces with full training, the latter has something wrong.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.3 Autoregressive Video Generation
Orthogonal to the diffusion line is the autoregressive (AR) approach: tokenise video into a sequence of discrete codes and predict the next code. Two variants:

Discrete VAE / VQ-VAE tokenisation (Oord et al. 2017; Esser et al. 2021; P. Sun et al. 2024). A VQ-VAE maps each clip to a sequence of integer codes from a fixed codebook (e.g. 16 384 entries). A transformer is trained with a next-token-prediction loss on these codes; sampling decodes from codes back to pixels. The original VQ-VAE-based video generators (Video VQ-VAE, NUWA-XL) date to 2021–2022; the more capable modern examples are below.
Continuous AR with a diffusion head (Li et al. 2024; Tian et al. 2024). Predict the parameters of the next frame’s distribution autoregressively, but parameterise that distribution as a small diffusion model. Hybrid; recent and less proven for video specifically.

The autoregressive line is appealing for two reasons:

Token interface unification with LLMs. A video tokeniser turns video into the same token stream as text, so a single transformer can read a video and write a video — exactly the understanding + generation unification that Janus-Pro pursued in



Inherits LLM infrastructure. Speculative decoding, prefix caching, FlashAttention, pipeline parallelism — every win the LLM community gets transfers for free.

The headline open-source examples:

VideoPoet (Kondratyuk et al. 2024) (Google, Dec 2023). The first large-scale (~8B-param) autoregressive video LM. Predicts a unified stream of image tokens + audio tokens + text tokens, enabling text-to-video, image-to-video, video stylisation, and audio-to-video in a single model. Uses MAGVIT-v2 (Yu et al. 2023) as the video tokeniser, which crucially improved tokeniser quality to the point AR video matched diffusion on FVD.
LlamaGen (P. Sun et al. 2024) (ByteDance, Jun 2024). Image-only but architecturally the cleanest demonstration: a vanilla LLaMA transformer with a high-quality VQ tokeniser produces images at Stable-Diffusion quality. The video extension is implicit in the Janus-Pro line — Janus-Pro (Chen et al. 2025) uses the same VQ tokeniser approach for image generation, embedded in a unified understanding/generation transformer (see 1).
MAGI-1, Cosmos-1 (NVIDIA, late 2024) — recent autoregressive video models for world simulation; smaller community footprint than the diffusion line but increasingly relevant for robotics and embodied AI.

As of mid-2026 the diffusion-DiT line is still ahead on raw video quality (Sora, Veo 3, CogVideoX 1.5), but the AR + diffusion-head hybrids are closing the gap, and the unification argument keeps this line architecturally alive.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.4 Closed-Source Flagships
Brief mentions to anchor the architecture discussion in the public state of the art. None of these have full disclosed weights but most have technical reports.

Sora / Sora 2 (OpenAI 2024) (OpenAI). The reference text-to-video DiT, 1080p, up to ~1 minute. Sora 2 (Sep 2024) adds synchronised audio generation and improved long-clip coherence.
Veo / Veo 2 / Veo 3 (Google DeepMind 2024) (Google DeepMind). 4K-capable, 8-second prompts with strong physics. Veo 3 (May 2025) added native audio (dialogue, sound effects) at video-generation time and now matches or exceeds Sora 2 on most evaluation axes.
Movie Gen (Polyak et al. 2024) (Meta, Oct 2024). 30B-parameter text-to-video DiT trained on a curated 100M-video corpus; also generates synced audio and allows video editing (text-guided edits to a given clip).
Genie / Genie 2 / Genie 3 (Bruce et al. 2024) (Google DeepMind). Action-conditioned world model — given an image, the model generates playable video where the user can control the agent. Conceptually distinct from the text-to-video flagships above — more an interactive world simulator than a film generator.
Runway Gen-3 / Gen-4, Pika 2.0, Luma Dream Machine (2024–2025). Commercial generators with strong consumer features (motion brushes, style transfer, character LoRAs) and undisclosed architectural details.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.5 Open-Source Landscape (2024–2026)
The open-weights line has been moving extremely fast since CogVideoX. The current shortlist, all DiT-based unless noted:

CogVideoX-2B / 5B / CogVideoX 1.5-5B (Yang et al. 2024) (Aug 2024 → Nov 2024) — see Section 15.2.1. 5 B-param DiT, Apache-2.0; the academic baseline.
Mochi 1 (Genmo AI 2024) (Genmo, Oct 2024) — 10 B-param DiT with asymmetric attention (text tokens get cheaper attention); Apache-2.0. Strong on motion realism.
HunyuanVideo (Kong et al. 2024) (Tencent, Dec 2024) — 13 B-param DiT with a dual-stream attention layout (image tokens and text tokens are processed in parallel then fused); Apache-2.0. The first open model to challenge closed-source quality in side-by-side preference tests.
Wan 2.1 / Wan 2.2 (Wan Team, Alibaba 2025) (Alibaba, Feb 2025 / Jul 2025) — 14 B-param DiT with high-compression 3D VAE; Apache-2.0. Multilingual prompts (English + Chinese) work natively.
LTX-Video (HaCohen et al. 2024) (Lightricks, Nov 2024) — 2 B- param DiT optimised for speed: produces 5-second 768×512 clips in 4 seconds on an H100. Trades quality for inference latency in the same way SDXL Turbo did for images.
Open-Sora / Open-Sora-Plan (Zheng et al. 2024; Lin et al. 2024) (PKU + HuaWei + community, 2024–2025) — community reimplementations of the inferred Sora recipe. Useful for ablations and for understanding what a high-quality DiT pipeline looks like end-to-end; not yet competitive with the curated commercial models.
Stable Video Diffusion (SVD) / SVD-XT / Stable Video 4D (Blattmann, Dockhorn, et al. 2023) (Stability AI, 2023–2024) — the U-Net line. SVD-XT generates 25-frame clips; Stable Video 4D adds multi-view generation (4 views × 8 frames). Still widely used for image-to-video where the input is a still image.

The convergence in 2025–2026 is striking: every open generator uses a DiT with a 3D-VAE latent, T5-XXL or LLM text conditioning, and trains on a filtered re-captioned video corpus (closely mirroring the data evolution of Section 14.9 in Chapter 14). The differences sit in (i) parameter count, (ii) attention layout (joint vs dual-stream), (iii) precise VAE compression ratio, and (iv) inference-time tricks (Mochi’s asymmetric attention, LTX’s speed-optimised solver).

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.6 Evaluation
Video generation evaluation is in a much worse state than video understanding evaluation, because there is no single “correct” output. The 2024–2026 reporting suite is:

Distributional metrics

Fréchet Video Distance (FVD) (Unterthiner et al. 2018) (2018). The video analogue of FID: compute I3D features for real and generated clips, fit Gaussians, measure 2-Wasserstein distance between them. Reported on UCF-101 and MSR-VTT. Strong correlation with human preference for content quality, weak correlation with temporal consistency.
Inception Score (IS) / Kinetics-FID / CLIP-FID — variants on the FID theme with different feature extractors. Less common in 2024–2026.

FVD has known issues — sensitive to clip length, frame rate, and the choice of I3D checkpoint — but it is the only reported number for nearly every paper, so it persists.


Compositional / dimension-decomposed metrics

VBench / VBench++ (Huang et al. 2023) (2024). The dominant evaluation suite for 2024–2026 generation papers. Breaks down generation quality into 16 dimensions — subject consistency, background consistency, temporal flickering, motion smoothness, dynamic degree, aesthetic quality, imaging quality, object class, multiple objects, human action, colour, spatial relationship, scene, appearance style, temporal style, overall consistency — each scored by a small dedicated evaluator (CLIP, ViCLIP, MUSIQ, RAFT, ViT-based classifiers). The headline number is a weighted mean; the per- dimension breakdown lets papers argue about which aspect their model is good at.
EvalCrafter (Liu et al. 2023) (2024). A similar dimension-decomposed benchmark with ~700 prompts × 17 metrics. Often reported alongside VBench.
VideoScore (He et al. 2024) (2024). A learned LLM-based evaluator trained on human preference data; emerging as a single- number sanity check.



Human preference
Side-by-side preference tests against a strong baseline (typically Sora, Veo, or CogVideoX-5B). Almost every 2025–2026 paper reports this in addition to FVD + VBench, because the automatic metrics still fail to discriminate among the top open models. The standard protocol: 50–100 prompts × 3–5 raters, blinded A/B comparison, report win rate.


Prompt sets
The standard ones:

VBench prompts (~950 prompts across the 16 dimensions).
EvalCrafter prompts (~700 prompts).
T2V-CompBench (K. Sun et al. 2024) — adversarial compositional prompts (e.g. “a red cube on top of a blue cylinder, rotating while a yellow ball orbits”); designed to expose compositional failures that pretty pictures hide.



Recommendations
For a 2026 video-generation paper:

FVD on UCF-101 + MSR-VTT — legacy but expected.
VBench (full 16 dimensions + headline mean) — the de facto 2024–2026 default.
A human-preference A/B against a flagship — Sora 2, Veo 3, or CogVideoX 1.5-5B depending on what is fair (closed vs open weights).
Sanity check on a compositional prompt set (T2V-CompBench or one of the VBench compositional sub-axes) — to confirm the model has not collapsed to “pretty but wrong”.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.7 Open Problems and Future Directions
Brief, because the chapter is intentionally short.

Long-form video. Most open models cap out at 5–10 seconds. Sora showed 1 min, Veo 3 nominally supports 8 s, Movie Gen ~16 s — but coherent narrative over a minute is still rare. The open frontier is autoregressive chunked generation (generate \(k\) seconds, condition the next chunk on the last) vs one-shot long-context DiTs.
Controllability. Text alone is a weak control signal for video. Pose / depth / camera-trajectory control (Video-ControlNet, CameraCtrl), reference-image identity preservation, and structured edits (Movie Gen’s text-guided editing) are active research lines.
Physics. Top-of-leaderboard models still produce subtle physics violations (objects passing through each other, gravity glitches, fluid dynamics implausibilities). The 2025–2026 wave of world model generators (Genie 3, Cosmos) explicitly trades generality for physical plausibility.
Audio. Veo 3 and Movie Gen generate synced audio; Sora 2 does not yet. Joint video+audio generation is the most likely next flagship axis — the model needs to know which sound goes with which visible event.
Evaluation honesty. VBench is increasingly gameable — papers optimise for high VBench scores rather than for human preference. The community is working on more adversarial prompt sets (T2V-CompBench, Movie Gen Bench) but no clean replacement exists yet.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.8 Summary
Video generation in 2024–2026 has converged on a tight stack: a 3D-VAE that compresses pixels to a low-dimensional latent, a Diffusion Transformer (DiT) that denoises that latent, and a T5-XXL or LLM text encoder that injects prompts via cross-attention. Within that stack, three families differ in how much video training they do — train from scratch (Sora, CogVideoX, HunyuanVideo), fine-tune from an image model (Make-a-Video, Stable Video Diffusion), or adapt for free (Text2Video-Zero) — but the architecture is increasingly the same. The autoregressive line (VideoPoet, Janus-Pro, MAGI/Cosmos) is the credible orthogonal alternative, especially for unified understanding+generation models.
Compared with video understanding (Chapter 12), the generation field is roughly 18 months behind on data quality and benchmark consolidation. There is no MVBench-equivalent for generation in 2026 — VBench is closest, but every paper has its own headline number and human preference is still the ground truth. As the infrastructure and data converge, expect the next two years to look much like the understanding side did in 2024: rapid architectural convergence, a stable evaluation suite, and a sharper focus on the remaining hard axes — long form, controllability, physics, and honest evaluation.

title: 15  Video Generation
text:
15.9 Interview Questions
Q: What is the core architectural difference between Sora/CogVideoX and earlier video diffusion models like VDM or Imagen Video?
VDM and Imagen Video use a U-Net denoiser with 3D convolutions and factorized spatiotemporal attention — spatial and temporal processing are largely separate operations. Sora and CogVideoX replace the U-Net with a Diffusion Transformer (DiT), tokenizing the video into 3D spacetime patches and applying full self-attention jointly across all spatial and temporal positions. This lets the same architecture handle variable-length, variable-resolution video (and degenerate to image generation at \(T=1\)), and benefits from transformer scaling laws — at the cost of higher per-step compute than the factorized U-Net pattern.

Q: Describe how Make-a-Video generates video without training a video diffusion model from scratch.
Make-a-Video inserts (2D+1) convolutional and attention layers into a pretrained text-to-image diffusion model: each 2D conv is followed by a temporal 1D conv initialized to the identity, and each spatial attention layer is followed by a temporal attention layer. The image weights stay frozen (or lightly fine-tuned); only the new temporal layers are trained on video data. Because the temporal layers initialize as identity functions, the model initially behaves exactly like the image model on individual frames — a stable starting point that preserves image generation quality while learning motion cheaply.

Q: Why does almost every video generator use a 3D VAE rather than the 2D VAE from image diffusion?
A 2D VAE compresses each frame independently, so a video tensor is still \(T\) times larger than a single image latent — the dominant cost for video diffusion. A 3D VAE compresses space and time jointly (e.g. \(8{\times}8{\times}4\)), giving an additional ~4× reduction along the temporal axis on top of the spatial compression. This is what makes it feasible to run a transformer or U-Net over the latent at all; without it, even a modest 16-frame clip would have a sequence length 16× larger than the equivalent image.

Q: VBench reports 16 separate dimensions instead of one number. Why, and what’s the risk?
Video quality is multi-axis: a model can have excellent per-frame aesthetics but flicker badly (low temporal consistency), or move very little because static frames score well on most metrics (low “dynamic degree”). A single averaged score hides these trade-offs and can be gamed — e.g., a model that barely moves scores well on subject/background consistency. The 16-dimension breakdown lets a paper show which axis it improves, but the flip side is that papers increasingly optimize directly for VBench sub-scores rather than for human preference, which is why human A/B testing remains mandatory alongside it.

Q: Compare the autoregressive and diffusion approaches to video generation. Why might unification with LLMs matter beyond raw quality?
Diffusion generates a clip by iterative denoising of a continuous (or VAE) latent and currently leads on raw visual quality (Sora, Veo 3, CogVideoX 1.5). Autoregressive generation tokenizes video into discrete VQ codes and predicts them one at a time, like text — currently behind on quality but improving rapidly with better tokenizers (MAGVIT-v2). The unification argument is architectural: an AR video model uses the same token interface as an LLM, so a single transformer can both understand video (read tokens, write text — Chapter 11) and generate it (read text, write tokens), and inherits every LLM-serving optimization (speculative decoding, KV-cache reuse, prefix sharing) for free. This is why Janus-Pro and the broader “unified” model line bet on AR despite the current quality gap.

Q: How does classifier-free guidance behave differently for video versus image generation?
CFG blends conditional and unconditional denoiser outputs, \(\hat{\boldsymbol{\epsilon}} = \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing) + w[\boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\mathbf{c}) - \boldsymbol{\epsilon}_\theta(\mathbf{x}_t,\varnothing)]\), trading diversity for prompt fidelity. For video, the practical guidance scale is typically higher (6–9 vs. 4–7.5 for images) because the temporal-consistency requirement makes under-conditioned samples noticeably worse — a video that drifts off-prompt over time looks like a different video halfway through, which is far more jarring than a single off-prompt image. Over-guidance also has a video-specific failure mode: oversaturated, low-motion (“frozen”) clips, since high guidance pushes toward the conditional mode at the expense of the diversity that produces natural motion.

title: 3D Data
text:
Overview
2D images are projections of a 3D world. Recovering that third dimension—and building models that reason natively in 3D—is central to robotics, autonomous driving, augmented reality, and a growing share of computer vision research. This part covers the geometry, representations, and learning algorithms needed to work with 3D data.
Chapter Scope:
Interview Relevance: 3D understanding is central to roles at Waymo, Tesla, and Aurora (autonomous driving), Meta Reality Labs and Apple (AR/VR and spatial computing), Boston Dynamics and Figure (robotics), and Stability AI (3D generative models). Expect questions on camera projection, the NeRF-vs-Gaussian trade-off, and how to handle the permutation invariance of point clouds.
Prerequisites: Part II (CNNs, Vision Transformers). Familiarity with linear algebra (matrix decompositions, homogeneous coordinates), and 2D convolution.

title: 3D Data
text:
3D Scene Representations (§11.1): Point clouds, voxels, meshes, and implicit surfaces
Camera Geometry (§11.2): Intrinsics, extrinsics, and the perspective projection pipeline
3D Reconstruction (§11.3): Structure-from-Motion, Neural Radiance Fields, and 3D Gaussian Splatting
Point Cloud Learning (§11.4): PointNet and PointNet++ for unordered 3D sets
Human Pose Estimation (§11.5): 2D and 3D joint localization and body model fitting

title: 16  3D Data Understanding
text:
16.1 3D Scene Representations
A 3D scene can be represented in several fundamentally different ways. The choice of representation determines which operations are efficient, what inductive biases are present, and how the representation interacts with deep learning pipelines.
Point Cloud: An unordered set of 3D points \(\mathcal{P} = \{(\mathbf{x}_i, \mathbf{f}_i)\}_{i=1}^N\) where \(\mathbf{x}_i \in \mathbb{R}^3\) is a spatial coordinate and \(\mathbf{f}_i\) is an optional per-point feature (e.g. color, normal). Point clouds are the native output of LiDAR sensors and multi-view stereo. They are memory-efficient and geometrically faithful, but unstructured—standard convolutions do not apply directly.
Voxel Grid: A regular 3D grid \(\mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times H \times W \times C}\) with \(C\) features per cell. Enables direct application of 3D convolutions. The \(O(D^3)\) memory cost makes high-resolution grids prohibitive; sparse voxel representations (SparseConvNet, MinkowskiNet) address this by storing only occupied cells.
Mesh: A surface represented by vertices \(V \subset \mathbb{R}^3\) and faces \(F \subseteq V^3\) (typically triangles). Compact and artist-friendly; standard in rendering pipelines. Difficult to interface with gradient-based learning due to the combinatorial topology.
Implicit Surface: A scalar field \(f_\theta : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}\) whose zero-level set defines the surface. Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and occupancy networks are the most common variants. Resolution-free and differentiable; surfaces are extracted at inference via marching cubes.
Neural Radiance Field / 3D Gaussian: Continuous volumetric representations that encode both geometry and appearance; covered in detail in Chapter 12.
Interview Insight: “Why not just use voxels for everything?” Voxel resolution scales cubically — a \(512^3\) grid at float32 requires 512 MB for geometry alone, before any features. Point clouds and implicit representations are the practical answer for high-resolution 3D.
