Going from full fine-tuning to LoRA removes the gradient and optimizer-state memory for the base model (~650 GB saved) by training only the small adapters; going from LoRA to QLoRA further shrinks the dominant remaining cost — the frozen base weights — via 4-bit quantization. The net effect: a 65B model becomes fine-tunable on a single consumer/prosumer GPU (e.g., a 48 GB card) rather than requiring a multi-node cluster — a major driver of open-source LLM fine-tuning accessibility.

title: 22  Large Language Models
text:
22.9 Tool Use and Applications
Several frameworks extend an LLM’s capabilities by interleaving generation with external tool calls:

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG): given a prompt, retrieve relevant documents from an external database (e.g., via embedding similarity search, Section 23.1) and prepend them to the prompt before the LLM generates its answer — grounding generation in up-to-date or proprietary information without retraining.
Program-Aided Language Models (PAL): the model generates code (e.g., Python) representing the reasoning/computation needed to answer the prompt; the code is executed by an interpreter, and the result is fed back to the model to produce the final answer — offloading arithmetic/logical steps the model itself performs unreliably.
ReAct (Reasoning and Acting): the model interleaves free-text reasoning traces with discrete actions (e.g., Search[entity], Lookup[string], Finish[answer]), observing the result of each action before deciding the next reasoning step or action — repeating until a final answer is produced.

title: 22  Large Language Models
text:
22.10 Ethical Concerns

Toxicity: mitigated through careful training-data curation, dedicated guardrail/classifier models that filter generated text, and diverse human annotator pools (to avoid encoding a narrow set of cultural norms as “safe”).
Hallucination: mitigated by grounding generation in independent, verifiable sources (e.g., RAG) rather than relying solely on parametric knowledge.
Intellectual property / privacy: addressed via machine unlearning (removing the influence of specific training examples post-hoc) and filtering/blocking approaches at both training-data and generation time.

title: 22  Large Language Models
text:
22.11 Interview Questions
Q: Why does RoPE generalize better to longer sequences than learned absolute positional embeddings?
Absolute positional embeddings assign a distinct, independently-learned vector to each position index — positions beyond the maximum seen in training have no learned embedding at all. RoPE instead encodes position as a rotation applied to query/key vectors, and the attention dot product \(\langle R_m q, R_n k\rangle\) depends only on the relative offset \(m-n\) via the rotation’s algebraic structure — a property that holds for any \(m,n\), including offsets larger than those seen during training, giving at least some degree of length extrapolation “for free.”

Q: What’s the difference between MHA, MQA, and GQA, and why does it matter for serving?
All three differ only in how many distinct \((K,V)\) projection pairs exist relative to the number of query heads \(h\): MHA uses \(h\) (one per head), MQA uses \(1\) (all heads share), and GQA uses \(g\) with \(1 < g < h\) (groups of heads share). This directly scales the KV-cache size (the dominant inference memory cost at long contexts/large batches) by a factor of \(h/g\). MQA/GQA trade a small amount of quality for a large reduction in memory bandwidth and footprint during generation — critical for serving long-context models at scale.

Q: Walk through the LoRA forward pass and explain why \(B\) is initialized to zero.
LoRA replaces \(h = W_0 x\) with \(h = W_0 x + BA x\), where \(W_0\) is frozen and only \(A \in \mathbb{R}^{r\times k}\), \(B \in \mathbb{R}^{d\times r}\) are trained, with \(r \ll d,k\). Initializing \(B = 0\) (with \(A\) initialized randomly, e.g., Gaussian) ensures \(\Delta W = BA = 0\) at the start of training, so the adapted model is identical to the pre-trained model before any fine-tuning steps — training starts from a known-good point and gradually learns a low-rank perturbation, rather than starting from a randomly perturbed (and likely worse) model.

Q: How does DPO avoid training a separate reward model, and what does it give up compared to PPO-based RLHF?
DPO derives a closed-form expression for the optimal RLHF policy as a function of the reward, then substitutes this back into the Bradley-Terry preference model — the reward terms cancel into log-probability ratios between the policy and a frozen reference model. The result is a simple binary classification loss directly on the policy’s log-probabilities of preferred vs. dispreferred completions, with \(\beta\) playing the role of the RLHF KL-penalty coefficient. What’s given up: DPO is trained on a fixed, offline preference dataset sampled from \(\pi_{\text{ref}}\), whereas PPO-based RLHF can sample new completions from the current policy during training (online), potentially exploring regions of output space the offline dataset doesn’t cover.

Q: Why is QLoRA able to fine-tune a 65B model on a single GPU when full fine-tuning needs ~780 GB?
Full fine-tuning’s memory is dominated by gradients and Adam optimizer states for all 65B parameters (24 bytes/param total). LoRA already removes most of this by freezing the base model and training only ~0.1% of parameters as low-rank adapters — but the frozen 16-bit base weights (130 GB) still dominate. QLoRA additionally stores those frozen weights in 4-bit NF4 (~33 GB), since they’re never updated and don’t need gradient/optimizer storage — only the small adapter matrices need full-precision gradients and Adam states. The combination removes both major cost drivers: optimizer states (via freezing) and base-weight precision (via quantization), leaving a total in the tens of GB.

title: 23  Text Embedding Models & Evaluation
text:
23.1 Text Embedding Models
Many NLP tasks — semantic search, clustering, deduplication, named entity linking, retrieval-augmented generation (Section 22.7) — require a fixed-size semantic representation of a document, sentence, or token, such that semantically similar texts map to nearby vectors. This chapter covers how such embedding (representation) models are built and trained, and how language models and embeddings are evaluated.
The dominant paradigm for training embedding models is contrastive learning (Part: Self-Supervised Learning): pull together the representations of positive pairs (e.g., a sentence and its paraphrase, or a query and a relevant document), and push apart the representations of negative pairs (unrelated texts).

title: 23  Text Embedding Models & Evaluation
text:
23.1.1 Cross-Encoder
The most direct way to score a pair of sentences with a pre-trained Transformer (e.g., BERT) is to concatenate them and pass the pair jointly through the model, with a classification head on top:






Figure 23.1: A cross-encoder concatenates sentence A and sentence B as a single input to a shared encoder (e.g., BERT), with a classifier head producing a similarity/relevance score.



This is accurate (the model can attend jointly across both sentences) but has two major drawbacks:

No standalone sentence embeddings — the model only produces a pairwise score, not a vector representation of either sentence in isolation.
Quadratic inference cost for retrieval/clustering: finding the most similar pair among \(n\) sentences requires \(\binom{n}{2}\) forward passes through the full encoder — for \(n=10{,}000\), that’s ~50 million forward passes, intractable for real-time search.



23.1.2 Bi-Encoder
A bi-encoder instead encodes each sentence independently (with shared weights) and pools the token embeddings (e.g., mean pooling) into a single sentence vector, comparing two sentence vectors via cosine similarity:






Figure 23.2: A bi-encoder independently encodes sentence A and sentence B, pools each into a fixed-size vector, and compares the two vectors with cosine similarity.



\[\text{sim}(u,v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}\]
Because each sentence’s embedding is computed independently of any other, embeddings for an entire corpus can be precomputed once and indexed (e.g., with approximate nearest-neighbor search) — retrieval then costs one forward pass for the query plus a fast vector lookup, not \(O(n^2)\) encoder passes.
Training losses:
Pairwise MSE loss — given a labeled similarity score \(y_i \in [0,1]\) for sentence pair \(i\), regress the cosine similarity toward it:
\[\mathcal{L}_{\text{MSE}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left(\text{sim}(u_i, v_i) - y_i\right)^2\]
This works but is sensitive to class imbalance between positive and negative pairs — and labeled positive pairs are typically much scarcer than negatives.
InfoNCE loss (preferred in practice) — for an anchor \(u_i\) with positive \(v_{i^+}\) and a batch of \(M\) candidates (the positive plus in-batch negatives):
\[\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{InfoNCE}} = -\log \frac{\exp(\text{sim}(u_i, v_{i^+})/\tau)}{\sum_{j=1}^{M} \exp(\text{sim}(u_i, v_j)/\tau)}}\]
where \(\tau > 0\) is a temperature that sharpens (small \(\tau\)) or smooths (large \(\tau\)) the distribution over candidates. The denominator sums over all candidates in the batch (including the positive itself), so this is effectively an \(M\)-way classification: “pick out the true positive among \(M\) candidates.”
Negative mining: the choice of negatives strongly affects what the model learns:

Easy negatives: other (unrelated) sentences randomly sampled from the batch — trivial to distinguish, weak training signal once the model is reasonably good.
Semi-hard negatives: sentences identified as topically related (but not equivalent) by another embedding model — harder to distinguish, stronger signal.
Hard negatives: explicitly labeled contradicting/related sentence pairs from human annotation — the strongest (and most expensive) signal.

Labeled data sources: natural language inference (NLI) datasets provide sentence pairs labeled as entailment (same meaning), contradiction, or neutral (neither implies the other). Entailment pairs become positives; contradiction and neutral pairs become negatives. These datasets are high-quality but small.


23.1.3 Training Methods

Domain-adaptive MLM: before contrastive fine-tuning, continue pre-training (masked language modeling) on an in-domain corpus — adapts the base encoder’s vocabulary and representations to the target domain (e.g., legal, biomedical text) without requiring any labeled pairs.
Supervised — SBERT (Sentence-BERT): fine-tune a bi-encoder on labeled sentence pairs (e.g., NLI data) with the losses above — the canonical approach when sufficient labeled pairs exist.
Semi-supervised — Augmented SBERT: labeled (“gold”) pairs are scarce, but a cross-encoder (accurate but too slow for retrieval) can be trained on them; use that cross-encoder to label additional unlabeled pairs (“silver” data), then train a bi-encoder (SBERT) on the combined gold + silver dataset — distilling the cross-encoder’s accuracy into a fast bi-encoder.
Unsupervised — TSDAE (Transformer-based Sequential Denoising Auto-Encoder): corrupt input sentences (e.g., randomly delete/shuffle tokens), encode the corrupted sentence into a single vector with the bi-encoder, and train a decoder to reconstruct the original sentence from that vector — requires no labels, and the resulting encoder produces useful sentence embeddings.
LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): a classical (non-neural) topic-modeling baseline — represents a document collection as mixtures over latent topics, where each topic is itself a distribution over words, with both distributions governed by Dirichlet priors. Useful as a cheap, interpretable baseline for document representation/clustering.

title: 23  Text Embedding Models & Evaluation
text:
23.2 Evaluation

23.2.1 Metrics
These metrics compare model outputs for a given task (e.g., two summarization models) — they are not meaningful for comparing models across different tasks.
ROUGE (Recall-Oriented Understudy for Gisting Evaluation) — for a generated text and a reference text:

ROUGE-N Recall \(= \dfrac{\#\text{overlapping } n\text{-grams}}{\#\,n\text{-grams in reference}}\), ROUGE-N Precision \(= \dfrac{\#\text{overlapping } n\text{-grams}}{\#\,n\text{-grams in generated}}\), ROUGE-N F1 \(= \dfrac{2PR}{P+R}\).
ROUGE-L replaces \(n\)-gram overlap with the Longest Common Subsequence (LCS) between generated and reference text: Recall \(=\frac{\text{LCS}}{\#\text{unigrams in reference}}\), Precision \(=\frac{\text{LCS}}{\#\text{unigrams in generated}}\), F1 the harmonic mean of the two.

BLEU (Bilingual Evaluation Understudy) — BLEU-N is the precision of \(n\)-grams (with clipping, so a generated \(n\)-gram can’t be “matched” more times than it appears in the reference); the overall BLEU score is (a brevity-penalized) combination of BLEU-1 through BLEU-4.
Perplexity — the exponentiated cross-entropy between the true data distribution and the model’s predictions:
\[\boxed{\text{PPL}(W) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \log P(w_i \mid w_{<i})\right)}\]
Intuitively, perplexity is the (geometric-mean) effective branching factor of the model’s predictive distribution — “the number of equally-likely word choices the model is choosing among at each step.” A perplexity of 1 is a perfect (deterministic) model; a perplexity equal to the vocabulary size corresponds to a uniform-random model.


23.2.2 Benchmarks
Benchmarks aggregate many tasks into a single suite, enabling comparison across models (and, to a degree, across task types):

GLUE (General Language Understanding Evaluation, 2018) — a suite of sentence- and sentence-pair classification tasks.
SuperGLUE (2019) — a harder successor to GLUE, with tasks requiring more reasoning.
MMLU (Massive Multitask Language Understanding, 2021) — multiple-choice questions across 57 academic/professional subjects, evaluated zero/few-shot.
BIG-bench (2022) — a large, crowd-sourced collection of tasks (with “BIG-bench Lite” and “BIG-bench Hard” subsets) probing capabilities expected to emerge at scale.
HELM (Holistic Evaluation of Language Models, 2022) — evaluates models across accuracy, calibration, robustness, fairness, bias, toxicity, and efficiency simultaneously, rather than accuracy alone.
TOFU (Task of Fictitious Unlearning, 2024) — benchmarks machine unlearning: how completely can a model be made to “forget” specific training examples (e.g., for privacy/IP compliance, Section 22.7) without degrading general performance.

Interview Insight: Single-number leaderboards (e.g., aggregate MMLU score) are convenient but lossy — a model’s rank can vary substantially across HELM’s individual axes (accuracy vs. robustness vs. toxicity), and benchmarks saturate or leak into training data over time (motivating newer, harder, or more holistic suites like BIG-bench Hard and HELM). When asked to evaluate or compare LLMs, anchor the discussion to which capability a benchmark actually measures, not just its headline number.

title: 23  Text Embedding Models & Evaluation
text:
23.3 Interview Questions
Q: Why is a bi-encoder preferred over a cross-encoder for large-scale semantic search, despite being less accurate per-pair?
A cross-encoder requires both texts as joint input, so comparing a query against \(n\) candidates costs \(n\) full forward passes (and comparing all pairs in a corpus costs \(O(n^2)\)) — infeasible beyond small \(n\). A bi-encoder encodes each text independently into a fixed vector; corpus embeddings can be precomputed and indexed once, reducing query-time cost to one encoder pass plus an approximate nearest-neighbor lookup, which scales to millions of documents. In practice, a common pattern is to use a bi-encoder for fast first-stage retrieval and a cross-encoder to re-rank only the top-\(k\) candidates — combining bi-encoder scalability with cross-encoder accuracy.

Q: Why is InfoNCE generally preferred over pairwise MSE for training sentence embeddings?
Pairwise MSE regresses the cosine similarity directly toward a target label, which requires reliable similarity scores and is sensitive to the (typically severe) imbalance between abundant negative pairs and scarce labeled positive pairs. InfoNCE instead frames training as in-batch classification — given an anchor and its positive among \(M\) in-batch candidates (mostly negatives), maximize the softmax probability assigned to the positive. This only requires knowing which pairs are positive (not a calibrated similarity score), naturally leverages many negatives per positive from within a batch, and the temperature \(\tau\) gives direct control over how sharply the model is pushed to separate positives from negatives.

Q: What is Augmented SBERT, and what problem does it solve?
Labeled sentence-pair data (e.g., from NLI datasets) is accurate but scarce, while a cross-encoder trained on that scarce data is accurate but too slow for retrieval. Augmented SBERT uses the cross-encoder as a labeling function for a much larger pool of unlabeled pairs (producing “silver” labels), then trains a bi-encoder (SBERT) on the combination of gold (human-labeled) and silver (cross-encoder-labeled) pairs. This is effectively knowledge distillation from an accurate-but-slow cross-encoder into a fast bi-encoder, while also addressing the small-labeled-data problem.

Q: Why can’t ROUGE/BLEU scores be used to compare models across different tasks, but MMLU can?
ROUGE and BLEU measure \(n\)-gram (or LCS) overlap between a generated output and a task-specific reference — their absolute values depend heavily on the nature of the reference texts for that task (e.g., summarization references vs. translation references have very different length and vocabulary distributions), so a ROUGE score of 0.4 on one task is not comparable to 0.4 on another. MMLU (and similar benchmarks) instead measure accuracy on a fixed, multiple-choice format spanning many subjects — the metric (accuracy) has the same meaning and scale regardless of subject, making aggregate scores meaningfully comparable across models and (within MMLU) across subject areas.

Q: What does perplexity actually measure, and what’s a key limitation of using it to compare models?
Perplexity is \(\exp\) of the average negative log-likelihood the model assigns to held-out text — equivalently, the effective number of equally-likely choices the model is “choosing between” at each token, on average. Lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the true continuation. The key limitation: perplexity is only comparable between models that share the same tokenizer/vocabulary — a model with a coarser tokenization (fewer, longer tokens) will tend to have higher per-token perplexity than one with finer tokenization, even if both predict the underlying text equally well, since the “difficulty” of each prediction step differs.

title: Vision-Language
text:
Overview
Vision-language (VL) models learn joint representations of images and text, enabling tasks that require reasoning across both modalities: retrieval, captioning, visual question answering, grounding, and text-to-image generation. This chapter covers how VL models are architected (modality fusion strategies), how they are pre-trained (contrastive, masked-token, and generative objectives), the major model families built on each objective, and how pre-trained VL models are adapted to downstream tasks.
Chapter Scope:
Interview Relevance: Vision-language modeling is central to roles at OpenAI (GPT-4V, DALL-E), Google DeepMind (Gemini, PaLI), Meta (Flamingo, LLaVA-style assistants), and any team building retrieval, captioning, or multimodal assistant products. Expect questions on CLIP’s contrastive objective and its variants (SigLIP, FILIP), the trade-offs between fusion strategies, how Q-Former / Perceiver Resampler connect frozen vision encoders to frozen LLMs, and emergent capabilities of large multimodal models.
Prerequisites: Part II (CNNs, Vision Transformers), Part III (Self-Supervised Learning — contrastive learning foundations). Familiarity with the Transformer attention mechanism and autoregressive language modeling.

title: Vision-Language
text:
Vision-Language Tasks and Pre-Training (§16.1–16.2): task taxonomy, modality fusion architectures, and pre-training objectives
Models (§16.3): CLIP/ALIGN, SigLIP, BEiT-3, and Large Multimodal Models (GIT, BLIP-2, Flamingo, LLaVA)
Transfer Learning and Knowledge Distillation (§16.4–16.5): adapting pre-trained VL models to downstream tasks
Vision Foundation Models (§16.7): unifying vision tasks via free-text outputs and visual prompting

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
text:
24.1 Modalities and the Vision-Language Setting
Modality: two data sources correspond to different modalities if the representation of at least one cannot be mapped unambiguously into the other — a pixel grid and a token sequence encode fundamentally different information and cannot be losslessly converted into each other.
Vision-Language (VL) modeling learns statistical patterns relating image and text data. Modern VL models are pre-trained on large image-text datasets via a general pretext task, then adapted to downstream tasks of interest via transfer learning or knowledge distillation.

24.1.2 Task Examples
The same generic architecture — a visual encoder \(h(\cdot)\), a language encoder \(g(\cdot)\), and a combination function \(f(\cdot)\) — instantiates each task below by varying the inputs and output of \(f(\cdot)\).









Figure 24.1: Text-to-Image Retrieval: \(f(\cdot)\) outputs an image-caption similarity score.

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
text:
24.2 Pre-Training






Figure 24.12: Overview: VL model pre-training (contrastive, generative, and alignment objectives), transfer learning (prompt tuning, feature adaptation), and knowledge distillation to task-specific architectures.



Two challenges dominate VL pre-training:

Data Alignment: learning the semantic correspondence between the two modalities.
Complexity: the computational cost of training and serving a large multimodal model.

VL models differ primarily along two axes: architecture (how the modalities are fused) and pre-training objective (what signal drives the alignment).

24.2.1 Architecture: Modality Fusion






Figure 24.13: The three modality-fusion architectures: (a) Two-Tower / Late Fusion, (b) Two-Leg / Intermediate Fusion, (c) One-Tower / Early Fusion.











Fusion
Description
Examples




Late Fusion (Two-Tower)
Two independent encoders process each modality separately; outputs combined only via a similarity score (e.g. dot product)
CLIP, ALIGN


Intermediate Fusion (Two-Leg / Cross-Attention)
Two separate networks, connected by cross-attention layers between modalities
Flamingo, BLIP-2


Early Fusion (Single-Tower / Self-Attention)
A single encoder embeds both modalities into a shared token sequence, processed by joint self-attention
BEiT-3, VisualBERT



Interview Insight: “Which fusion strategy for retrieval vs. reasoning?” Late fusion is the only architecture that scales to retrieval over millions of images — embeddings are pre-computed once and compared via a single dot product at query time. Early and intermediate fusion enable much richer cross-modal reasoning (needed for VQA, captioning, grounding) but require a full forward pass through the joint model for every query, making them unsuitable for large-scale retrieval.


24.2.2 Pre-Training Objectives

Contrastive Learning: distinguish a matched (image, caption) pair from mismatched pairs.
Masked Token Learning: predict masked input tokens (image patches and/or text tokens) from the unmasked context.
Generative Learning: autoregressive next-token prediction on the language output, conditioned on the image via cross-attention.

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
text:
24.3 Models

24.3.1 A. Contrastive Learning Objective

24.3.1.1 CLIP / ALIGN (2021)
Architecture: dual encoder — a Transformer text encoder and a ResNet or ViT image encoder, projecting both modalities into a shared embedding space.
Training: given a batch of \(N\) (image, caption) pairs, encode each into normalized embeddings \(\mathbf{v}_i, \mathbf{t}_i\) and minimize the symmetric InfoNCE loss over the \(N \times N\) similarity matrix \(S_{ij} = \mathbf{v}_i^\top \mathbf{t}_j / \tau\): \[\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{CLIP}} = \frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^N \left[-\log\frac{\exp(S_{ii})}{\sum_{j=1}^N \exp(S_{ij})} -\log\frac{\exp(S_{ii})}{\sum_{j=1}^N \exp(S_{ji})}\right]}\] where \(\tau\) is a learnable temperature. The two terms are the image→text and text→image classification losses: each image must pick out its matching caption among the \(N\) in the batch, and vice versa.






Figure 24.14: CLIP training: the \(N \times N\) matrix of cosine similarities between image and text embeddings; the diagonal entries are the positive pairs.



Inference: for zero-shot classification, encode each class label as a text prompt (e.g. “a photo of a {class}”) and assign the image to the class whose text embedding has the highest cosine similarity with the image embedding.






Figure 24.15: CLIP zero-shot inference: class names are embedded as “a photo of a {object}” prompts, and the image is assigned to the class with the highest image-text similarity.



Scaling: data size, batch size, and model size all improve accuracy — larger batches give a harder contrastive task (more negatives per positive), which is one reason CLIP-style training benefits disproportionately from scale.






Figure 24.16: CLIP’s contrastive “bag of words” objective reaches a given zero-shot ImageNet accuracy with far fewer images processed than a transformer language-modeling objective.



Interview Insight: “Why does CLIP need such large batch sizes?” Every other sample in the batch serves as a negative for the contrastive loss. Small batches give few, easy negatives — the model can satisfy the loss without learning fine-grained distinctions. Large batches (32k+ in the original CLIP) make the discrimination task hard enough to drive useful representation learning.


24.3.1.2 Improvements Combining CLIP with Other Objectives

FLIP (2022): randomly drops a large fraction of image patches before encoding, reducing compute and acting as data augmentation — the efficiency gains can be reinvested as accuracy gains at a fixed compute budget.
CoCa (2022): trains a single model with both a contrastive loss (image-text matching) and a captioning (generative) loss, unifying the two paradigms.
Florence (2021): a unified image representation pre-trained with a contrastive objective, transferable across classification, retrieval, detection, and captioning.
DeCLIP (2022): supplements the contrastive signal with self-supervision (image-image, text-text) and nearest-neighbor supervision, improving data efficiency.
FILIP (2021) — fine-grained alignment between image patches and text tokens. Given \(N\) image patch embeddings \(\{\mathbf{v}_k\}\) and \(M\) text token embeddings \(\{\mathbf{t}_r\}\), the image-text similarity is the average, over image patches, of the maximum similarity to any text token: \[\text{sim}(\mathbf{V}, \mathbf{T}) = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^N \max_{r=1,\ldots,M} \mathbf{v}_k^\top \mathbf{t}_r\] This token-level max-similarity replaces the single global cosine similarity in the InfoNCE loss, giving a much finer-grained training signal than CLIP’s pooled embeddings.







Figure 24.17: FILIP’s cross-modal late interaction (left) computes token-wise image-to-text and text-to-image similarities. The token-level attention maps (right) localize which image patches each word attends to — much sharper than CLIP’s global similarity.





24.3.1.3 SigLIP (Sigmoid Loss for Language-Image Pre-training, 2023)
SigLIP keeps CLIP’s dual-encoder architecture but replaces the softmax-based InfoNCE loss with a pairwise sigmoid loss. Each (image, text) pair in the batch is treated as an independent binary classification — match or non-match — rather than a multi-way classification over the batch: \[\boxed{\mathcal{L}_{\text{SigLIP}} = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{j=1}^N \log\sigma\!\left(z_{ij}\,(t\,\mathbf{v}_i^\top\mathbf{t}_j + b)\right)}, \qquad z_{ij} = \begin{cases} +1 & i = j \\ -1 & i \neq j \end{cases}\] where \(t\) is a learnable temperature, \(b\) a learnable bias, and \(\sigma\) the sigmoid function.






Figure 24.18: CLIP’s softmax loss normalizes over all \(N\) pairs in each row/column of the similarity matrix; SigLIP’s sigmoid loss treats every \((i,j)\) pair as an independent binary classification.



Why it matters:

SigLIP outperforms CLIP at small batch sizes — the per-pair loss doesn’t degrade when there are fewer negatives.
SigLIP is more memory-efficient at very large batch sizes, because the sigmoid loss decomposes over individual \((i,j)\) pairs — no global softmax normalization (and the associated cross-device all-gather of the full similarity matrix) is required.







Figure 24.19: Zero-shot ImageNet accuracy vs. batch size: the sigmoid loss matches or exceeds the softmax loss across the range, with its advantage most visible at small batch sizes.





24.3.1.4 SigLIP2 (2025)






Figure 24.20: SigLIP2 architecture: alongside the sigmoid image-text matching loss (SigLIP v1), an EMA teacher provides self-distillation/masked-prediction targets (SILC/TIPS), and an autoregressive decoder adds a captioning loss (LocCa).



SigLIP2 combines SigLIP’s sigmoid image-text matching objective with auxiliary self-supervised losses that improve un-pooled (per-patch) image features:








Auxiliary Objective
Type of Loss
Primary Benefit




Captioning-based Pretraining (LocCa)
Image-to-Text, Region-to-Text
Localization — image captioning, referring expression prediction, and grounded captioning force the vision encoder to be location-aware


Self-Distillation (Global-Local)
Self-Supervised
Dense feature semantics — a student matches a teacher’s full-image representation from local crops, encouraging consistent local-to-global features


Masked Prediction
Self-Supervised
Richer per-patch representations — the student predicts teacher features of masked patches







24.3.2 B. Masked Token Learning Objective

24.3.2.1 BEiT / BEiT-2 / BEiT-3 (2021–2023)
Pre-training task: BEiT-3 extends BERT-style masked modeling to image tokens, text tokens, and image-text pairs in a unified manner — randomly masking 15% of tokens in unimodal text, 50% of tokens in text paired with images, and 40% of image patches (block-wise masking, as in BEiT).
Model: a Multiway Transformer — shared self-attention modules followed by three modality-specific feed-forward “experts” (vision, language, vision-language), allowing a single backbone to specialize per modality while sharing the attention computation.






Figure 24.21: BEiT-3’s Multiway Transformer: images, text, and image-text pairs share a multi-head self-attention module, then route through modality-specific feed-forward “experts” (V-FFN, L-FFN, VL-FFN).



Data: ~21M image-text pairs for multimodal pre-training, plus 14M unimodal images (ImageNet-21K) and 160GB of text corpora (Wikipedia, BookCorpus, OpenWebText, CC-News, Stories).
Advantage over contrastive pre-training: masked-token pre-training requires a much smaller batch size. BEiT-3 uses batches of 6,144 samples total (2,048 images + 2,048 texts + 2,048 image-text pairs) — orders of magnitude smaller than the 32k+ batches needed for contrastive learning, because the loss is computed per-token rather than relying on in-batch negatives.




24.3.3 C. Generative Objective and Large Multimodal Models (LMMs)
The generative objective is an autoregressive loss on the language output, with the image injected via cross-attention from text tokens to image features: \[\mathcal{L}_{\text{gen}} = -\sum_{l=1}^{L} \log p_\theta(y_l \mid y_{<l}, \mathbf{X}_{\text{img}})\]






Figure 24.22: The language model predicts each next token from the visual tokens and all preceding text tokens; the causal attention mask (right) allows every token to attend to the visual tokens but only to earlier text tokens.



This objective underlies most modern Large Multimodal Models (LMMs), which connect a pre-trained vision encoder to a pre-trained (often frozen) LLM via a lightweight connection module.






Figure 24.23: The generic LMM stack: a (frozen) vision encoder, a trainable connection module, and a (frozen) language model.













GIT (2022)
BLIP-2 (2023)
Flamingo (2022)




Language Model
From scratch
Frozen: FLAN-T5 / OPT
Frozen: 70B Chinchilla


Connection Module
—
Q-Former (trained)
Perceiver Resampler + gated cross-attention (trained)


Vision Encoder
Pre-trained: Florence/CLIP
Frozen: EVA/CLIP
Frozen: NFNet (CLIP-like)









Figure 24.24: GIT: image features from a pre-trained image encoder are prepended to the text embeddings, and a Transformer text decoder autoregressively generates the output text.



Q-Former (BLIP-2) — a trainable module connecting a frozen image encoder to a frozen LLM, itself composed of an image Transformer and a text Transformer sharing self-attention:






Figure 24.25: BLIP-2’s two-stage training: (1) the Q-Former learns vision-language representations from a frozen image encoder; (2) the Q-Former’s output queries are fed to a frozen LLM as a generative bridge.




The image Transformer takes a fixed number of learnable query tokens as input (à la DETR), which interact with frozen image features via cross-attention.
Stage 1 (representation learning): jointly optimizes three losses — Image-Text Contrastive learning, Image-grounded Text Generation, and Image-Text Matching (binary classification with hard negatives).
Stage 2 (generative pre-training): a linear projection maps the query embeddings into the LLM’s input embedding space; the projected queries are prepended to the text sequence as “soft visual prompts,” and the frozen LLM is trained to generate captions conditioned on them.







Figure 24.26: Q-Former internals: the same learned queries interact with image features via cross-attention and with text via self-attention, under different attention masks for each Stage-1 loss (bidirectional for ITM, multi-modal causal for image-grounded generation, uni-modal for the contrastive loss).



Perceiver Resampler (Flamingo) — converts a variable-length (and for video, spatiotemporal) sequence of vision-encoder features into a fixed small number of tokens (64), via cross-attention from a fixed set of learnable query tokens to the vision features — the same query-based compression idea as Q-Former and DETR.
Flamingo chains the Perceiver Resampler with newly-initialized, trainable gated cross-attention layers inserted between the frozen LLM’s self-attention blocks: \[\mathbf{h}' = \mathbf{h} + \tanh(\alpha)\cdot \text{CrossAttn}(\mathbf{Q}=\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{K}=\mathbf{V}=\mathbf{X}_{\text{img}})\] The gate \(\alpha\) is initialized to zero, so at initialization the block is the identity — the frozen LLM’s behavior is preserved until the cross-attention layers learn to use the visual input. Flamingo accepts an interleaved sequence of images and text and generates text.






Figure 24.27: Flamingo architecture: each image/video is independently encoded by a frozen vision encoder and a trainable Perceiver Resampler, then injected into the frozen LLM via trainable GATED XATTN-DENSE layers interleaved between the LLM’s blocks.









Figure 24.28: Flamingo’s interleaved chat-like input: a few-shot prompt of images and text lets the frozen LLM generalize to new questions about the final image, including comparisons across images.



LLaVA (Large Language-and-Vision Assistant, 2023) — a single LLM consumes both text tokens and image tokens (projected into the language embedding space by a linear layer), with two-stage training:

Stage 1 — Lightweight alignment: only the projection matrix is trained, on a subset of Conceptual Captions (CC3M).
Stage 2 — Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): both the projection matrix and the LLM are updated on visual instruction data (multi-turn chat) and Science QA (multimodal reasoning).







Figure 24.29: LLaVA architecture: image features \(\mathbf{Z}_v\) from a frozen vision encoder are mapped by a trainable projection \(\mathbf{W}\) into the language embedding space (\(\mathbf{H}_v\)), then concatenated with the language instruction tokens \(\mathbf{H}_q\) and fed to the language model \(f_\phi\) to produce the response \(\mathbf{X}_a\).




24.3.3.1 LMM Improvements

Architecture: LLM backbone size matters most for final performance. Vision encoder size matters less than its training data and representation quality — a CLIP-pretrained encoder is the strongest single choice, and mixing multiple vision encoders can further help.
Visual tokens — higher resolution matters:

Multi-crop / dynamic high resolution: tile a high-resolution image into multiple fixed-size crops, each encoded independently, to support resolutions beyond the encoder’s native input size.







Figure 24.30: Dynamic high resolution: the input image is split into crops (and separately resized to a low-resolution overview), each encoded independently and flattened into the LLM’s input sequence.




Token reduction: with up to \(576 \times 5\) visual tokens for a multi-crop high-res image, strategies include adaptive sampling, nested/elastic token organization, and stacking tokens across layers (rather than only along the sequence at the input layer) to keep sequence length tractable.

Visual prompts: vision foundation models (Grounding DINO, SAM, SEEM) provide grounding signals, injected via two strategies:

Feature-based: points, masks, boxes encoded and passed as additional tokens to the LLM.
Pixel-based: points, masks, boxes overlaid directly on image pixels — simpler to implement and apply.

Training strategy: the best recipe is to fully fine-tune the model on high-quality “recap” data, after an initial projector-only warm-up followed by fine-tuning on general data.
Video: LLaVA-NeXT extends the dynamic-high-resolution mechanism (originally for high-resolution images) to handle multiple frames, trained with Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) on high-quality video data. At inference, relative positional embeddings across frames support longer videos than seen during training.






Figure 24.31: LLaVA-NeXT extends multi-patch processing for high-resolution images (left) to multi-frame processing for video (right), reusing the same split-encode-flatten pipeline across frames.




Emergent abilities: large VL models (e.g. Flamingo) display capabilities — implicit counting, arithmetic, celebrity recognition, OCR — that are emergent: absent in smaller models, present only once scale crosses some threshold, and not directly optimized for during pre-training.






Figure 24.32: Examples of Flamingo’s emergent few-shot abilities: visual dialogue, OCR-based reasoning, arithmetic, counting, multilingual captioning, and reasoning about “out of distribution” images (e.g. a 3D-rendered flamingo).

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
text:
24.4 Transfer Learning
Pre-trained VL models often underperform on downstream tasks due to mismatches in data distribution (image and text statistics of the target task) and training objective (the pretext task differs from the downstream task). Four strategies adapt a pre-trained VL model:







Strategy
Description




Prompt Tuning
Learn a continuous text prompt prepended to the input sequence, and/or a visual prompt added to the input image; the backbone is frozen


Feature Adaptation
Insert a small trainable network (e.g. a few linear layers, as in CLIP-Adapter) after the frozen encoders, trained with the task-specific loss


Fine-Tuning
Update the whole model (or a subset of layers) on task-specific data


Instruction Fine-Tuning
Fine-tune on machine-generated instruction-following data, improving zero-shot performance on novel instructions









Figure 24.33: Prompt Tuning: (a) a learnable continuous text prompt is prepended to the class label; (b) a learnable visual prompt is added to the input image. The frozen encoders are unchanged.









Figure 24.34: Feature Adaptation (CLIP-Adapter): a small trainable network is inserted after the frozen image encoder, and its output is combined with the original visual features before the classification loss.



Instruction tuning for VL (LLaVA): for each MS-COCO (image, 5 captions) pair, a text-only GPT-4 generates instruction-following data from the captions alone — conversations, detailed descriptions, and complex-reasoning Q&A — without ever seeing the image. A pre-trained VL model is then fine-tuned on this synthetic (image, instruction, response) data.






Figure 24.35: Examples of the three types of LLaVA instruction-tuning data generated from MS-COCO captions and bounding boxes: (1) multi-turn conversations, (2) detailed descriptions, and (3) complex reasoning.

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
text:
24.5 Knowledge Distillation
Transfer learning preserves the original model architecture; knowledge distillation instead transfers the learned representations of a large, generally pre-trained VL model into a task-specific architecture.
Example — object detection and semantic segmentation: region-level (Faster R-CNN, DETR) and pixel-level (segmentation) knowledge is distilled from the image-level representations of a generic pre-trained VL model (e.g. CLIP), bridging the gap between the VL model’s global image-text alignment and the dense, localized predictions required by detection/segmentation.

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
section: 24.7 Vision Foundation Models: Unifying Vision Tasks
text:
24.7 Vision Foundation Models: Unifying Vision Tasks
Language models unified many language tasks under a single architecture (decoder LLMs), and conversational LLMs (ChatGPT) enabled human-AI interaction. Vision tasks, by contrast, vary widely in input, output, and task granularity (image-level, region-level, pixel-level), making a single unifying architecture harder to design. Three lines of work address this:






Figure 24.36: Vision tasks vary along three axes: (a) input type (static/dynamic, single/multi-modal), (b) task granularity (image-, region-, pixel-level), and (c) output type (spatial vs. semantic).




Free-text task unification (GroupViT, MaskCLIP, OpenSeg): replace fixed class label sets with free-text language, allowing a single model to handle arbitrary categories specified at inference time via text.






Figure 24.37: Replacing fixed class labels with a text encoder over concept names (“language”) unifies classification, detection, and segmentation models (CLIP, GLIP, MaskCLIP) with their label-based counterparts (ViT, DETR, Mask2Former) across the granularity axis.



Output unification across granularities (UniTab, Pix2Seq v2, Unified-IO, UniPerceiver-v2, X-Decoder): represent diverse outputs (bounding boxes, masks, captions, labels) in a common sequence format, allowing one model/decoder to serve detection, segmentation, and captioning.
Human-AI interaction via prompting (SegGPT 2023, SAM 2023, SEEM 2024): text and visual prompts (points, boxes, scribbles) let a user interactively specify the segmentation/detection target at inference time.






Figure 24.38: Prompting-based interaction lets a single model move flexibly along both the granularity axis (image/region/pixel) and the label-vs-language axis at inference time, rather than requiring a separately trained model for each combination.

title: 24  Vision-Language Multimodal Models
text:
24.8 Interview Questions
Q: Why does CLIP require very large batch sizes, and how does SigLIP address this?
CLIP’s InfoNCE loss treats every other image-text pair in the batch as a negative; small batches give few, easy negatives, so the contrastive task is too easy to drive fine-grained representation learning — accuracy scales strongly with batch size (32k+ in the original CLIP). SigLIP replaces the batch-wide softmax with a per-pair sigmoid loss, treating each (image, text) pair as an independent binary classification. This removes the dependence on a large pool of in-batch negatives (so SigLIP is competitive at small batch sizes) and avoids the cross-device communication needed to normalize a softmax over the full batch (so it’s more memory-efficient at very large batch sizes).

Q: Compare late, intermediate, and early fusion for vision-language models. When would you choose each?
Late fusion (CLIP, ALIGN) — two independent encoders combined only via a similarity score — is the only architecture that scales to retrieval over millions of images, since embeddings can be pre-computed offline. Early fusion (BEiT-3) — a single joint encoder over both modalities — gives the richest cross-modal interaction (best for VQA, reasoning) but every input pair requires a full joint forward pass, making it unsuitable for large-scale retrieval. Intermediate fusion (Flamingo, BLIP-2) — separate encoders connected by cross-attention — is a middle ground, commonly used in LMMs where a frozen LLM and frozen vision encoder are connected by a small trainable bridge.

Q: How do the Q-Former (BLIP-2) and Perceiver Resampler (Flamingo) compress visual information, and why is this compression necessary?
Both use a fixed, small set of learnable query tokens that cross-attend into the (potentially long) sequence of vision-encoder features, producing a fixed-size set of output tokens (e.g. 64 for Flamingo) regardless of input resolution or, for video, frame count. This compression is necessary because feeding raw per-patch (and per-frame) vision features directly into the LLM would make the input sequence prohibitively long — especially for high-resolution images or video, where the token count scales with \(H \times W\) (and \(\times T\)).

Q: Why does BEiT-3’s masked-modeling objective allow much smaller batch sizes than CLIP’s contrastive objective?
Contrastive losses derive their training signal from in-batch negatives — the loss is only meaningful with many negatives per positive, requiring large batches. Masked-token prediction derives its signal per-masked-token, from a cross-entropy loss against the ground-truth token/patch — each training example provides a dense, self-contained supervision signal independent of batch composition. BEiT-3 uses batches of ~6K total samples vs. 32k+ for CLIP-style training.

Q: What does it mean for an ability to be “emergent” in large VL models? Give an example.
An ability is emergent if it is absent (near chance performance) in smaller models but appears once model/data scale crosses some threshold — and was not an explicit training objective. Flamingo exhibits emergent few-shot abilities like implicit counting, arithmetic from images, celebrity recognition, and OCR — none of which were directly supervised, but which arise from the combination of a large frozen LLM’s priors and visual grounding.

Q: LLaVA’s instruction-tuning data is generated by a text-only GPT-4 that never sees the images. How is this possible, and what’s the risk?
GPT-4 is given the MS-COCO captions (typically 5 per image) as a dense textual proxy for the image content, and asked to generate conversations, detailed descriptions, and complex-reasoning questions consistent with those captions. The risk is that the generated instructions and answers can only be as accurate as the captions — any visual detail not captured in the captions cannot be reflected in the generated data, and caption errors or omissions propagate into the instruction-tuning set.

Q: Why is fine-grained alignment (FILIP) useful beyond global CLIP-style contrastive learning?
CLIP’s loss operates on a single pooled embedding per image and per caption, which can match on coarse, global similarity while missing whether specific objects or attributes mentioned in the caption are actually present and localized in the image. FILIP’s token-level max-similarity — matching each image patch to its closest text token, averaged over patches — forces the model to learn correspondences at the level of objects and words, giving denser supervision and a representation more useful for localization-sensitive downstream tasks.

title: Time Series
text:
Overview
A time series is a sequence of observations indexed by time. Unlike i.i.d. data, consecutive observations are correlated — a property that both enriches the structure and constrains the methodology. This part covers the statistical foundations needed to reason about temporal data, classical and deep learning models for forecasting, and the practical considerations that distinguish time series engineering from standard supervised learning.
Chapter Scope:
Interview Relevance: Time series forecasting is central to roles at Amazon (demand forecasting, Alexa), Google (Search trends, ads), Meta (Feed engagement, infrastructure capacity), and virtually every fintech and trading firm. Expect questions on how to handle non-stationarity, how to prevent data leakage in temporal splits, the trade-off between autoregressive and multi-horizon models, and the architectural differences between LSTM, TCN, and Transformer-based approaches.
Prerequisites: Foundations (neural networks, optimization). Familiarity with probability and basic statistics (expectation, variance, covariance). Chapter 15 also requires knowledge of attention mechanisms from Part II.

title: Time Series
text:
Time Series Fundamentals (§14): Problem formulation, autocorrelation, stationarity, data handling, classical models (ARIMA family), and evaluation metrics
Deep Learning for Time Series (§15): Recurrent networks (LSTM, GRU), temporal convolutions (TCN), MLP residual stacks (N-BEATS), probabilistic autoregressive models (DeepAR), attention-based models (TFT, PatchTST), and state space models (Mamba)

title: 25  Time Series Fundamentals
text:
25.1 Problem Formulation
A time series is a sequence \(\{x_t\}_{t=1,\ldots,T}\) of observations indexed by time. The core structural assumption is that consecutive observations are statistically dependent — the defining property that separates time series from i.i.d. regression problems.
Univariate time series: a single time-dependent variable, \(x_t \in \mathbb{R}\).
Multivariate time series: \(M\) variables recorded at each time step, \(\mathbf{x}_t \in \mathbb{R}^M\).
Endogenous variables: quantities the model explains or predicts (the target).
Exogenous variables: external covariates used as inputs but not predicted (e.g., predicting temperature with humidity and wind speed as exogenous inputs).
Core tasks:
Forecasting setup: given a context window of \(p\) past observations, predict a forecast horizon of \(h\) future values. The pair \((x_{t-p+1:t},\, x_{t+1:t+h})\) is one training sample.

title: 25  Time Series Fundamentals
text:
25.2 Core Concepts

25.2.1 Autocorrelation
Autocorrelation measures the linear correlation of a time series with a lagged copy of itself. The Autocorrelation Function (ACF) at lag \(k\) is: \[\boxed{\rho_k = \frac{\mathrm{Cov}(x_t,\, x_{t-k})}{\mathrm{Var}(x_t)} = \frac{\displaystyle\sum_{t=k+1}^T (x_t - \bar{x})(x_{t-k} - \bar{x})}{\displaystyle\sum_{t=1}^T (x_t - \bar{x})^2}}\]
\(\rho_k \in [-1, 1]\): values near \(\pm 1\) indicate strong linear dependence at lag \(k\); near 0 indicates none.
The Partial Autocorrelation Function (PACF) at lag \(k\) measures the correlation between \(x_t\) and \(x_{t-k}\) after removing the linear effect of all intermediate lags \(\{x_{t-1}, \ldots, x_{t-k+1}\}\).
ACF/PACF as model selection tools:



Pattern
Suggests




ACF decays slowly, PACF has sharp cutoff at lag \(p\)
AR(\(p\))


ACF has sharp cutoff at lag \(q\), PACF decays slowly
MA(\(q\))


Both decay slowly
ARMA(\(p\), \(q\))





25.2.2 Stationarity
A time series is weakly stationary (covariance-stationary) if: 1. \(\mathbb{E}[x_t] = \mu\) is constant (no trend) 2. \(\mathrm{Var}(x_t) = \sigma^2\) is constant (no variance drift) 3. \(\mathrm{Cov}(x_t, x_{t-k}) = \gamma_k\) depends only on lag \(k\), not on \(t\)
Stationarity matters because most forecasting methods assume that the statistical relationship between past and future is stable. A series with a trend or growing variance violates this assumption.
Testing for stationarity: the Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test has null hypothesis \(H_0\): the series has a unit root (is non-stationary). Rejecting \(H_0\) (low \(p\)-value) supports stationarity.
Removing non-stationarity: differencing — replacing \(x_t\) with \(\nabla x_t = x_t - x_{t-1}\). Applying differencing \(d\) times is denoted the \(I(d)\) operation. First-order differencing (\(d=1\)) eliminates linear trends; second-order (\(d=2\)) eliminates quadratic trends: \[x'_t = x_t - x_{t-1} \quad \text{(first-order differencing)}\] \[x''_t = x'_t - x'_{t-1} = x_t - 2x_{t-1} + x_{t-2} \quad \text{(second-order differencing)}\]


25.2.3 Seasonality
Seasonality is a recurring pattern at a fixed period \(s\) (e.g., \(s=12\) for monthly data with yearly seasonality, \(s=7\) for daily data with weekly seasonality). Multiple seasonal periods can co-occur (e.g., hourly electricity demand has daily and weekly cycles).
Seasonal differencing removes seasonality of period \(s\): \[x_t^{(s)} = x_t - x_{t-s} \quad \text{(seasonal differencing)}\]
Combining seasonal and first-order differencing removes both seasonality and a linear trend: \[x_t'^{(s)} = x_t^{(s)} - x_{t-1}^{(s)} = x_t - x_{t-1} - x_{t-s} + x_{t-s-1} \quad \text{(seasonal + first-order differencing)}\]

title: 25  Time Series Fundamentals
text:
25.3 Data Handling

25.3.1 Sliding Window
Models are trained on sample sequences extracted from the raw time series via a sliding window: for each time step \(t\), extract the pair \((\text{context}: x_{t-p+1:t},\; \text{target}: x_{t+1:t+h})\) and advance \(t\) by one step (or by a stride \(> 1\) for efficiency).


25.3.2 Temporal Train / Validation / Test Split
Never shuffle time series data. Shuffling causes future data to leak into the training set, inflating all metrics.
Temporal splits are defined by cutoff timestamps:

Training set: all samples whose context window ends before the training cutoff \(\tau_{\text{train}}\).
Validation set: samples between \(\tau_{\text{train}}\) and \(\tau_{\text{val}}\) (used for hyperparameter tuning).
Test set: samples after \(\tau_{\text{val}}\) (used only for final evaluation).

The target sequences of training samples may extend past \(\tau_{\text{train}}\) — what must not happen is the context window of a training sample seeing data from after \(\tau_{\text{train}}\).
Interview Insight: “Why can’t we shuffle time series?” Shuffling breaks temporal causality — a training sample that includes future observations relative to its context would give the model access to information it cannot have at inference time, yielding optimistic metrics that do not transfer to real deployment.

title: 25  Time Series Fundamentals
text:
25.4 Classical Models

25.4.1 Simple Moving Average
The Simple Moving Average (SMA) of window size \(k\) predicts the next value as the mean of the most recent \(k\) observations: \[\hat{x}_{t+1} = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_{t-i}\]
No learned parameters; serves as a strong baseline for slowly-varying series.


25.4.2 Simple Exponential Smoothing
Simple Exponential Smoothing (SES) is a weighted average where exponentially decaying weights assign more importance to recent observations: \[\hat{x}_{t+1} = \alpha x_t + (1-\alpha)\hat{x}_t = \alpha \sum_{j=0}^{t-1}(1-\alpha)^j x_{t-j}, \qquad \alpha \in (0,1)\]
Unrolling the recursion \(k\) steps shows the exponentially decaying weights explicitly: \[\hat{x}_t = \sum_{i=1}^{k} \underbrace{\alpha(1-\alpha)^{i-1}}_{\text{exponential smoothing}} \cdot\, x_{t-i} + (1-\alpha)^k \hat{x}_{t-k}\]
\(\alpha\) close to 1: weights concentrated on recent observations (tracks changes quickly, noisier). \(\alpha\) close to 0: weights spread across history (smoother, slower to adapt). Also known as the Exponential Moving Average (EMA).


25.4.3 ARIMA
ARIMA(\(p\), \(d\), \(q\)) — AutoRegressive Integrated Moving Average — combines three components:
AR(\(p\)): current value is a linear combination of the \(p\) most recent values plus white noise: \[x_t = c + \phi_1 x_{t-1} + \cdots + \phi_p x_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t\]
MA(\(q\)): current value is a linear combination of the \(q\) most recent error terms: \[x_t = \mu + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \cdots + \theta_q\varepsilon_{t-q}\]
I(\(d\)): apply \(d\)-th order differencing \((1-B)^d x_t\) to achieve stationarity, where \(B\) is the backshift operator (\(Bx_t = x_{t-1}\)).
The full ARIMA model in compact form: \[\boxed{\phi(B)(1-B)^d x_t = c + \theta(B)\varepsilon_t}\]
where \(\phi(B) = 1 - \phi_1 B - \cdots - \phi_p B^p\) and \(\theta(B) = 1 + \theta_1 B + \cdots + \theta_q B^q\) are the AR and MA lag polynomials, and \(\varepsilon_t \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)\) is white noise.
Written out explicitly on the \(d\)-times-differenced series \(\Delta^d x_t = (1-B)^d x_t\), this is: \[\Delta^d x_t = \phi_0 + \phi_1 x_{t-1} + \cdots + \phi_p x_{t-p} + \varepsilon_t + \theta_1\varepsilon_{t-1} + \cdots + \theta_q \varepsilon_{t-q}\]


25.4.4 SARIMA
SARIMA(\(p, d, q\))(\(P, D, Q\))\(_s\) — Seasonal ARIMA — extends ARIMA by adding seasonal AR, MA, and differencing terms at period \(s\): \[\Phi(B^s)\phi(B)(1-B^s)^D(1-B)^d x_t = \Theta(B^s)\theta(B)\varepsilon_t\]
where \(\Phi, \Theta\) are the seasonal lag polynomials of orders \(P\) and \(Q\) acting at period \(s\).


25.4.5 Box-Jenkins Procedure
Systematic method for selecting ARIMA parameters:

Stationarity: visual inspection for trend/seasonality; ADF test; difference until stationary.
Order identification: inspect ACF/PACF plots to guess \(p\) and \(q\) (see table above).
Estimation: fit ARIMA(\(p\), \(d\), \(q\)) by MLE or nonlinear least squares.
Diagnostic checking: residuals should be white noise — no significant ACF/PACF, Ljung-Box test \(p\)-value \(> 0.05\).
Refinement: if diagnostics fail, return to step 2 and revise model order.

title: 25  Time Series Fundamentals
text:
25.5 Evaluation Metrics
All metrics below are computed over a forecast horizon of \(h\) steps, where \(y_{t+k}\) is the ground truth and \(\hat{y}_{t+k}\) is the forecast.
MAE (Mean Absolute Error): \[\text{MAE} = \frac{1}{h}\sum_{k=1}^h |y_{t+k} - \hat{y}_{t+k}|\] Interpretable in the original units. Robust to outliers (linear penalty). Not scale-invariant — cannot compare across series with different magnitudes.
RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error): \[\text{RMSE} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{h}\sum_{k=1}^h (y_{t+k} - \hat{y}_{t+k})^2}\] Penalizes large errors more than MAE (quadratic penalty). Popular in competitions; sensitive to outliers.
MAPE (Mean Absolute Percentage Error): \[\text{MAPE} = \frac{100\%}{h}\sum_{k=1}^h \frac{|y_{t+k} - \hat{y}_{t+k}|}{|y_{t+k}|}\] Scale-independent; easy to interpret as a percentage. Undefined when \(y_{t+k} = 0\); asymmetric (over-penalizes under-forecasts for small values).
SMAPE (Symmetric MAPE): \[\text{SMAPE} = \frac{200\%}{h}\sum_{k=1}^h \frac{|y_{t+k} - \hat{y}_{t+k}|}{|y_{t+k}| + |\hat{y}_{t+k}|}\] Mitigates MAPE’s asymmetry. Still poorly behaved near zero; bounded in \([0\%, 200\%]\).
MASE (Mean Absolute Scaled Error): \[\text{MASE} = \frac{\text{MAE}}{\dfrac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t=2}^T |y_t - y_{t-1}|}\] Scales MAE by the in-sample naïve one-step forecast error (mean absolute first-difference). Scale-independent, well-defined for zero targets, and directly comparable across time series of different scales. The recommended default for comparing models across datasets.

title: 25  Time Series Fundamentals
text:
25.6 Interview Questions
Q: What is the difference between univariate and multivariate time series forecasting, and when does modeling cross-variable dependencies matter?
Univariate forecasting predicts one variable from its own history. Multivariate uses multiple variables jointly. Cross-variable dependencies matter when one variable Granger-causes another (e.g., promotions causing demand spikes), when lead-lag relationships exist (e.g., energy prices affecting consumption with a delay), or when multiple correlated series share common latent drivers. However, richer multivariate models also have more parameters and require more data — when cross-variable correlations are weak, univariate models with exogenous inputs (ARIMAX, N-BEATSx) often outperform full joint models.

Q: Why must time series train/val/test splits be temporal, not random?
Random shuffling breaks temporal causality: a training sample could include observations from after its test counterpart, meaning the model implicitly sees “the future” during training. This inflates training-set metrics and produces models that generalize poorly to real deployment (where the future is genuinely unknown). Temporal splits preserve causal ordering by strictly partitioning based on timestamps.

Q: How do you determine the order \((p, d, q)\) for an ARIMA model?

\(d\): apply the ADF test; difference until stationary. (2) \(p\): look at the PACF of the stationary series — the last significantly non-zero lag suggests \(p\). (3) \(q\): look at the ACF — the last significantly non-zero lag suggests \(q\). Validate by fitting, checking residual whiteness (Ljung-Box test), and comparing models on AIC/BIC. Both criteria penalize model complexity: AIC = \(-2\ell + 2k\), BIC = \(-2\ell + k\ln n\) where \(\ell\) is log-likelihood and \(k\) is the number of parameters.


Q: When should you use MASE instead of MAPE for model evaluation?
MAPE is undefined when targets equal zero (division by zero) and is heavily asymmetric — under-forecasts are penalized more than over-forecasts of the same magnitude. MASE avoids both issues: it scales errors by the naïve one-step forecast error, is well-defined at zero, and is symmetric. Use MASE whenever you compare across multiple time series of different scales, or whenever zero or near-zero values appear in the target.

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text: 26.1 Recurrent Models
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.1.1 LSTM
Long Short-Term Memory (Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997) is a recurrent architecture designed to capture long-range dependencies through an explicit cell state \(\mathbf{c}_t\) that persists across steps, modulated by three learned gates.
At each time step \(t\), given input \(\mathbf{x}_t\) and previous hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}\):
\[\mathbf{f}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f[\mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_f) \quad \text{(forget gate)}\] \[\mathbf{i}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i[\mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_i) \quad \text{(input gate)}\] \[\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_c[\mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_c) \quad \text{(candidate cell)}\] \[\mathbf{o}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o[\mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t] + \mathbf{b}_o) \quad \text{(output gate)}\]
\[\boxed{\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t, \qquad \mathbf{h}_t = \mathbf{o}_t \odot \tanh(\mathbf{c}_t)}\]
Forget gate \(\mathbf{f}_t\): decides which part of the old cell state to discard. When \(\mathbf{f}_t \approx 1\), the cell state is passed through unchanged — enabling gradient flow over long sequences and preventing vanishing gradients.
Input gate \(\mathbf{i}_t\): controls how much of the new candidate \(\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t\) to write into the cell state.
Output gate \(\mathbf{o}_t\): controls what portion of the cell state is exposed as the hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t\).
Interview Insight: “How does LSTM solve the vanishing gradient problem?” In a vanilla RNN, \(\partial \mathbf{h}_t / \partial \mathbf{h}_0 = \prod W^T\) which vanishes exponentially for typical weight matrices. LSTM’s cell state update \(\mathbf{c}_t = \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \cdots\) creates an additive highway through time — the gradient of \(\mathbf{c}_t\) w.r.t. \(\mathbf{c}_{t-1}\) is \(\mathbf{f}_t\), which can remain close to 1, giving gradients a path that doesn’t vanish.


26.1.2 GRU
Gated Recurrent Unit (Cho et al., 2014) is a simplified alternative to LSTM with no separate cell state and two gates instead of three:
\[\mathbf{r}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_r[\mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t]) \quad \text{(reset gate)}\] \[\mathbf{z}_t = \sigma(\mathbf{W}_z[\mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t]) \quad \text{(update gate)}\] \[\tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t = \tanh(\mathbf{W}_h[\mathbf{r}_t \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1};\, \mathbf{x}_t])\] \[\boxed{\mathbf{h}_t = (1 - \mathbf{z}_t) \odot \mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{z}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{h}}_t}\]
The update gate \(\mathbf{z}_t\) interpolates between carrying the old hidden state forward (\(\mathbf{z}_t \to 0\)) and replacing it with the new candidate (\(\mathbf{z}_t \to 1\)). The reset gate \(\mathbf{r}_t\) controls how much past state influences the candidate.
GRU has fewer parameters than LSTM and often performs comparably on time series tasks; preferred when training data is limited.


26.1.3 Limitations of RNNs

Sequential computation: each step depends on the previous hidden state — parallelization across time is impossible during training.
Fixed-size bottleneck: the hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_t \in \mathbb{R}^d\) must compress the entire history into a fixed-dimensional vector, which limits capacity for very long sequences.
Quadratic gradient decay over long horizons: even with gating, gradients from very distant past steps are attenuated.
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.2 Temporal Convolutional Networks
Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) apply 1D convolutions with two key modifications to handle long-range temporal dependencies.
Causal convolutions: the convolution kernel is zero-padded on the right so the output at time \(t\) depends only on \(x_{\leq t}\), preserving temporal causality.
Dilated convolutions: a dilation factor \(d\) spaces out the receptive field without increasing kernel size. For a kernel of size \(k\) at dilation \(d\): \[y_t = \sum_{i=0}^{k-1} w_i \cdot x_{t - d \cdot i}\]
Stacking layers with exponentially increasing dilation \(d = 1, 2, 4, \ldots, 2^{L-1}\) gives a receptive field of \(2^L(k-1) + 1\) steps with only \(O(L \cdot k)\) parameters and \(O(L)\) depth. This enables very long effective context windows at low parameter cost.
WaveNet (van den Oord et al., 2016) introduced this architecture for audio generation. For time series forecasting, TCN-style stacks of dilated causal convolutions have been shown to match or outperform LSTM on many benchmarks, with the added benefit of full parallelism during training.
Advantages over RNNs: training is fully parallelizable (no sequential dependency); the receptive field is explicit and controlled by architecture rather than implicit and learned; stable gradients.
Disadvantage: the receptive field is fixed by architecture — extending the context window requires adding layers or increasing dilation, not just runtime adjustments.
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.3 N-BEATS
N-BEATS (Neural Basis Expansion Analysis for Interpretable Time Series, Oreshkin et al., 2019) was the first deep learning model to outperform classical statistical methods on established benchmarks, while providing decomposable forecasts.

26.3.1 Architecture
The model is a stack of basic blocks, each sharing the same structure. A block receives a context sequence, produces:

A backcast \(\hat{\mathbf{x}}_l\) — a reconstruction of the input it can explain.
A forecast \(\hat{\mathbf{y}}_l\) — a prediction of the future.







Figure 26.1: N-BEATS architecture. Left: a basic block applies a fully-connected stack to the input, then projects to backcast and forecast coefficients \(\theta^b, \theta^f\) via two separate heads. Center: a stack of \(K\) blocks processes residuals sequentially, each subtracting its backcast from the input before passing it to the next block. Right: \(M\) stacks are summed to produce the global forecast.



Residual stacking: each block processes the residual left unexplained by all previous blocks: \[\mathbf{x}_{l+1} = \mathbf{x}_l - \hat{\mathbf{x}}_l\]






Figure 26.2: Residual stacking between consecutive blocks: block \(l\) produces backcast \(\hat{x}_l\) and forecast \(\hat{y}_l\); the residual \(x_{l+1} = x_l - \hat{x}_l\) becomes the input to block \(l+1\), and forecasts are accumulated via summation.



The final forecast is the sum of individual block forecasts: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}} = \sum_l \hat{\mathbf{y}}_l\]
Basis expansion: within each block, an MLP stack maps the input to coefficient vectors \(\boldsymbol{\theta}^b, \boldsymbol{\theta}^f\), which are projected through basis functions \(\{\psi_k^b\}, \{\psi_k^f\}\): \[\hat{\mathbf{x}}_l = \sum_k \theta_k^b \psi_k^b(\mathbf{t}_\text{in}), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{y}}_l = \sum_k \theta_k^f \psi_k^f(\mathbf{t}_\text{out})\]


26.3.2 Interpretable Configuration
Two stacks with interpretable basis functions:
Trend stack — polynomial basis over the forecast time vector \(\mathbf{t} \in [0, 1]^h\): \[\psi_k^f(t) = t^k, \quad k = 0, 1, \ldots, p_{\max}\]
Substituting into the forecast equation gives, for stack \(s\) and block \(\ell\), a low-order polynomial in \(t\) — capturing slowly varying trend: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{s,\ell} = \sum_{i=0}^{p} \theta^f_{s,\ell,i}\, t^i\]
Seasonality stack — Fourier basis: \[\psi_{2j}^f(t) = \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi j t}{H}\right), \quad \psi_{2j+1}^f(t) = \sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi j t}{H}\right), \quad j = 1, \ldots, \lfloor h/2 \rfloor\]
Substituting gives a truncated Fourier series, capturing periodic patterns: \[\hat{\mathbf{y}}_{s,\ell} = \sum_{i=0}^{\lfloor H/2 \rfloor - 1} \theta^f_{s,\ell,i} \cos(2\pi i t) + \theta^f_{s,\ell,i+\lfloor H/2 \rfloor} \sin(2\pi i t)\]
This decomposes forecasts into trend and seasonal components, analogous to classical additive decomposition — but the components are learned, not prescribed.
Generic configuration: identity basis (\(\psi_k = \mathbf{e}_k\), standard basis vectors), typically a deeper network. Achieves higher accuracy but sacrifices interpretability.
Limitations: - Strictly univariate (N-BEATSx extends to exogenous variables). - Trained on a single time series — cannot generalize across series at different scales; requires sufficient history to extract training pairs.
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.4 DeepAR
DeepAR (Salinas et al., 2020) is a probabilistic autoregressive model based on LSTM, designed to scale across many heterogeneous time series simultaneously.

26.4.1 Model
For time series \(i\) at step \(t\), the model takes as input the previous observation \(z_{i,t-1}\) (scaled) and exogenous covariates \(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}\): \[\mathbf{h}_{i,t} = \text{LSTM}\!\left(\mathbf{h}_{i,t-1},\; \left[\tfrac{z_{i,t-1}}{\nu_i};\, \mathbf{x}_{i,t}\right]\right)\]






Figure 26.3: DeepAR unrolled over time. At each step, the LSTM hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_{i,t}\) is conditioned on the previous target \(z_{i,t-1}\) and covariates \(x_{i,t}\), and decodes to the parameters \(\theta_{i,t}\) of the output likelihood \(\ell(z_{i,t} \mid \theta_{i,t})\).



The LSTM hidden state \(\mathbf{h}_{i,t}\) is decoded to the parameters of a likelihood: \[p(z_{i,t} \mid \mathbf{h}_{i,t}) = \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu(\mathbf{h}_{i,t}),\; \sigma^2(\mathbf{h}_{i,t})\right)\]
Training minimizes the negative log-likelihood over all observed steps.
Per-series scaling: \[\nu_i = 1 + \frac{1}{t_0}\sum_{t=1}^{t_0} z_{i,t}\] is one plus the mean value over the context window (the \(+1\) avoids division by zero for series that are identically zero). Dividing inputs by \(\nu_i\) and multiplying outputs by \(\nu_i\) handles series at different scales (e.g., clothing sales vs. furniture sales differing by orders of magnitude).
Inference: sample \(z_{i,t}\) autoregressively from \(p(z_{i,t} | \mathbf{h}_{i,t})\) for \(t = T+1, \ldots, T+h\); repeat \(S\) times to produce Monte Carlo forecast intervals.
Cold start: because DeepAR learns a global model shared across series, it can forecast a new series with little or no history by relying on covariates and the patterns learned from similar series — an advantage over single-series models like N-BEATS.
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.5 Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT)
TFT (Lim et al., 2021) is a multi-horizon forecasting model that handles heterogeneous input types through a combination of recurrent layers, attention, and gating mechanisms.






Figure 26.4: TFT prediction overview: a single model conditions on past observations, static covariates (e.g., store location, product info), and known future inputs (e.g., holidays, store closures) to produce a multi-step forecast.




26.5.1 Input Types
TFT distinguishes three categories of inputs:

All inputs are projected to a common embedding dimension \(d\) via variable-specific linear layers. Static embeddings are used to initialize LSTM states.


26.5.2 Architecture






Figure 26.5: TFT architecture. Static metadata, past inputs, and known future inputs each pass through Variable Selection Networks before an LSTM encoder-decoder. The temporal fusion decoder then applies static enrichment, masked interpretable multi-head attention, and position-wise feed-forward layers (via Gated Residual Networks) to produce quantile forecasts.




Variable Selection Network (VSN): per-time-step gating over all input features → weighted sum of embeddings, plus a scalar importance weight per variable (used for post-hoc interpretability).
LSTM encoder–decoder: processes the context window (encoder) and generates a representation of the forecast horizon (decoder) using known future inputs.
Interpretable Multi-Head Attention over decoder positions: standard scaled dot-product attention with a single shared \(\mathbf{V}\) projection across heads, so attention weights are directly comparable across heads. The attention map over time steps reveals which past periods matter most for each forecast step.
Quantile output: rather than a point forecast, TFT predicts quantiles \(\{q_{0.1}, q_{0.5}, q_{0.9}\}\) (or any set) via quantile loss (pinball loss): \[\mathcal{L}(q) = \frac{1}{Th}\sum_{i,t} \max\!\left(q\,(y_{i,t} - \hat{y}_{i,t}^{(q)}),\; (q-1)(y_{i,t} - \hat{y}_{i,t}^{(q)})\right)\]

Interview Insight: “Why does TFT use quantile regression rather than Gaussian output like DeepAR?” Quantile regression makes no distributional assumption about the forecast error — useful when the error distribution is skewed or multimodal. Gaussian output is simpler and enables analytic credible intervals but may be miscalibrated for asymmetric targets.
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.6 PatchTST
PatchTST (Nie et al., 2023) applies a standard ViT backbone to time series via two structural innovations.






Figure 26.6: PatchTST overview. (a) Each channel of a multivariate series is patched and embedded independently, then processed by a shared Transformer encoder. (b) Supervised backbone: patch embeddings flow through the Transformer encoder to a flatten-and-linear head producing the forecast. (c) Self-supervised backbone: a subset of patches is masked, and the model reconstructs them — analogous to masked image modeling in MAE.




26.6.1 Patching
Split a length-\(L\) time series into overlapping patches of size \(P\) with stride \(S\): \[N = \left\lfloor \frac{L - P}{S} \right\rfloor + 1 \quad \text{patches}\]






Figure 26.7: Patching a univariate series into overlapping windows of size \(P\). Each colored block is a patch, linearly projected to a single token — reducing the Transformer’s input sequence length from \(L\) to \(N\).



Each patch is linearly projected to a \(d\)-dimensional embedding — analogous to how ViT embeds image patches. This reduces the sequence length fed to the Transformer from \(L\) to \(N \ll L\), bringing attention complexity from \(O(L^2)\) to \(O(N^2)\) while also improving temporal locality (each token represents a local window rather than a single noisy time step).


26.6.2 Channel Independence
For multivariate time series, each variable (channel) is processed independently through the same shared Transformer backbone — no cross-variable attention. Motivation: temporal attention maps are driven by the local shape of a time series; different variables can have very different temporal patterns, and forcing a single shared attention map across variables degrades representation quality. Shared weights still enable transfer across channels.






Figure 26.8: Spectrograms (left) and raw signals (right) for different channels of a multivariate series. Each channel exhibits a distinct frequency profile and temporal pattern, motivating channel-independent processing rather than a single shared cross-channel attention map.





26.6.3 Self-Supervised Pre-training
PatchTST can be pre-trained via masked patch prediction: randomly mask a fraction of patches and train the model to reconstruct them (analogous to BERT/MAE). The pre-trained backbone is fine-tuned for downstream forecasting with a linear projection head. Self-supervised pre-training is particularly valuable when labeled forecasting data is scarce.
Interview Insight: “What is the trade-off between channel independence and channel mixing in multivariate forecasting?” Channel independence (PatchTST, N-BEATS per-channel) is more robust when cross-variable correlations are weak or unstable — fewer parameters to overfit, and no risk of spurious cross-variable interactions. Channel mixing (iTransformer, multi-variate LSTM) can be beneficial when strong stable correlations exist (e.g., correlated sensor readings), but requires more data to learn meaningful cross-channel attention.
crumbs: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series

title: 26  Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
26.7 State Space Models
State Space Models (SSMs) represent a time series via a latent state \(\mathbf{h}_t\) evolving under linear dynamics. The continuous-time formulation: \[\dot{\mathbf{h}}(t) = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{h}(t) + \mathbf{B}x(t), \qquad y(t) = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{h}(t) + Dx(t)\]
Discretized with step size \(\Delta\) via zero-order hold: \[\boxed{\mathbf{h}_t = \bar{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \bar{\mathbf{B}}x_t, \qquad y_t = \mathbf{C}\mathbf{h}_t + Dx_t}\] \[\bar{\mathbf{A}} = e^{\Delta \mathbf{A}}, \qquad \bar{\mathbf{B}} = (\Delta\mathbf{A})^{-1}(e^{\Delta\mathbf{A}} - \mathbf{I})\Delta\mathbf{B}\]
S4 (Gu et al., 2021) parameterizes \(\mathbf{A}\) as a structured matrix (diagonal plus low-rank) that enables \(O(N \log N)\) computation via convolution. S4 demonstrates that SSMs can match Transformers on long-range sequence modeling tasks while maintaining linear inference time per step.
Mamba (Gu & Dao, 2023) extends S4 with input-selective state transitions: \(\mathbf{B}\), \(\mathbf{C}\), and \(\Delta\) are functions of the input \(x_t\) (computed by small linear projections), making the state transition content-dependent rather than fixed. This allows the model to selectively remember or forget information based on the current input, analogous to the gating mechanism in LSTMs but derived from continuous-time dynamical systems.
