title: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models
text:
32.2 The Adapter Recipe
The dominant architecture for audio understanding is a three-part sandwich, and it is worth writing down precisely because almost everything reduces to it.
Let \(\mathbf{X}\) be audio, \(f_\theta\) a pretrained audio encoder (Section 27.8.1), and \(\mathcal{P}_\phi\) a learned projector. The audio is converted to a sequence of vectors in the LLM’s embedding space and prepended to the text embeddings:
\[
\mathbf{H} = \mathcal{P}_\phi\big(f_\theta(\mathbf{X})\big) \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times d_{\text{LLM}}},
\qquad
p(\mathbf{y}) = \prod_{i} p_{\text{LLM}}\big(y_i \mid \mathbf{H}, \mathbf{e}(\mathbf{y}_{<i})\big)
\tag{32.1}\]
The LLM is unmodified. It receives what it takes to be \(M\) ordinary token embeddings and continues as usual. This is the same trick that made vision-language models work, transplanted without alteration.
The projector’s real job is rate reduction, and the arithmetic explains most design choices. Whisper’s encoder emits 50 vectors per second; a one-minute clip is 3,000 positions, which would dominate any reasonable context. Projectors therefore downsample aggressively — by stacking adjacent frames before a linear map, by strided convolution, or by cross-attending a fixed number of learned queries into each window (a Q-Former). Typical operating points land between 5 and 12 vectors per second, a factor of 4–10 reduction.
Three systems established the design space.
SALMONN (Tang et al. 2024) uses two encoders in parallel — Whisper for speech and BEATs for general audio events — concatenated frame-by-frame and read by a window-level Q-Former, with LoRA adaptation of the LLM. The dual encoder is the point: a speech encoder trained on transcription is systematically poor at non-speech audio, which is exactly the WavLM/HuBERT specialisation of Section 27.3.2 reappearing one level up. SALMONN also reported task over-fitting — after instruction tuning, the model collapses toward the tasks it was tuned on and loses the emergent cross-modal abilities it briefly had — and proposed a lightweight activation-tuning stage to recover them. That failure recurs throughout this chapter.
Qwen-Audio (Chu et al. 2023) attacked the same problem from the data side, training one encoder across more than thirty tasks with a hierarchy of tags identifying task, language, and annotation granularity, so that supervision from heterogeneous datasets could be shared rather than interfering. Qwen2-Audio (Chu et al. 2024) dropped the tag hierarchy for natural-language prompts, and Qwen2.5-Omni (Xu et al. 2025) extended the same backbone to vision and to speech output.
LTU (Gong et al. 2024) made the case that the interesting capability is not classification but reasoning about audio — answering open-ended questions about what is happening and why — and built the instruction corpus to train it. Audio Flamingo (Kong et al. 2024; Ghosh et al. 2025) pursued in-context learning and long-audio understanding in the same spirit.
crumbs: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models

title: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models
text:
32.3 Training and Catastrophic Forgetting
Training proceeds in stages, and the recipe is stable across systems.

Modality alignment. Freeze the LLM, train the projector alone on large-scale ASR and audio-captioning data. The objective is simply to make Equation 32.1 produce embeddings the LLM can read.
Instruction tuning. Unfreeze partially — typically LoRA on the LLM, and often the encoder’s upper layers — and train on audio question-answering and multi-task instruction data.
Speech output, where applicable: train the generation path (Section 31.9), usually with the understanding path frozen.
Preference optimisation and duplex adaptation, increasingly standard.

The central difficulty is stage 2. Speech-centric training degrades the model’s text abilities, and the degradation is severe enough to be the principal reported obstacle. Speech-IFEval (Lu, Kuan, et al. 2025) isolates it by separating instruction-following from speech perception, and finds that most speech-aware LLMs “struggle with even basic instructions, performing far worse than text-based LLMs”, and are unstable under paraphrases of the same prompt. A model that hears well but can no longer follow a formatting instruction is not obviously an improvement on a cascade.
Two mitigations are in current use. The first is architectural conservatism: keep the LLM frozen and push all adaptation into the projector, which preserves text ability at the cost of how much audio detail can reach the model — Freeze-Omni (Wang et al. 2024) takes this position explicitly. The second is to fix the data. DeSTA2.5-Audio (Lu, Chen, et al. 2025) observes that forgetting is largely caused by training targets written in a style the backbone LLM would never produce, and has the backbone generate its own training targets from audio metadata, so that fine-tuning reinforces rather than overwrites its native distribution. Reported gains hold across Dynamic-SUPERB, MMAU, SAKURA, Speech-IFEval, and VoiceBench simultaneously, which is the kind of broad result that suggests a real mechanism rather than benchmark tuning.






WarningThe synthetic-data trap



Most audio instruction corpora are built by synthesising speech from text with a TTS system. Such data has no genuine paralinguistic variation — no real emotion, no real hesitation, no real room. A model trained on it can only learn that audio is a lossy encoding of text, which is precisely the failure the whole paradigm exists to avoid. This is a plausible mechanism behind Section 32.5, and it is self-inflicted.
crumbs: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models

title: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models
text:
32.4 Speaking: Interleaving, Streams, and Duplex
Models that emit audio face a decision about how text participates in generation. Nearly all of them use text somehow, and why is the interesting part.
Text-scaffolded generation is the near-universal pattern. Rather than modelling audio tokens alone, the model predicts text and audio jointly, with text leading:
\[
p(\mathbf{a}, \mathbf{w}) = \prod_{t} p\big(w_t \mid \mathbf{w}_{<t}, \mathbf{a}_{<t}\big)\,
p\big(\mathbf{a}_t \mid \mathbf{w}_{\leq t}, \mathbf{a}_{<t}\big)
\tag{32.2}\]
Two families implement Equation 32.2 differently. Interleaving alternates chunks of text and audio tokens in one sequence — the approach of SpeechGPT (Zhang et al. 2023), AudioPaLM (Rubenstein et al. 2023), and GLM-4-Voice (Zeng et al. 2024). Parallel streams predict text and audio at the same position on separate channels, which is Moshi’s inner monologue (Section 31.9.6). Mini-Omni (Xie and Wu 2024) and LLaMA-Omni (Fang et al. 2025) occupy points in between, generating text and audio concurrently to keep latency low.
The empirical finding is consistent and slightly deflating: the text stream carries most of the reasoning. Moshi’s ablations show the inner monologue improves linguistic quality substantially. Volhejn’s reading of this is that most of the intelligence is delegated to text while the audio streams degenerate into an integrated ASR and TTS — which, if true, means the architecture is a cascade wearing a different coat. I think that is too strong as a general claim, but it is the right worry, and no current system clearly refutes it.
Full duplex is the other axis. A half-duplex model processes one turn at a time; a full-duplex model listens and speaks simultaneously, which is what makes interruption, backchannelling (“mm-hm”), and overlap representable at all. Modelling both participants’ audio as parallel streams (Section 31.9.6) replaces an explicit turn-taking state machine with next-token prediction, and dGSLM (Nguyen et al. 2023) demonstrated the idea before speech LLMs existed by modelling two-channel spontaneous dialogue directly. Full-Duplex-Bench (Lin et al. 2025) gives the behaviours their own metrics: pause handling, backchannelling, turn-taking, and interruption management.
crumbs: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models

title: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models
text:
32.5 The Modality Gap
Here is the phenomenon, in the cleanest available form. Ask a natively speech-capable model, in a high-pitched voice, “Am I speaking in a low voice or a high voice?” It will generally fail — not by refusing, but by answering as though it had read a transcript. Volhejn reports this for Gemini, ChatGPT’s Advanced Voice Mode, Qwen, and Moshi alike.
This is a strange failure. The information is unambiguously present in the input, the model was trained on audio, and the question is trivial. Four mechanisms plausibly contribute, and they are not mutually exclusive.
Tokenisation discards it by construction. Semantic tokens are defined by invariance to speaker and channel — the demonstration in Section 30.7, where fixing semantic tokens and resampling the rest yields the same words in a different voice, shows this directly. A model whose loss is dominated by semantic tokens is trained to ignore exactly the cues in question. The layer-wise result of Section 27.5 says the same thing about encoders: representations optimised for content actively suppress paralinguistic nuisance variables.
Text scaffolding makes audio vestigial. If Equation 32.2 lets the model route all reasoning through text, gradient pressure on the audio path to encode anything beyond phonetic content is weak.
The training data has no variation to learn from. The synthetic-data trap above.
Scale asymmetry. Text corpora are trillions of tokens; transcribed and instruction-annotated speech is orders of magnitude smaller, and the annotated paralinguistic slice smaller still.
The measurements support a sharper diagnosis than “the model cannot hear”. SAKURA (Yang et al. 2025) evaluates multi-hop reasoning over speech and audio and finds that models fail to integrate audio information into a reasoning chain even when they extract the relevant information correctly. Perception is not the bottleneck; integration is. Consistently, a 2026 layer-wise study (Yang et al. 2026) finds that paralinguistic and semantic information occupy identifiable and distinct layers of these models, and that fine-tuning selected layers with an auxiliary classification head restores paralinguistic awareness more effectively than fine-tuning everything. The information is present and localisable; the model is simply not in the habit of using it.
That is a more optimistic reading than the phenomenon first suggests. It says the gap is a training and objective-design problem rather than a representational impossibility.

A striking side-effect of this architecture is that a set of previously separate research areas collapsed into prompting. Each once had its own models, losses, and leaderboards; each is now a question you ask.

Two caveats keep this from being the whole story. Specialised models still win on their own tasks, often by a wide margin, and the unified model’s advantage is breadth and compositionality rather than peak accuracy; Chapter 33 takes these tasks on their own terms, including the measurement problems the prompting framing inherits. And contrastive audio-text models remain a distinct and more efficient paradigm for retrieval-style problems: CLAP (Elizalde et al. 2023) aligns audio and text in a shared embedding space, giving zero-shot classification over an open label set at a fraction of the cost of generative inference.

32.7 Evaluation
Evaluating these models is harder than evaluating either parent, because the output is open-ended text about an open-ended input.

Benchmark
Measures

Three methodological problems are worth naming, because they affect how the numbers in these tables should be read.
Many questions are answerable from the transcript alone. If a benchmark item can be solved by an ASR-plus-text-LLM cascade, it measures nothing about audio understanding. The correct control is to run that cascade and report it as a baseline — a practice that is becoming standard but is still often omitted. Any claim that native audio processing helps should be a claim about the gap to that baseline.
Open-ended answers are usually scored by an LLM judge, which inherits the judge’s biases, is sensitive to answer formatting, and has received little meta-evaluation in this domain. This is the same problem flagged for synthesis in Section 31.12, and it is not better here.
Perception and instruction-following are routinely conflated. A model can fail an item because it did not hear correctly or because it ignored the output format. Speech-IFEval exists precisely to separate the two, and the finding that much of the apparent perception failure is really instruction failure should make one cautious about single-number leaderboards.

title: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models
text:
32.8 Open Problems

Closing the modality gap. The evidence in Section 32.5 suggests paralinguistic information is present but unused. Whether the fix is objective design, better data, selective adaptation, or richer tokenisation is the field’s central open question.
Forgetting without a trade-off. Every current method buys text ability with audio detail or vice versa. A training scheme that adds hearing without subtracting reasoning does not yet exist.
Beating the cascade convincingly. On most benchmarks a strong cascade remains competitive. Establishing where native processing genuinely wins — and by how much — is unresolved, and partly an evaluation problem.
Long-form audio. Rate reduction in Equation 32.1 makes minutes tractable and hours not. Meetings, lectures, and podcasts remain out of reach without chunking that destroys global structure.
Duplex behaviour is barely modelled. Knowing when to speak, when to stay silent, and when to yield is a skill with almost no supervision available, and Full-Duplex-Bench shows current systems handle it crudely.
Speaker attribution in multi-party audio. These models largely assume one speaker. Integrating diarization (Chapter 29) into a speech LLM, rather than bolting it on, is open.
Safety at the paralinguistic layer. A model that can hear emotion, health markers, age, and identity can also infer them without consent, and a model that can speak in any voice can impersonate. Neither the inference side nor the generation side has an accepted governance story.
Scaling laws. Nobody has mapped how audio-language capability trades off between audio hours, text tokens, parameters, and token rate.
crumbs: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models

title: 32  Speech and Audio Language Models
text:
32.9 Summary
Speech and audio language models are the convergence point of this part of the book: the encoders of Chapter 27 supply perception, the codecs of Chapter 30 supply a generation interface, and a pretrained text LLM supplies everything else. Three architectures divide the space — the cascade, which preserves text ability perfectly and discards everything not in the transcript; the adapter sandwich of Equation 32.1, which projects encoder features into the LLM’s embedding space and is essentially the vision-language recipe unchanged; and native token-in-token-out models that read and write audio directly.
The recurring technical difficulty is that teaching a language model to hear tends to make it worse at thinking. Instruction tuning on audio degrades text ability measurably, task-specific tuning collapses emergent generality, and the mitigations — frozen backbones, selective adaptation, self-generated training targets — all trade one capability against another.
The recurring scientific difficulty is the modality gap. A model that hears a high-pitched voice and cannot say so is failing at something its input contains and its architecture permits. The most useful recent finding is that this is not a perception failure: the information is extractable, and localisable to particular layers, but does not make it into the model’s reasoning. Tokenisers that define away paralinguistics, text scaffolding that renders the audio path vestigial, and synthetic training data with no genuine acoustic variation all push in the same direction. That the causes are identifiable and largely self-inflicted is the best reason to expect the gap to close.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.1 The Annotation Problem
Every chapter so far has treated audio as a carrier of words. Recognition extracts them, synthesis produces them, codecs compress the signal that contains them, and speech language models reason about them. This chapter is about everything else in the signal.
That residue divides into two families. Paralinguistic attributes are properties of the speaker and the delivery rather than the message: emotion, age, accent, health, arousal, whether the utterance is sincere. Non-speech audio is the rest of the acoustic world: a door closing, a siren, rain, a violin. They are conventionally separate research communities with separate venues, and this chapter treats them together because they share a difficulty that the tasks in earlier chapters do not have.
That difficulty is the label. Word error rate works because a transcript has a correct answer, and disagreement between annotators is rare and resolvable. Ask two people whether a speaker sounds angry or merely emphatic, or to describe a five-second recording in a sentence, and they will disagree — not through carelessness, but because the question does not have a single answer. Almost everything distinctive about this area follows from that.
Consider what a “ground truth” emotion label is. An annotator listens to an utterance and selects a category. A second annotator hears the same utterance and selects a different one. Neither is wrong. The label that reaches the dataset is usually the majority vote, which discards the disagreement and presents the result as though it were fact.
Three consequences follow, and they recur through every section below.
Reported accuracy is bounded by human agreement, which for categorical emotion is frequently in the range of 0.3–0.6 by chance-corrected measures such as Krippendorff’s \(\alpha\). A model reporting 75% accuracy against majority-vote labels on a corpus where annotators agree 60% of the time is reporting something other than what the number appears to say.
The majority vote is a lossy summary of a distribution. A clip where seven of ten annotators say angry and three say frustrated is genuinely different from one where ten of ten say angry, and collapsing both to angry throws away the distinction. Soft labels — training against the annotator distribution with a cross-entropy or divergence objective rather than a one-hot target — are the standard response, and are now common practice in emotion and sound-event work alike.
Evaluation must respect the same fact. Scoring a prediction against one reference when many are valid is the same structural problem as MOS in synthesis (Section 31.12.1) and as the one-to-many problem in generation (Section 31.2). It is the reason audio captioning needed its own metrics rather than borrowing image captioning’s, as Section 33.5 describes.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.2 Audio Classification Backbones
The non-speech side of the field was organised by one dataset. AudioSet (Gemmeke et al. 2017) is roughly two million ten-second YouTube clips labelled against an ontology of 527 sound classes, and it played the role for audio that ImageNet played for vision: large enough that pre-training on it transfers, and standard enough that everyone reports on it.



Table 33.1: Backbones for general audio classification.










Model
Idea
Why it mattered




PANNs (Kong et al. 2020)
Large CNNs (notably CNN14) trained on AudioSet, released as transferable feature extractors
Established AudioSet pre-training as the default starting point for audio tagging


AST (Gong et al. 2021)
Treat the spectrogram as an image; a pure ViT (Dosovitskiy et al. 2021) over patches, initialised from ImageNet weights
Removed convolutions entirely; the cross-modal weight transfer is the surprising part


SSAST (Gong et al. 2022)
Self-supervised AST pre-training by masked patch prediction
Removed the dependence on AudioSet labels


BEATs (Chen et al. 2023)
Iterative pre-training that alternates between learning an acoustic tokeniser and a masked-prediction model over its discrete labels
Brought HuBERT’s iterative refinement (Section 27.3.1) to general audio; the standard general-audio encoder, and SALMONN’s non-speech branch






Two observations are worth drawing out. AST’s initialisation from ImageNet weights works despite a spectrogram not being an image in any meaningful sense — its axes are time and frequency, not two spatial dimensions, and translation invariance along frequency is wrong for audio, since shifting a harmonic stack upward changes the sound. That it transfers anyway says something about how generic early ViT features are.
And BEATs closes a loop this book has traced twice. It is HuBERT’s insight — that the quality of a masked-prediction target can be improved by re-deriving it from the model you just trained — applied to general audio rather than speech (Section 27.3.1). The same idea reappears in codecs as semantic distillation (Section 30.7).

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.3 Weak Labels and Temporal Localisation
AudioSet labels are clip-level: a ten-second clip is marked as containing a dog bark, with no indication of when. Sound event detection requires the onset and offset. This is a mismatch between the supervision available and the output required, and it is the technical core of the non-speech side.
The standard formulation is multiple-instance learning. The model produces a frame-level probability \(y_t\) for each class and pools it to a clip-level prediction compared against the weak label. Max pooling is degenerate — it propagates gradient to one frame — and mean pooling dilutes short events, so the usual choice is attention pooling, in which the model learns its own weighting:
\[
\hat{y} = \frac{\sum_{t} y_t \, w_t}{\sum_{t} w_t},
\qquad w_t = \sigma\big(\mathbf{v}^{\top}\mathbf{h}_t\big)
\tag{33.1}\]
The frame-level \(y_t\) is never directly supervised; it emerges as the byproduct of explaining a clip-level label. That is an elegant trick and also a fragile one, since nothing forces \(y_t\) to be temporally accurate as long as the pooled value is right.
The DCASE challenge’s long-running Task 4 formalised the harder realistic setting: a small strongly-labelled set, a larger weakly-labelled set, and a large unlabelled set. The standard method is mean teacher (Tarvainen and Valpola 2017) — an exponential moving average of the student’s weights supplies consistency targets on unlabelled audio — imported directly from semi-supervised image classification, and structurally the same EMA-teacher device that data2vec uses for representation learning (Section 27.3.3).
Evaluation has its own subtlety. Event-based F-score with a fixed tolerance (“collar”) around each boundary depends heavily on an arbitrary collar width and on a chosen operating threshold. The polyphonic sound detection score (Bilen et al. 2020) replaces both with a threshold-independent, collar-free formulation that integrates performance across operating points and explicitly separates confusion between classes from missed detections. It is now the standard DCASE metric, and the reasoning behind it — that a metric which moves when you change an arbitrary hyperparameter is measuring the hyperparameter — generalises well beyond this task.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.4 Speech Emotion Recognition
Emotion is represented in two incompatible ways, and much confusion in this literature comes from comparing across them.
Categorical representations assign a discrete label from a small set (angry, happy, sad, neutral). They are intuitive and align with how people talk about emotion, but the categories are culturally specific and the boundaries are not sharp. Dimensional representations place an utterance in a continuous space, conventionally valence (pleasant–unpleasant), arousal (calm–excited), and sometimes dominance. They avoid forcing discrete choices and are the more defensible target, and they are scored with the concordance correlation coefficient, which rewards agreement in both correlation and absolute scale:
\[
\rho_c = \frac{2\,\rho\,\sigma_x \sigma_y}{\sigma_x^2 + \sigma_y^2 + (\mu_x - \mu_y)^2}
\tag{33.2}\]
Categorical work reports weighted and unweighted accuracy, the latter averaging per-class recall; the distinction matters because emotion corpora are severely imbalanced toward neutral.
Arousal is easy and valence is hard. Arousal correlates strongly with straightforward acoustics — energy, pitch range, speaking rate — so it was largely solved early. Valence does not: whether an utterance is pleasant or unpleasant often depends on what is being said. This “valence gap” defined the field for a decade.
The most instructive result here is that transformers closed the gap, and why. Wagner et al. (Wagner et al. 2023) fine-tuned wav2vec 2.0 and HuBERT variants on MSP-Podcast and obtained state-of-the-art valence prediction (CCC 0.638) without any explicit linguistic input. Their analysis of the mechanism is the part worth teaching: the models succeed because the transformer layers learn implicit linguistic information during fine-tuning, which is why they match multimodal systems that use transcripts explicitly. The model closed the valence gap by covertly learning to read.
That finding is a useful corrective in two directions. It explains an apparent capability without crediting the model with acoustic sensitivity it does not have, and it connects directly to Section 32.5: a system that appears to hear emotion may be routing through language, which is the same substitution that makes audio language models insensitive to pitch.
The same study is unusually careful about robustness and fairness, and reports a distinction worth carrying: the models were fair with respect to biological sex groups but not with respect to individual speakers. Aggregate group parity and per-speaker reliability are different properties, and a system can have the first without the second.






WarningIEMOCAP results are frequently not comparable



IEMOCAP has been the field’s default corpus for fifteen years, and papers using it differ on choices that change results by many points: whether to merge excited into happy to reach the conventional four classes, whether to use improvised or scripted sessions or both, and whether the split is speaker-independent. A great many reported comparisons are therefore between different tasks wearing the same name. MSP-Podcast, larger and drawn from natural speech, is the better modern default.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.5 Audio Captioning and Language-Aligned Audio
Automated audio captioning asks for a free-text description of a clip — “a dog barks twice as a car passes” — which is the general-audio analogue of the open-ended understanding that audio language models aim at. The standard corpora are AudioCaps and Clotho (Drossos et al. 2020), the latter deliberately multi-reference, with five captions per clip.
Captioning inherited its metrics from image captioning, and they did not transfer. Zhou et al. (Zhou et al. 2022) built human-judgement benchmarks for audio captions — using pairwise comparisons rather than absolute ratings, precisely because pairwise judgements achieve better annotator agreement — and found that SPICE, CIDEr, and SPIDEr (Liu et al. 2017) correlate poorly with human assessment. Their replacement, FENSE, combines Sentence-BERT similarity with a learned error detector that penalises fluent but incorrect sentences, and improves agreement with human judgement by 14–25%. The methodological lesson is the same one Section 31.12 reaches from a different direction: a borrowed metric requires validation in its new domain, and this one was used for years without it.

33.5.1 Contrastive Audio-Text Models
The other way to connect audio to language is not to generate text but to align the two in a shared embedding space. CLAP (Elizalde et al. 2023; Wu et al. 2023) applies the CLIP recipe to audio: an audio encoder \(f\) and a text encoder \(g\) trained on paired data with a symmetric contrastive objective over a batch,
\[
\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}
\left[
\log \frac{e^{\,s(a_i, t_i)/\tau}}{\sum_{j} e^{\,s(a_i, t_j)/\tau}}
+
\log \frac{e^{\,s(a_i, t_i)/\tau}}{\sum_{j} e^{\,s(a_j, t_i)/\tau}}
\right]
\tag{33.3}\]
with \(s(a,t) = \cos\big(f(a), g(t)\big)\) and temperature \(\tau\).
What this buys is an open label set. Classification becomes ranking a set of text prompts against the audio embedding, so the classes need not be fixed at training time and adding a new one costs nothing. It also gives text-to-audio retrieval directly, and — as Section 31.12 noted for FAD — a general-purpose audio embedding space that turns out to correlate with human perceptual judgement better than codec latents do.
CLAP and audio language models are complementary rather than competing. CLAP is a single forward pass per candidate and is the right tool for retrieval, tagging, and filtering at scale; a generative model is the right tool when the answer is a sentence rather than a ranking.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.6 Other Paralinguistic Inferences
A short catalogue, since these share the machinery above and differ mainly in what is being inferred and at what risk.
Speaker traits — age, sex, accent, native language — are standard classification over speaker embeddings (Section 29.1.1) or SSL features. Speech pathology and health covers dysarthria, Parkinsonian speech, and a large and methodologically contested literature on inferring depression and cognitive decline. Spoofing and deepfake detection is the countermeasure side of Section 31.10: the ASVspoof series (Wang et al. 2024) is the standard evaluation, and its central finding across editions is that detectors generalise poorly to attack types they were not trained on — which is why the synthesis chapter treats passive detection as substantially unsolved.
Two of these have a property the others do not: the inference is about a person, and can be made without their knowledge. That is the subject of Section 33.8.

33.7 Evaluation



Table 33.2: Benchmarks for audio understanding.









Benchmark
Scope




DCASE challenges
The organising annual event for detection and classification of acoustic scenes and events; defines the tasks, data, and metrics most of this chapter uses


HEAR (Turian et al. 2022)
Holistic evaluation of audio representations: one frozen encoder, many downstream tasks spanning speech, music, and environmental sound


SUPERB (Yang et al. 2021)
The speech-side equivalent (Section 27.6), including emotion and speaker tasks


AudioSet tagging (mAP)
The default general-audio classification benchmark


Clotho / AudioCaps with FENSE

MMAU, AIR-Bench (Section 32.7)

HEAR is worth singling out for its design. It freezes the encoder and varies only a shallow downstream head across a deliberately heterogeneous task set, which tests generality rather than task-specific tuning — the same protocol as SUPERB, and it revealed the same thing: no single encoder wins everywhere, and speech encoders and general-audio encoders have genuinely different strengths. That result is what forces SALMONN’s dual-encoder design (Section 32.2).

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.8 Validity, Fairness, and Regulation
This is the one area in this book where the most important open problem is not technical.
Construct validity. Supervised learning assumes the label denotes something real and stable. For emotion that assumption is contested within psychology itself. Barrett et al. (Barrett et al. 2019) reviewed the evidence on inferring emotional state from facial movements and concluded that the mapping is far weaker and more context-dependent than the “universal expression” model assumes. Their review concerns faces rather than voice, so it is not direct evidence about speech — but the argument it makes is structural, about whether a fixed set of expressions reliably signals a fixed set of internal states, and it applies to vocal expression for the same reasons. A model can be an excellent predictor of annotator labels while those labels are a poor measure of what the speaker felt, and no amount of accuracy resolves the difference.
Fairness. Systems inherit the demographic composition of their training data, which for paralinguistics is usually unknown and rarely balanced. The distinction from Section 33.4 is the operative one: parity across broad groups does not imply reliability for individuals, and it is individuals who are affected.
Regulation. The EU AI Act prohibits placing on the market or using AI systems that infer emotions in the workplace and in education, outside narrow medical and safety exceptions, and treats emotion recognition as high-risk in other contexts. This is one of the few places where a research area in this book has been directly restricted by law, and the stated rationale is the validity concern above rather than a general objection to the technology. Anyone building in this area should read the operative text rather than a summary of it, including this one.
The practical position I would take is that these systems are defensible for aggregate, consented, low-stakes uses — retrieval, content description, accessibility, research on populations — and difficult to defend for individual consequential decisions about people who did not consent to being measured.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.9 Open Problems

Labels that reflect uncertainty. Soft labels are a partial answer. Training and evaluation protocols that treat annotator disagreement as signal rather than noise are still not standard.
Robustness across corpora. Cross-corpus emotion recognition degrades sharply, which suggests models learn corpus-specific recording and elicitation artefacts alongside the target attribute.
Disentangling acoustics from language. The Section 33.4 finding that valence performance rests on implicit lexical learning means we do not currently know how much genuinely acoustic affect recognition is achievable.
Weak supervision without temporal degradation. Equation 33.1 produces frame-level outputs that nothing supervises; better inductive biases or cheap forms of temporal supervision remain open.
Generalisation of spoofing countermeasures to unseen attacks, which every ASVspoof edition has identified and none has closed.
Polyphony and overlap. Real acoustic scenes contain many simultaneous sources; most benchmarks under-represent dense overlap.
Do audio LLMs subsume this? They are broad and weak; specialised models are narrow and strong. Whether the general model eventually dominates, as it did in text, is unresolved — and Section 32.5 suggests the paralinguistic part is exactly where it currently does not.

title: 33  Audio Understanding Beyond Words
text:
33.10 Summary
What remains in an audio signal after the words have been removed is the subject of two research communities that share one problem: their labels are constructions rather than facts. Annotators disagree irreducibly about emotion and about how to describe a sound, so majority-vote targets discard real information, reported accuracies live under a ceiling set by human agreement, and metrics borrowed from domains with unique correct answers mislead.
The non-speech side was organised by AudioSet and by a progression of backbones — PANNs, AST, BEATs — whose trajectory recapitulates the rest of the book: convolutional to transformer, supervised to self-supervised, and finally to iterative masked prediction over learned discrete targets, which is HuBERT’s idea transplanted to general audio. Its distinctive technical problem is supervision that is weaker than the required output, addressed by multiple-instance learning with attention pooling and by semi-supervised consistency training, and evaluated by a score designed not to move when you change an arbitrary threshold.
The speech side’s clearest lesson is a negative one. Transformers closed the long-standing valence gap in emotion recognition, but the mechanism was implicit lexical learning rather than acoustic sensitivity — the model learned to read. That is the same substitution of language for audio diagnosed in Section 32.5, appearing here in a task where it was measured precisely, and it should make one cautious about any claim that a model has learned to hear something when reading would also have sufficed.
Finally, this is the part of the field where the binding constraint is not architecture or data but whether the quantity being predicted exists as labelled. That question is unresolved in psychology, and it has now been answered provisionally in law.
